Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36(8)(a), I have the honour to table, in both official languages, the government's responses to five petitions. These returns will be tabled in an electronic format.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Patrick Weiler (West Vancouver—Sunshine Coast—Sea to Sky Country, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the seventh report of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Oceans, entitled “Review of the Fisheries Act: policy and legislative considerations and recommendations”.
Pursuant to Standing Order 109, the committee requests that the government table a comprehensive response to this report.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to present the official opposition's dissenting opinion for the seventh report of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Ocean report, entitled “Review of the Fisheries Act: policy and legislative considerations and recommendations”.

Conservatives of the official opposition were motivated to submit this dissenting report to ensure that Canadians are provided the whole story of the evidence we received and the whole story of the harms caused by the 2019 changes.

When the Liberals introduced these changes, they said the changes were necessary to restore lost protections, yet when they were asked what harms had been caused by the supposed lost protections, the Liberal government provided no proof. The Liberals charged ahead with changes that have not only hurt harvesters and supply chains that depend on fisheries, but they have also undermined Canada's national interest in our sovereignty and our independence.

At a time when Canadians are concerned for independence and progressive growth, the reality is that major projects and even the government's own strategies for energy emissions reductions and natural resources are directly hampered and put in limbo by Liberal legislation like the 2019 changes to the Fisheries Act.

Conservatives appreciate all participants in the study, especially those who spoke honestly, despite facing possible retributions. I thank all Canadians who participated in this study, because they care. Conservatives also care, and we urge everyone to read this dissenting report. We have made recommendations to strengthen the Fisheries Act and allow for a stronger and more independent Canada.

Mr. Speaker, since 2012, the First Nations Education Steering Committee, British Columbia and Canada have worked together on the British Columbia Tripartite Education Agreement to promote successful education outcomes for first nations learners.

The petitioners note that education is a fundamental human right, and the BCTEA is the primary source of funding for first nations students of schools based on the public education system in British Columbia. It was expected that renewed funding commitments would be confirmed in the spring economic update, as the agreement is set to expire on June 30, 2026. Canada instead confirmed that the funding for the proposed renewed BCTEA was not secured and that the status quo funding was confirmed for only a one-year extension.

Therefore, the petitioners in Mission—Matsqui—Abbotsford call upon the government to approve the proposed renewed BCTEA and associated funding commitments for a 10-year term in the fall budget to ensure that the education of first nations students is not needlessly disrupted.
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise today to table this petition on behalf of constituents of my riding.

The petitioners cite that Canada's national inventory identifies more than 1,300 wrecked, abandoned and hazardous vessels, including more than 900 in British Columbia. These vessels pose serious risks to marine ecosystems, fisheries, indigenous food harvesting, coastal communities, navigation and public safety.

The petitioners highlight that coastal communities continue to experience vessels grounding, sinking or breaking apart in sensitive marine habitats, resulting in pollution and fisheries closures. Preventing vessels from becoming environmental hazards is safer and less costly than emergency response, salvage and remediation after they sink or break apart; that existing federal vessel removal and disposal programs are inadequately funded, limited in scope or have expired; that Canada lacks a comprehensive strategy and sufficient infrastructure for the responsible retirement, recycling and disposal of end-of-life vessels; and that Washington state demonstrates a proactive approach using dedicated vessel registration revenues to help address vessels before they become abandoned or hazardous.

The petitioners call on the government to establish a permanent national strategy for the prevention, removal, recycling and responsible disposal of wrecked, abandoned and hazardous vessels; create a self-sustaining vessel retirement and turn-in program funded in whole or in part through vessel registration fees; restore and expand federal funding for timely vessel removal; and improve federal procurement and response processes so qualified regional marine contractors can be deployed quickly to prevent environmental damage and invest in Canadian vessel recycling and disposal infrastructure, including capacity in coastal British Columbia.

PersonSpeaking.Affiliation: Hon. Marjorie Michel (Minister of Health, Lib.)

Content.ParaText: moved that Bill S-5, An Act respecting the interoperability of health information technology and to prohibit data blocking by health information technology vendors, be read the second time and referred to a committee.

She said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise today to speak to Bill S-5, the connected care for Canadians act. Timely and secure access to personal health information is critical to saving lives and improving care for Canadians. This act is part of our government's plan to build up and protect the health care system and empower Canadians to have more control over their health.

The main focus of Bill S-5 is patient safety. When health care systems are not interconnected, they are not only inefficient, but they also pose a clinical risk for Canadians. Things like undetected allergies, incomplete medication history and lost or delayed test results can lead to misdiagnosis and potentially life-threatening consequences.

Even today, fewer than 13% of Canadians say they have electronic access to all their medical records. In Canada, in 2026, the fax machine remains the primary means for sharing health information between health care facilities. Only 52% of health care providers say that they share their patients' health information electronically outside their office. The main obstacle they cite is a lack of interoperability. Consider what that means for patients.

Patients should not have to remember their entire medical history or repeat it every time they consult a new health care provider. Furthermore, health care providers should not have to rely on incomplete information to make clinical decisions. A survey by the Canadian Medical Association found that 92% of practising physicians in Canada said that the lack of coordination between health care systems was hindering their ability to provide care. That is unacceptable, and it needs to change.

Through Bill S-5, we can make technology work for Canadians, improving lives, improving care and building a more efficient health care system ready for the future. Australia and the European Union have already implemented similar legislation or regulations. Their residents have benefited from connected health care for years. If we act now, we can ensure that Canadians have access to the connected care they need and deserve.

I would like to clarify what this bill would do. At present, the sharing of health information in Canada is hampered by the lack of common standards across the country. Bill S-5 would promote interconnected health care by requiring IT vendors in Canada's digital health sector to adopt common data standards. It would also prohibit data blocking.

Data blocking means restricting access to, use of or sharing of health information among authorized parties, such as patients and their health care providers, when privacy laws would otherwise permit it.
In other words, Bill S-5 would help identify the barriers preventing patients and their health care providers from securely accessing the health information they need, when they need it.
All of this would be achieved while preserving existing privacy protections and personal information safeguards.
Access to health information is not a matter of convenience. It is a necessity. Data saves lives, especially when a full medical history is needed in an emergency.

Let me share the stories of real patients and their families. They have experienced the devastating consequences of disconnected care in Canada. Theresa lost her son, Dan, who was only 17, after two visits to the emergency department. She believes real-time access to his file would have helped the family flag critical details sooner.

Another patient requiring an urgent surgical procedure outside her home province was compromised because the local medical team could not access vital records from her home province. Without this essential medical history, clinicians were unable to safely perform the procedure.

There is the story of Greg Price, whose legacy has been an inspiration for many of us working on this legislation. Greg was a healthy engineer from Alberta who faced systemic failures in our health care system. Like many others, he experienced delays due to poor coordination and inaccessible health information. He died of cancer in 2012. He was 31.
This is why today's legislation is so important. We need to break down those silos, so we are changing the rules and we are building the health data infrastructure Canadians deserve.

Bill S‑5 would also reduce the day-to-day administrative burden on our health care professionals. According to a survey conducted by the Canadian Medical Association, physicians report that they waste an average of 86 minutes a day searching for patient data. That is almost an hour and a half a day. Time spent printing and sorting documents is time that health care professionals do not spend on what they should be doing and what they want to do: caring for people.

Several OECD countries modernized their data laws years ago to allow for the secure transmission of health data, but Canada is lagging behind. This is important not only for patient care but also for the future of innovation within our health care system.

Canada has implemented a near-universal medical records system. Things have to change, especially in light of artificial intelligence. Realizing the transformative potential and the growing importance of artificial intelligence, the Government of Canada recently published Canada's new national artificial intelligence strategy, known as “AI for All”. Health and life sciences are one of the priority sectors under the strategy, given AI's potential to improve patient care, accelerate diagnostics and support the development of new treatments.

However, AI's effectiveness depends on the quality of the data it uses. To unleash AI's potential in the health care field, it must have access to anonymized, standardized high-quality data that can be used responsibly and shared in total safety.
With Bill S-5, we can create the standardized database that is essential to a modern health care system.

Fragmented digital health systems lead to costly requirements across various regions. Health information technology vendors have to build customized models to make their products work in every province and territory. This limits their ability to grow in the Canadian market. Vendors have been clear about the need to address interoperability challenges in Canada.

By establishing clear and consistent national requirements, Bill S-5 would make Canada more predictable and attractive for businesses in the digital health sector. Rather than having to adapt to different requirements in each province and territory, vendors could operate within a single internationally harmonized framework. This would reduce complexity while encouraging innovation and investment. It would also help Canadian businesses grow domestically and compete globally.

Canadians must also be able to trust that their personal medical records will be secure and protected. That is exactly what Bill S-5 aims to do. The bill would not amend federal, provincial or territorial laws governing the use of personal health information. Access to personal health information would continue to be governed by existing privacy laws, and only authorized users would be able to access their patients' medical records.

It is important to note that Bill S-5 also respects indigenous data sovereignty and will in no way alter the ownership, control or governance of the health data of first nations, Inuit, and Métis peoples.

As technology evolves, it is essential to protect Canadians' privacy. That is why our government has also introduced Bill C-36, the protecting privacy and consumer data act, to modernize Canada's private sector privacy legislation for the digital age. Bill C-36 reinforces our commitment to responsible innovation, economic growth, and the protection of Canadians' rights in the digital age.

Co-operation with the provinces and territories is key. I am already working with my provincial and territorial counterparts to develop the regulations. However, the federal framework will not apply to provinces and territories that already have similar conditions. I welcome our shared commitment to interoperable digital solutions that enhance connectivity in our health care system.
Gaps in access to and sharing of health data create unnecessary and unacceptable risks. Canadians continue to face challenges when navigating the health care system.
Canadians strongly support change and want better access to their own health data.
This bill is part of our government's plan to build up and protect the health care system and empower Canadians to have more control over their health.
This is great news for our country. That is why I am calling on all members of the House to work together to pass Bill S‑5.
I want to thank the Senate for voting to pass it.

Madam Speaker, I was really struck by my colleague's comment that 92% of practising physicians have been hampered by lack of access to information about their patients. The Canadian Medical Association and other medical organizations have been calling for this for a decade. The Competition Tribunal, in June 2022, identified the behaviour of electronic medical record providers as being anti-competitive, and of course we had Bill C-72 before the previous Parliament.
My question for the minister, given that the Liberals let Bill C-72 die on the Order Paper when they called an election last January, is, what took them so long?

Madam Speaker, what I can say is that when I took office, work had already been done on the bill. It had died on the Order Paper, but I immediately revived it. We started discussions with the provinces and territories to ensure that we could move the bill forward. The bill was first introduced in the Senate, and now that the Senate has passed it, we are moving it forward in the House.

I understand what my colleague is saying, and I agree that this has taken too long. However, I think now is the time, and we cannot wait any longer. Given all of the technological advances, such as AI, if we do not have good data, then we will be at risk, and Canada will fall even further behind.

Madam Speaker, I admit that the bill's objective is laudable, but there is a major problem here. I am sure members know what I am going to say next. This bill fails to acknowledge that health falls under the exclusive jurisdiction of Quebec and the provinces. Quebec already has laws that implements proposals similar to the ones found in this bill. I do not see how the Bloc Québécois can approve a bill like this unless it is amended to explicitly acknowledge that health falls under Quebec's jurisdiction and that it is Quebec's responsibility, not the federal government's.
I would like to hear my colleague's thoughts on that.

Madam Speaker, I was expecting a question along those lines. My colleague did not hear my speech, but I made it very clear that any provinces and territories that already have their own regulations will not have to opt out of Bill S-5. The federal government will not interfere with the delivery of health care services by the provinces and territories. The law is complementary, applying only in cases where a province or territory does not already have comparable legislation. At present, Quebec and Ontario already have their own legislation in place.
Madam Speaker, Dr. Margot Burnell, the past president of the CMA, stated:

Quote.QuotePara: When personal health information can travel freely and securely between patients, clinics, hospitals and labs, people will have better health outcomes and doctors will have more time to focus on care. It also makes it easier for patients to manage their own care in partnership with doctors and other health professionals.

Content.ParaText: I know this is echoed by the new, incoming president.

The government has been working on a pan-Canadian interoperability road map for years. What is the difference this time, and what concrete timeline would the government commit to so Canadians are not still hearing about the promise of connected care in five years or 10 years from now? This is something the NDP has been calling on for a long time, and I have been working with the minister on it.
Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for working with us to move this bill forward. I know how important this bill is to him.

Today is a positive step forward. The bill has already passed the Senate and is now before the House, which will refer it to a committee. Once the bill has been passed, we will be able to develop the regulations. We have already started working with the provinces and territories, but this will allow us to formalize that work. While it will still take several months to put the regulations in place, if the bill is passed quickly, I expect the entire process could be completed in less than a year.

Madam Speaker, I would like to begin by congratulating my esteemed colleague, the Minister of Health, for all her leadership on this issue. I can tell her that, yes, we have been waiting a long time for this bill, but now we are truly moving in the right direction, and we are doing so quickly. The Canadian government is playing a leadership role. It is not responsible for managing hospitals, but it has a role to play in health care and public health.

I would like her to elaborate on an issue that we do not talk about often enough: the fact that data is important to health research, which is, in turn, important to clinical care, benefiting both patients and health care professionals.
Madam Speaker, I have been talking about data ever since I became the Minister of Health.

Reliable data is essential to making good health care decisions with respect to both service delivery and research. When data is harmonized, researchers can collect it in the same way across the country. This bill will help us do that. It will harmonize how data is collected. All the data will speak the same language, and researchers will be able to analyze it in a consistent fashion. This bill will be beneficial in that regard.
Madam Speaker, I was interested in the point the minister made about Ontario and Quebec already having legislation that this legislation would not supersede.

This interested me in particular because, as a physician practising in Ontario, I know that the clinical notes from one hospital that I worked at over the last few years in Guelph, Ontario, could be viewed in the region west of Toronto, but I also worked in Kingston, Ontario, over that time, and clinical notes from my other work in Guelph could not be viewed in that region. Even Ontario has not resolved this problem within the province.

I wonder if we are talking about whether Ontario has legislation that calls for this, or about whether Ontario has a reality of interoperability between all the regions in Ontario. Would Bill S-5 affect Ontario as it stands today or not?
Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for the question because it allows me to clarify a few things.

Yes, Ontario and Quebec already have a legislative framework in this area. However, the data is still blocked by the vendors. Unblocking this data will allow us to share it, and that is what makes all the difference, both within a single province and between provinces. Bill S-5 will still have an impact in Ontario.

What I meant to say is that Ontario and Quebec have already adopted legislation to improve the interoperability of their own health care systems. They have already started putting procedures in place. However, Bill S-5 will require vendors to unblock data, and sharing the data is going to change things.
Madam Speaker, my colleague's question is important. Earlier, the minister quoted a passage stating that the bill will not a apply to provinces that have their own system.
Could she table that wording? I cannot find it in the bill.
Madam Speaker, we can certainly clarify that.
Madam Speaker, I want to thank the hon. minister for her leadership on this very important bill. We all know that this bill is going to save lives across Canada.
I would also like to ask the minister a question about access to our own health data. We know that Canadian patients want access to their own medical records.
How might Bill S-5 facilitate that?

Madam Speaker, nearly 25% of Canadians currently have access to their health data, and the same mechanism will apply here. Bill S-5 will require vendors to unblock data, which will enable the various health care systems to make the data available to doctors and patients.

Madam Speaker, the minister's enthusiasm for the bill is very well appreciated. The issue of health information technology is very near and dear to my heart, and not always in a happy way. Without naming any names of any particular institutions, one of the hospitals that I worked at for a long time foisted on physicians a health information technology solution without asking the physicians, the pharmacists or the nurses if they should do this or whether it was a good idea. They spent millions of dollars on it, and it frankly ruined our professional lives when it did not work at all.

It is important to have good intentions. It is important to be enthusiastic about those intentions, but it is really important that the solutions that end up hitting the ground actually work for the people who use them and for the people those professionals serve. We have to be really careful about a bill like this. The possibility of causing more problems than it solves is a real and present danger.

It is always a great honour to be in the chamber. It is always a great honour to speak on behalf of the people of Kitchener South—Hespeler. It is a great honour to give the Conservative response to the minister's speech. This is, I believe, the first piece of legislation pertaining to health care in the 45th Parliament.

It has been a long time coming. It has been a year and a half. I am a bit sad to say this is a bill that is warmed over from the last Parliament, when it somehow did not make it through. It has been years coming, and for that reason I would hold it to an even higher standard than if it were invented de novo.

The bill before us today, Bill S-5, has the admittedly laudable goal of making it illegal for health information technology companies to engage in what the bill defines as data blocking, that is, stopping the exchange, or impeding the exchange, of personal health information between authorized health information technologies.

In sharp contradistinction to many of the government bills that we have been debating over this past month, or even this past week, this is a very short bill. I commend it for that reason. It is perhaps only five pages long, in one language. Even though it is easy to read the bill, which I am grateful for, it is very difficult for me to understand how it could, in fact, work.

I spent 95% of my clinical career in hospitals. There are three electronic medical record vendors that hospitals in Canada use very commonly: Epic, Cerner and Meditech. All three, I am sorry to say, are American companies. All three are subject to a 2016 law passed by the Obama administration called the Cures Act. My understanding is that the Cures Act is very similar, both in its intent and its operations, to the bill before us today, Bill S-5.

Of course, it would be ideal, internationally, that all three of these systems be able to transmit patient health information between each other, obviously with the consent of the patient involved, but it is a really hard problem. This morning, for instance, my office printer was on the fritz. I was unable to send data, this speech, from my computer to the printer in my office. I had to get a friend in the lobby to print it for me, and that is a much simpler problem than all of the health information in all of Canada.

Software vendors and Bill S-5 can have the best of intentions, but the problem of data interoperability is just a hard problem. Let us take, for instance, Meditech. Currently, Meditech has multiple products, multiple product families and different versions of each currently operating in the wild. There is Meditech 6.0, Meditech 6.1, Meditech Expanse, Meditech Expanse 2.1, Meditech Expanse 2.2. Different hospitals may choose to invest more or less money, or use one product family over another. They may choose to update whichever product family they are using often or not, depending on their own IT and human resources.

I imagine it is a full-time job, nay several full-time jobs, at Meditech headquarters just to make sure that its own systems can communicate with each other in an interoperable fashion. That is not for a lack of trying. How much work, how many people and how much money will it take to make the Meditech system talk to the Epic system, to make both talk to Cerner and to make all three talk to the 10 to 15 major players in the European market? How much of a barrier of entry to one day starting a Canadian competitor would all of this entail?

Let us drill down on a small part of the problem to understand the full scale of the problem. In my work as an ICU physician, any individual patient might have literally tens of thousands of data points stored in the EMR from just one day. Just their vital signs, such as heart rate, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, body temperature and blood pressure, might be recorded and time-stamped continuously, providing thousands of data points before we even speak of medications, diagnostic imaging, clinical notes, blood work, etc.

Each of these data points has to be filed or coded in some agreed upon, legible way in order to be interoperable. Even to zero in on just blood pressure, there are multiple numbers that go into a blood pressure reading and different numbers one might want to store, such as the systolic, the diastolic and the mean arterial pressure. There are different ways of measuring a blood pressure, namely a sphygmomanometer or a blood pressure cuff, or invasive arterial monitoring. Sometimes we are measuring both continuously throughout the day.

One system might store, code and display the cuff systolic and the intra-arterial map every 15 minutes. My system might store, code and display only the cuff three times a day, or when an intra-arterial pressure is available, it might store that, superseding the other. It seems almost impossible to have a government regulatory body come in and say which one is correct. The sphygmomanometer, the intra-arterial blood pressure monitor, the EKG and the pulse oximeter all measure a patient's heart rate, and three of the four measure it continuously. How do we impose a system that ensures that each health vendor will store those in mutually comprehensible ways?

Let us consider a patient on continuous EKG monitoring. Literally every beat of their heart comes with multiple measurable waveforms depending on which EKG is looked at. Each monitoring system will come with different alarms and different ways of storing who responded to each alarm, how long the alarm went off, who turned it off and why they turned it off.

I cannot imagine setting one standard for how all of this ought to be captured. This is not like saying all smart phones have to use a USB-C plug. There are so many more inputs and outputs to a human body that constitute health information. When I speak of monitoring vital signs, I am speaking of a fraction of a fraction of all the forms of data that go into health and health care.

I have just now been speaking about electronic medical records, only one of the types of software we would find in a hospital. There are also prescription management systems, diagnostic imaging systems and scheduling systems, all of which contain personal health information. By the way, health care centres like hospitals are just one sort of organization that uses some classes of devices and some sorts of information technology on those devices.

Bill S-5 seems to seek to regulate all sorts of other devices. For instance, I am wearing an Apple Watch. It went off, and the Speaker got mad at me. It also stores personal health information of mine on it, such as my heart rate. If someone has a CPAP machine at home or a blood sugar monitor, the bill would seem to make demands on those device manufacturers as well.

This is just the present state of things. Health information technology is changing now at a faster and faster rate. A friend of mine runs an AI-powered ultrasound diagnostics start-up company for use by combat medics to see if a soldier in the field has a pneumothorax in real time. It is a pocket-sized device. It is an amazing invention. He worked so hard on it. He employs so many fantastic Canadian scientists who are designing it and making it better every day. I understand that he spends about 0% of his time making sure that whatever data is stored on that device in a battlefield somewhere can talk to Cerner, Epic and Meditech. He is trying to save lives by making something that has never existed before. How can he expect that whatever data his invention ends up outputting 10 years from now will be legible by these legacy systems?

I am hoping that this House will take seriously the scale of the problem that Bill S-5 is trying to make go away. As I said earlier in my speech, the bill closely follows the approach that the Obama administration took in 2016, 10 years ago. Did this approach work in that milieu?

If it pleases the House, I would love to table at some point a paper from November 2025 published in the Journal of the American Medical Association and written by Everson et al., entitled “EHR Interoperability Experiences Reported by Family Physicians”. The scientists surveyed more than 8,000 family doctors, asking them what their experience with health information interoperability has been like eight years after the Cures Act. I am sorry to say that despite the best of intentions, the results in this paper are dismal. Only 8% of the family doctors surveyed reported ideal interoperability. From my reading of the paper, it seemed that a majority of the doctors went so far as to give up on accessing outside clinical documentation. I hope we can talk more about this study at committee. Perhaps we could invite the authors of it to committee, should the bill succeed at second reading.

If it is the case that the U.S. administration, after eight years of trying, largely failed to regulate the big American health information technology vendors I mentioned, Cerner, Meditech and Epic, how can we expect that the Canadian federal government would succeed in regulating those same American health information technology vendors into making their systems interoperable? As I said, most Canadian hospitals use information technology from these American providers. Many of the Canadian hospitals I have personally worked at, however, cannot afford to use the latest systems or subscribe to the most up-to-date features from each of these vendors.

Is it really possible that Canadian regulators will be able to bully these gigantic corporations? Cerner is, in fact, by the way, the health information branch of Oracle, one of the largest tech companies in the world. Are we going to be able to demand that Oracle change what it is doing into solving what I fear may be an unsolvable problem when we are currently shopping in its bargain bin? Is it the case that the federal government has a good track record generally in the field of IT systems management? Who among us here could forget the $2.6-billion boondoggle that we now call the Phoenix pay system? Who could forget the $60-million arrive scam scandal? Who could forget the most recent scandal of all, the $300 million blown on the unworkable PrescribeIT program?

I, for one, am not going to forget the PrescribeIT scandal. I think anyone who is familiar with my parliamentary work knows about PrescribeIT by now, because it has been the biggest part of what I have been working on over the last year. In brief, not to belabour the point, as I know the health minister is very familiar with it, it was a 10-year-long attempt by an organization called Canada Health Infoway, which receives funding both from provinces and from the federal government, to solve a simple problem.

Ten years ago, when she introduced the legislation that gave the money for PrescribeIT, the minister of health at the time, Jane Philpott, called it the axe the fax program. Members are aware, of course, how much Liberals like rhyming three-word slogans such as axe the fax.

Right now, in our country, physicians fax prescriptions to pharmacies. That was the case in 2016 when Jane Philpott introduced the legislation. Canada Health Infoway spent $300 million and took 10 years to make just this small class of health information transfer digitally between a doctor's office or hospital and a pharmacy. We have investigated this matter at committee in some detail. To this day, I do not understand how it is that Canada Health Infoway invented something other than a digital fax, which has existed since 1998. Indeed, by its own admission, it invented nothing. It gave Telus $80 million to provide and manage the software platform, which already existed. That was a good deal for Telus. To this day, our study of this matter at committee having been truncated, I still have no idea what became of the other $220 million. It had a $300-million budget. It bought the software and had Telus managing it for $80 million. I do not know where the $220 million went.

After all of that money and all of that time, physicians and pharmacists in our country, by and large, refused to use the solution. Canada Health Infoway seems to have spent a decade designing, or not designing but ordering, a software solution from Telus, without bothering to check in with frontline workers whether they liked the product or whether they would agree to use the product. The product was free, and still over 95% of physicians in our country declined to use the product. That is really bad and frankly activates my PTSD from my home hospital, which had foisted an information management system on us all those years ago. Of all the dogs that have never hunted, the PrescribeIT dog really did not hunt. It was a free solution that 95% of physicians and pharmacists declined to take up.

With Phoenix, arrive scam and PrescribeIT, there is not a good track record. Maybe the federal government is about to turn over a new leaf and provide IT systems that work and that people want to use. I wish I could believe that, but do members know who it plans to put in charge of Bill S-5? Can anyone in the House guess? It is Canada Health Infoway, the totally corrupt organization that just blew $300 million on a failed solution. I know this is the Liberals' plan by word of mouth, but I also know it from Senate testimony. This bill is called Bill S-5 because it came from the Senate. It has already gone through Senate committee hearings, and that has been the clear message. They had the now interim CEO of Canada Health Infoway give testimony. It is their intention to oversee the regulation of this perhaps unsolvable problem.

For those who have not heard, Canada Health Infoway just fired its CEO because he came to the health committee to answer questions about PrescribeIT. He refused to answer the most basic questions about what he accomplished with his nearly $1-million salary. He would not even answer what his salary was. We had to get that information by other means. Its current CEO is the former vice-president, whom he hired.

The $300-million PrescribeIT boondoggle is not even Canada Health Infoway's total spend over the last decade. I believe the organization was in receipt of $1 billion of public money over this time, yet when we had the chair of the board at the health committee and I asked him what it accomplished with the other $700 million, he was unable to describe a single tangible achievement. This is a big problem. Even acknowledging that PrescribeIT did not work, acknowledging that the CEO of Canada Health Infoway was a big problem and acknowledging the extent to which the health minister took credit or did not for his dismissal, even after all that occurred, she planned to reward Canada Health Infoway with another $50 million of funding this year.

I came to question period week after week and asked why she would give it this money. To her credit, the minister halted that funding, acknowledging that this organization is in a serious state of disrepair. This is a big problem when we talk about Bill S-5. It is, to my understanding, still the Liberals' intention to have Canada Health Infoway lead the charge on regulating into existence a solution that is maybe not even possible when they have not accounted for the last $1 billion they spent.

Do I support Bill S-5 in principle? Of course I do. Of course health information technology should be interoperable. Of course no patient should ever have their care suffer because data transfer between institutions is hard. Do I believe that the government, with its track record of IT boondoggles and its track record with Canada Health Infoway, will succeed in getting this job done with this piece of very short legislation? I fear I do not. I want to hear more about it at committee. I certainly want to hear more from Canada Health Infoway on what its plan was, but I cannot say that I have great faith that it will work out.

Solving a problem like the one I have described is not a matter of intention. For instance, I do not want anyone in this country to be sad. If we were to make a law that no one is allowed to be sad anymore, it would not work. That was the question I asked the minister. She said it seemed to be the case that Bill S-5 would not even apply to Ontario because Ontario already has legislation with this intention. However, the reality in Ontario, as I described in my question, is not that health information technologies are interoperable. In the discussion and debate we have in this House, I would love for the government to explain why it will succeed where Ontario has failed if it already has similar legislation.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, I appreciate that the member clearly indicated that how health information technology is handled is absolutely critical and that he supports the principle of the legislation. I am encouraged by that.

In terms of the whole mismanagement area, it was the Harper government that brought in Phoenix. There is no escaping that. In other words, there are ways in which, no doubt, we can learn from past experiences in order to advance the principle of a good idea.

I appreciate the member's knowledge, I must say. I am quite impressed with his background and his understanding of the urgency of this. I believe that it would be best addressed at the committee stage. I wonder if he could provide his thoughts on whether he thinks this legislation will pass, given that the Senate has already supported it in principle.

Madam Speaker, I think this is becoming a bit of a running gag. After literally every speech I give in this House, the member for Winnipeg North stands and says, “but Stephen Harper”. I suspect that he checks under his bed for Stephen Harper before he goes to sleep at night.

In general, I criticized the federal government trying to do things that cannot be done. This is a vast country. If this problem were solvable, it would be solvable close to home at a low level. If a single province cannot get this done within its borders, I do not understand how any federal government, Stephen Harper's or otherwise, would be able to achieve that.

Is it still a good idea to do something that is well-intentioned but doomed to failure? Part of the answer to that is how much money the Liberals plan to spend on their well-intentioned, doomed project.
Madam Speaker, looking over the bill, we can see that it will be implemented by order in council.. Looking at the provision governing such orders, we find the following in clause 7:

Quote.QuotePara: The Governor in Council may, by order, make any provision of this Act or the regulations applicable in any province or territory if the Governor in Council is satisfied,

Content.ParaText: Already, we see that discretionary power comes into play.

Quote.QuotePara: after applying the criteria and the process provided for in the regulations,

Content.ParaText: We pass the laws, but regulations never come back before legislators.

Quote.QuotePara: that the province or territory does not have requirements that are substantially similar to or exceed those established under this Act.

Content.ParaText: A moment ago, the minister said the bill would not apply in the provinces or territories that already have legislation. However, through regulations and orders in council, the bill also allows her to satisfy herself that federal action is nonetheless required.
The territories' and the provinces' jurisdiction over health, however, is constitutionally established. Does my colleague not see that as a potentially dangerous discretionary power?

Madam Speaker, I think it is dangerous. There are two major dangers that I see. One is to free enterprise. If we have some giant regulator, unaccountable to the House, making decisions about what constitutes interoperability, how is that going to affect my friend? He is a professor of medicine. He is, frankly, a genius. He is trying to develop this ultrasound AI-powered technology. It would be easy for the regulator to put restrictions on him that would make it almost impossible for him to enter the market unless he lives up to the standard that the fat cats like Cerner and Meditech get the regulator to adopt. There is a real risk of protectionism and the choking out of health care innovation.

I have read the Canadian Constitution front to back a few times. It talks about hospitals being under provincial jurisdiction. We have the Public Health Agency, we have Health Canada, and we have the Canada Health Act. It seems that in many ways in this country, health care currently comes under federal jurisdiction, and the words “health care” do not appear in Canada's written constitution, at least.

Madam Speaker, it is important to hear from somebody like my colleague, who has the medical professional background that he does. He has very eloquently expressed a lot of the problems that currently exist. It is very reasonable for Canadians to expect that their data and their information would be available to them wherever they may be, and I think this is a problem that needs to be addressed. It has been a problem in Saskatchewan. It has been a problem in Ontario, as he has highlighted very well.

I passed a bill on the copyright side for interoperability, so I appreciate his talking about the need for data interoperability. I am just wondering, on that very specific point, if he has a little more to add to the remarks he made earlier.

Madam Speaker, something the member was driving at that I think is really important is the lens I would want this sort of bill to take. In medicine in general, we have struggled over the last several decades to be more patient-centred and less institutionally centred in our approach. I would love it if this health information technology bill put health information technology more in the hands of patients, if it adopted the patient-centred approach. Instead of a bill telling Epic and Cerner that they have to fulfill Canada Health Infoway's requirements on interoperability, I would love to see a bill that asks Cerner and Epic to put the health information in the hands of the patient to whom the information pertains, and then that patient could choose to hand it over to Epic or to Meditech if and when they see fit.

Madam Speaker, I was also very pleased and very interested by the speech we just heard from someone who obviously knows and cares very much about how health care systems work and should operate. I am curious to hear his point of view on the connection between research, science and health, health data and health clinical work. Does he believe that providing better access to data to researchers, scientists and health experts could lead to better development of technologies and better use of those technologies?
Madam Speaker, yes.
Madam Speaker, I have a fairly straightforward question. I hope we get the same sort of an answer.

The member talked originally about the principle of the legislation being something he appreciated. Then, when he answered my question, at the tail end he planted the seed of doubt as to whether the Conservatives would want to see the legislation go to committee. Can the member indicate whether the Conservative Party will be voting in favour of the legislation to go to committee?

Madam Speaker, my understanding is that the Liberal government has a majority in the House. The legislation will pass if the Liberal Party wants to pass it. I am honestly befuddled as to why the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader is so interested in whether we support the legislation. I am not in a position to speak for the Conservative Party today. For myself, I can say I have not made up my mind.

Madam Speaker, I am wondering what additional data the hon. member is looking for, in terms of what the government needs to provide in order to give not just Conservatives but Canadians comfort that the legislation would be implemented well and would provide for good, truly interoperable portable systems.
Madam Speaker, it comes down to trust. It is my understanding, based on the Senate testimony, that the intent is for Canada Health Infoway to lead this effort. I do not trust Canada Health Infoway.

It is a really, really difficult technical problem. I understand some things about health care. I understand not a lot of things about information technology. There are very few people, I think, who actually could make regulations that make sense. Unfortunately, I feel that many of them are currently in the employ of Cerner, Meditech and Epic. If more meat could be put on the bones regarding who would actually be doing the regulations, thinking about the regulations, and how much money it would cost to get those people to do it, then perhaps I would have some more trust in this approach overall.

Madam Speaker, the people who turned on their televisions last night saw us debating. If they tuned in this morning, they would see that we are still here. I say that for those who think we do not do a lot of work. Extended hours, when we finish in the early hours of the morning, means that we need to use our notes to ensure that we stay on topic.

With respect to Bill S‑5, I must remind the House of Quebec's responsibility in delivering health care services. To me, that is clear. For the past few weeks, I have been the Bloc Québécois health critic. I have never seen so much pressure from the Conservative Party, senators, the government party and lobbyists to centralize health care powers in Ottawa. Every time, I am told that it would make things so much easier.
Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order.
My colleague is a generous woman. I am sure she would be willing to share her time with me.
I believe the hon. member for Laurentides—Labelle is seeking unanimous consent to split her time.
Is it agreed?
Some hon. members: Agreed.
It is agreed.

Madam Speaker, setting aside any knee-jerk reaction I might have as a Quebec sovereignist to Ottawa's centralizing tendencies, there remains the broader issue of administering care and, above all, administering health care. I fully recognize that the sharing of information is critically important in health care. We need to be able to prevent epidemics, understand population movements and anticipate the long-term effects. I fully understand the importance of having an accurate picture of the public health situation. Take HIV/AIDS, for instance. In a study currently being conducted by our committee, officials from the Public Health Agency of Canada told us yesterday that they were having difficulty compiling data on the current situation in Canada.
That is why I encourage the provinces to work together and, with Ottawa's support, establish an effective framework for information sharing and exchange.

Quebec, whether as a province or as a country, has every interest in having access to reliable public health data at the North American level. That said, we should not ask Ottawa to dictate to the provinces how health care should be managed. Let us leave that to the provinces, public health agencies and health departments to determine together whether a common road map is the best way to collaborate.
The ideal would be for them to pool resources and expertise, because responsibilities are shared and solutions are developed collaboratively. That is the beauty of sharing.
Bill S‑5 could simply be based on a truly asymmetrical relationship and an uneven partnership, one that is more natural and in keeping with our federation.

In this case, it is the means I am questioning, not the end. Federal legislation that forces us to take on a subordinate role tells Quebeckers that the federal government wants to be the master in their house, whereas we want to be masters in our own house.

On this budget day, I would like to remind the House that “Maîtres chez nous” is more than a slogan. It represents the hopeful spirit of the Quiet Revolution, our collective drive as Quebeckers to assert ownership of the tools to build a modern, forward-thinking state that is committed to social progress.

The Trudeau government essentially stole our ideas. One might say that it drew inspiration from ideas such as child care and pharmacare. What we are seeing from the current government is something altogether different. It is appropriating symbols of national aspiration and collective emancipation. That is profoundly insulting.

When Quebec chose to take its destiny into its own hands, it did not wait for the federal government. It just did it. We have been proving that for decades. We built our own institutions, established our own frameworks and charted our own course. Now that the work is done, the federal government wants to tell us what to do. It should do the opposite and ask the provinces how this worthy objective can best be achieved. Instead, the same old reflexes persist. Unless the government is prepared, and this is important, to amend its bill to include a preamble stating that Quebec remains the primary architect of its health policies, we cannot support such a bill.

It is worth noting that Quebec already has its own digital health information system, known as the Health Booklet. This system allows all Quebec patients to access their list of medications, medical imaging and lab test results, and the services they have received since May 2026. Quebec has begun rolling out digital health records in the Mauricie region, the Centre-du-Québec region, and the northern part of the Island of Montreal. This project will enable the Quebec health care system to gradually phase out outdated technologies such as—I am embarrassed to say—the fax machine, and contribute to the digital transition of Quebec hospitals.
Going forward, patients will be able to access their medical information, appointment history and medical records through Mon dossier santé.

If the federal government really wants to support health care, I have an idea: Release the money. Unfortunately, the federal government cannot manage our emergency rooms, our CLSCs, our labour relations, the delivery of care or the priorities of our health care system, so we have a request. Every single year, we ask for more money in the form of health transfers. We firmly believe that 6% a year, for a total of $14 billion over five years, is not too much to ask, given all the tax dollars collected by Ottawa.

Yes, it is no secret that Quebec's health care system faces challenges, but it is up to the Quebec government to make its own decisions in the best interests of Quebeckers, in consultation with stakeholders on the ground who understand the real needs. My riding of Laurentides—Labelle has three hospitals, the Mont-Laurier hospital, the Rivière-Rouge hospital and the Sainte-Agathe-des-Monts hospital. They have enormous funding needs. In all three cases, private foundations are stepping in to make up for the funding shortfalls. Why? It is because, unfortunately, the federal government is not doing its part.

When it comes to equipment, it is quite remarkable that the community had to mobilize all its efforts just to secure access to an MRI machine, and even a CT scanner, only a few years ago. Rather than allocating funds for patient care, the federal government is just managing programs and telling others what to do. The federal government does not run a single clinic. Everyone has their own area of expertise.

When I talk to people, I ask them whether they would prefer option A or option B. Option A involves adding another layer of administration to Quebec's health care system. Option B involves Ottawa sending Quebec money so that we can provide care. Option B wins every time, both among health care professionals and among the public. People know that they pay more in taxes than what is transferred back to Quebec, so it is simple. Unless amendments are made, the Bloc Québécois will be voting against Bill S-5.

I will conclude as I began it. The government needs to let Quebec and the provinces manage their own health care systems and make their own decisions. Yes, let us work in partnership, but not by making Quebec and the provinces subordinate. Let us not go further down the road of an imposed federalism. We have had enough encroachments on provincial jurisdiction. As I always tell my colleagues, whenever provincial jurisdictions are at stake, I will be relentless, and my answer will always be no.
Madam Speaker, I thank our colleague for her excellent speech.

I would note two useful points. First, she said that the bill's objective is noble. Second, she said that the Canadian government has to show leadership in health care across the country, including in Quebec.

I would like to ask her whether she has had an opportunity in recent months to speak with researchers or experts in her riding who work on health data about the importance of having access to these data, and about the extent to which technological barriers put in place by large companies—barriers that often transcend the borders of a single province—can make accessing these critical data difficult, knowing full well that data can save lives.

Madam Speaker, my colleague is right to a large extent. Indeed, without data, how can we act? Scientists say that they want to do more, but that we have decades of data to compile before we can make changes.

That said, it matters who has the control. Consider, for example, a father who tells all his kids that he is going to manage everything and keep all the information to himself. We prefer self-determination. We believe that each of the children, the provinces and territories, should be trusted and provided with whatever they need to obtain that data. Then, these data can be pooled together to save lives.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate my colleague's speech on this important issue today. I was particularly interested in the part about health care transfers. It is not a big ask for the provinces in order to provide the health care that Canadians deserve. It does fall under provincial jurisdiction, but they are asking the federal government for health transfers.
I would like to know the member's opinion on the fact that we are spending more taxpayer dollars on servicing our debt than we are on health care transfers in this country.
Madam Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to say one thing. We often hear about the desire to build Canada strong, about development and about the need to work together.

I find it hard to understand why, when all the provincial and territorial premiers spoke out so loudly, forcefully and unanimously to say that they needed health transfers, it all came to nothing. It would have been such a great opportunity to show that the government does indeed want to build Canada strong.
Madam Speaker, when the pan-Canadian interoperability roadmap was announced, it was noted that:

Quote.QuotePara: Quebec has not signed any agreement with the federal government and is not bound by the conditions related to the document entitled “Working together to improve health care for Canadians”. Quebec remains fully committed to exercise its own responsibilities within its exclusive jurisdiction over health care and has not adhered to the pan-Canadian strategies concerning human resources, data and virtual care and mental health and intends to retain its full autonomy with regard to planning, organization and management of its health system. Quebec remains open, however, to share information and best practices with other governments in these areas.

Content.ParaText: The minister said earlier that she has the power to decide whether or not to impose the order in council. What I understood from my colleague's speech is that, unless the government explicitly states in the preamble to its bill that Quebec remains in charge of its health policies, she will not support the bill.
Madam Speaker, my colleague has such a way with words. He must have slept longer than I did yesterday, even though we were together.
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
Madam Speaker, we were together in the House. We did not sleep together.
I want to make this crystal clear: If the necessary firewalls are in place, if our responsibility for delivering services is clearly protected and if data is shared, we will obviously say yes.
Otherwise, there is too much margin for manoeuvre, and the autonomy of Quebec's health care sector could be negatively affected by these orders.

Madam Speaker, before I start my remarks, I would like to note a recurring trend. We are seeing more and more bills here in the House that originated in the Senate. As members know, the time allocated for debate on a bill is not unlimited, so I find it somewhat curious that the government continues to place so many Senate bills on the agenda.

Let me turn now to Bill S-5. As my colleague from Laurentides—Labelle said earlier, its objective is certainly commendable. No one can argue with it. Unfortunately, however, this bill reflects a familiar tendency to believe that Ottawa knows best, that Ottawa knows better than the provinces what is good for them in areas under their jurisdiction, and that Ottawa possesses more expertise when it comes to implementing policies. I must say, it is getting a bit tiresome.

There is a major problem, as my colleagues have pointed out. Despite what the Minister of Health said earlier, nowhere does this bill explicitly recognize Quebec's and the provinces' exclusive jurisdiction over the organization of health care delivery or the fact that Quebec can choose to develop its own digital infrastructure. If the Bloc Québécois is to support such a bill, it must include an explicit recognition.

I would like to point out that, as my colleague from Laurentides—Labelle said earlier, the Government of Quebec has already indicated its intention to deploy its own digital health infrastructure. Unfortunately, this bill in no way reflects the autonomy that Quebec claims with respect to health care. Moreover, to my knowledge, Quebec has not committed to following the pan-Canadian interoperability roadmap. The major stumbling block in Bill S‑5 is that it does not respect jurisdictions.
To convince my colleagues of this, I will reread clause 7(1), which my colleague from Montcalm referred to earlier. I hope the Minister of Health will listen to us.

Quote.QuotePara: The Governor in Council may, by order, make any provision of this Act or the regulations applicable in any province or territory if the Governor in Council is satisfied, after applying the criteria and the process provided for in the regulations, that the province or territory does not have requirements that are substantially similar to or exceed those established under this Act.

Content.ParaText: What does that mean, ultimately? It means that Ottawa is leaving the door wide open to tell the provinces how they should act. That is why I said in my introduction that this is, once again, a form of centralizing federalism. I will not use the term “predatory federalism”, but this is yet another form of federalism that is heavily focused on allowing Ottawa to define what is right and what constitutes good health care within the provinces' areas of jurisdiction.

This is very clear, and I want to make that point clear to the minister. In theory, Bill S-5 might not apply to Quebec, as my colleague said, but we must still speak out against clause 7, which would allow the government, by order, to effectively override provincial laws in areas that fall under provincial jurisdiction.

Unless the government is willing to amend its bill, I do not see how the Bloc Québécois can support it. At the very least, a preamble should be added that clearly specifies that Quebec remains in charge of its health care.

However, today is budget day, and we are always happy on budget day. This bill gives me the opportunity to talk about something that is central to the Canadian federation, and we will see it reflected in the budget: the perennial problem of health transfers. If we want to fix health care, we need to solve the funding problem. Year in and year out, and during every election campaign, when Quebeckers and Canadians are asked what their priorities are, health care is usually one of their top priorities.

I want to go back to the issue of health transfers because, in the great history of Canadian federalism and the injustices and inequities in relations between Quebec and Ottawa, one thing is glaringly obvious. I am talking about the infamous fiscal imbalance.

For those who do not remember what that is, I will explain. The Government of Quebec delivers virtually all social services and, in fact, Ottawa delivers very few services. There is EI, but that is paid for by workers. There is OAS, which is a social program. Ottawa participates very little in terms of social programs, although it takes up 60% of the tax room.

In the end, Ottawa always has much more money than its responsibilities require, while Quebec and the provinces never have enough because they have a smaller tax base. That is the fiscal imbalance in a nutshell.
Instead of piling on more and more health initiatives, encroaching on an area under provincial jurisdiction, Ottawa should focus on making health transfers more predictable and unconditional.

We will see whether there is any good news in the budget and whether health care transfers will live up to the expectations of Quebec and the provinces. Right now, if we look at the big picture, Quebec is spending about 42% of its total budget on health care. Back in the 1960s, when the public health care system was first established, 50¢ of every dollar invested in health care came from the federal government and 50¢ came from the provincial government. Today, the federal government's share is estimated at barely 22%. That means that, for every dollar invested, 22¢ comes from the federal government. Quebec has to cover the rest, and the infamous fiscal imbalance comes into play, as I mentioned earlier.

That said, 42% of the Government of Quebec's budget is a huge share. That means that Quebec has only about 58% of its total fiscal capacity left to address essential priorities, such as education, poverty, infrastructure, municipalities and support for Quebec businesses. We have been fighting long and hard over health care transfers in Canada. In 1980, the Mulroney government made the first drastic cuts to health transfers.

Then came the famous Liberal era, when there were budget surpluses. Where did those budget surpluses come from? They came from the recurring cuts Paul Martin made to health care. In the wake of the 1997-98 referendum, $2 billion in recurring funding was cut from the provinces. Jean Chrétien boasted to the G7 that he had balanced the budget, which is pretty cynical, really, because he got his surpluses by cutting transfer payments to the provinces. He added that he would not have to pay the political price for this, because the public believed—members may recall Lucien Bouchard's shift toward outpatient care—that the governments of Quebec and the other provinces were to blame for the shortcomings in health care services. However, it was the federal government that had just insidiously cut transfer payments and that was not shouldering its share of responsibility for health care.
It is budget day. I hope the federal government will see the light. It needs to put an end to the predatory federalism and accept its share of responsibility for health transfers.
Madam Speaker, better data collection and interoperability, and therefore better dialogue between systems, will ultimately benefit the health of Canadians, including Quebeckers.

As we know, these things do not happen in a vacuum. Some Quebeckers might have consultations in Ontario or New Brunswick, just as people from other provinces might have consultations in Quebec. I welcome the idea of having a health care system that is more connected in terms of data sharing, because it represents progress. In fact, if we look at the Quebec model for data management, it is already pretty much in line with what is set out in Bill S-5, and it will ensure greater consistency, and therefore comparability, of data right across the country.
I wish I could understand why my colleague appears to oppose improved data collection, which will benefit the entire population.

Madam Speaker, if somebody is getting their arm taken off, they are not going to worry about the pimple on their nose. In health care, having better data sharing is worthwhile. However, what people want is access to services.

Unfortunately, what we have been seeing within the federation for far too long are cuts to health care transfers. This makes it more difficult to access care, and it makes it harder for the provinces to manage other areas under their jurisdiction.
If my colleague wants to see results in health care, he should convince his government to invest as it should and to increase its participation through transfers. That is the best solution.

Madam Speaker, my colleague was right to raise the whole issue of chronic underfunding in health care, the lack of federal funding, and the federal government's fundamental inability to shoulder its fair share.

Going back to the bill, under clause 7, which my colleague mentioned, the bill would apply, by order, to a province such as Quebec if the minister determines that Quebec's existing measures do not meet the criteria. Whatever she wants to do, she will do by enforcing regulations that we have not seen, that we will never see, and that she can also amend at her discretion, by order.

The minister told us that she respects the way things are being done in Quebec. My colleague argued that the preamble should explicitly state that the minister intends to respect Quebec's constitutional jurisdiction. Can he tell us whether he is convinced that the minister's commitment will lead to a willingness to accept an amendment proposed by the Bloc Québécois?

Madam Speaker, a little while ago, I was listening to the Minister of Health, who said, in response to a question from the member for Montcalm, that she would table the clause demonstrating that the provinces' areas of jurisdiction will be respected.

After a close reading of the bill, it quickly becomes apparent that, and I can see that my colleague from Québec Centre agrees with me on this, the federal government is leaving the door open to the possibility of assessing the Quebec government's IT policies and deciding whether they are valid. That is completely unacceptable.

I therefore hold out little hope that the minister will see the light and amend the preamble to this bill to clearly affirm that health care falls within provincial jurisdiction and that the federal government should not interfere.

Madam Speaker, there seems to be some confusion in the remarks made by my colleague, for whom I have a great deal of respect. This has nothing to do with the decisions made by the Government of Quebec. What this bill aims to do is regulate the activities of organizations, including multinationals, that are unfortunately restricting access to data needed by patients and health care professionals.
Does my colleague acknowledge that there is some confusion in what he said? The Quebec government is not the target here; technology companies are.

Madam Speaker, I admit that I get confused sometimes, but as for this bill, I would invite my colleague from Québec Centre to reread clause 7. He will learn that the government is giving itself the option of enforcing a law in an area of jurisdiction that is not its responsibility.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Maggie Chi (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Health, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, it is great to see you here today. I will be sharing my time with the member for Bourassa.
I rise today to support Bill S-5, the connected care for Canadians act, which is crucial to establishing a connected health care system in Canada.

In Canada, health information is fragmented and is scattered among hundreds of health information systems across family doctor offices, hospitals, walk-in clinics and pharmacies. Bill S-5 would break down these digital barriers so a patient's health information could move securely and seamlessly wherever they receive care. It means that patients would no longer have to physically carry medical records from one doctor's appointment to another or repeatedly explain their medical history every time they seek care.

Bill S-5 is also about making the health care system work better for Canadians. It would unlock the potential of standardized and anonymized health data to accelerate medical breakthroughs and improve health outcomes for all Canadians. Health information in Canada is often stuck in separate digital systems that cannot be easily shared, first, because of data blocking, a practice that prevents authorized users from accessing health data even when privacy legislation allows it, and, second, because of a lack of common standards. For example, one hospital's database could record a patient's blood type using a numeric code, another could use an alphanumeric code, and a third hospital might use a written description. All three could mean exactly the same thing, but without common standards, their computer systems might not recognize each other's blood type entries.

To address this, Bill S-5 would require health information vendors in Canada to adopt common standards and would prohibit vendors from data blocking. These standards would be set out and maintained through regulations, with requirements that would ensure secure access for patients within the protection of existing security law. This is the approach used in other jurisdictions as well, such as Australia, the United States and the European Union.

Bill S-5 would build on the shared pan-Canadian interoperability road map, already endorsed by provinces and territories, and on the working together to improve health care for Canadians plan, which committed nearly $200 billion over 10 years, with modernizing health data as one of four shared priorities.

When somebody sees a new doctor, they are asked for their medical history. Bill S-5 would enable patients and their doctors to access health records electronically, no matter where in Canada patients receive care. This is connected care. Doctors' being able to access electronic health records is critical to the continuity of care. Without a seamless exchange of information between systems and providers, the burden of health information falls to patients and their families. Moreover, the lack of access to a patient's medical records increases the risks of misdiagnoses, medication errors, duplicate testing and treatment delays.

Take, for example, patients in rural and remote communities or patients with very complex conditions who are referred to hospitals in major urban centres for advanced diagnostic procedures, complex treatments and highly specialized medical care. Oftentimes these patients arrive in serious condition, usually with photocopies of their health records, and the information is often incomplete. Patients with a language barrier or limited medical familiarity shoulder the burden of coordinating their own care because there is no digital connection between our health information systems. In all these cases, important health information is often missing or inaccessible. Unfortunately, this happens very often.

Bill S-5 would help support these patients with a more coordinated and integrated health care system, with accurate and accessible data so doctors can make clinical decisions with complete information and provide the health care Canadians deserve. In today's rapidly evolving world of medical research and innovation, large, high-quality data sets are the foundation of medical breakthroughs such as accelerating drug discoveries and enabling earlier disease detection. For example, the quality, quantity and representativeness of the data sets largely determines how accurately a health AI model performs in real-world settings.

Our government's national AI strategy, AI for all, recognizes data as a strategic national asset that must be responsibly stewarded and mobilized to support innovation and productivity across the economy. Our health care system generates a vast amount of health data, spanning diverse populations, medical conditions and care settings.

By leveraging our standardized and anonymized health data, Canadian researchers have an opportunity to become global leaders in medical research and health innovation, driving medical breakthroughs and improving health outcomes for all Canadians. Currently, much of this data remains fragmented in disconnected systems. By securely unlocking its potential by applying common standards, our medical researchers can drive breakthroughs in disease detection, treatment and improved hospital efficiency.

For example, in my riding of Don Valley North, we are fortunate to have North York General Hospital, Canada's top-ranked community academic hospital. It partnered with a Canadian health AI company, and by leveraging the data it has collected from the emergency department, it has trained an AI model that analyzes real-time patient vitals, waiting times, triage assessments and hospital capacity to identify where patients can receive care sooner. This has cut the average emergency wait time by nearly 28%.

Data can save lives. The knowledge that can be unlocked from our health data sets has the power to transform our health care system. Better health data means a more accessible and innovative health care system. That is why Bill S-5 is such a consequential piece of legislation, and I believe it is a practical path forward that would serve the best interests of all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, setting aside the fact that, as we mentioned earlier, as soon as the pan-Canadian interoperability roadmap was announced, Quebec made it clear that it did not want any part of it, though it was open to data sharing, there is one issue that piques my curiosity from a purely technological standpoint.

This bill is about connecting all health care data from coast to coast to coast. Does my colleague have any technological opinions on how vulnerable this kind of system might be to cyber-attacks, like the one that hit sites like Hugging Face not so long ago?

Madam Speaker, that is an excellent question. As I mentioned in my speech, in a rapidly evolving world with a lot of cybersecurity threats, and with the development of AI, security is definitely top of mind for all of us. The legislation, at the core of it, would block the ability of vendors to block data, while respecting provinces' and territories' ability to also operate within their privacy laws and acts. We are very mindful of that. We will continue to work with the provinces and territories as we write out the regulations, while respecting the provincial and territorial jurisdictions.

Madam Speaker, I am curious as to whether the member for Don Valley North can comment on how a more connected health care system, through Bill S-5, could help Canadians facing barriers to care, especially those living in rural and remote communities across Canada.

Madam Speaker, I mentioned a few examples in my speech of frustration with always having to remember one's medical care record or the history of one's procedures. We have all experienced that. Sometimes we forget, sometimes we may have remembered things wrong, and it proves a hindrance to our care. Sometimes it causes delays, really dangerous delays. We heard the minister mention the example of Theresa and her family. We want to avoid that.

As we continue to have discussions with providers, doctors and clinicians are telling us about the importance of having the legislation passed because it would enable data sharing. It would enable more connected care. It would help them facilitate care that is more beneficial to the health outcomes of patients. We are very optimistic about the future of more connected care in Canada that the bill would enable.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, I believe it is important that we advance the legislation. Back in the nineties, I was the health care critic in the province of Manitoba.
