Even back then, we were talking about having better access and about patients being able to see their records. I see the legislation as modernizing something that is long overdue. It is in the patient's best interest. Could my colleague provide her thoughts on the patient's best interest and how the bill would support that?
Madam Speaker, I want to thank my friend and colleague for his long-time advocacy for creating this future of connected care in Canada.

Absolutely, that is the goal for all of us, to provide the reality of more connected care in our communities. For far too long, and far too often, we have heard frustrations about remembering one's medical records, having misdiagnoses, having mistreatments or delays. We all want that to improve. This bill would not only provide a path to that for clinicians and health authorities. It would also provide patients with the autonomy of having their personal data and more connected care for everybody .
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to Bill S-5.

I want to begin by having members imagine the following scene: A mother from Montreal North arrives at the emergency room with her son in the middle of the night. She knows his allergies, medications and most recent visits by heart, but the doctor on duty does not see any of that information on the patient's record. His record exists, but it is somewhere else, in another system, not in the system of this clinic, this CLSC or this hospital. It is in a different software program or sitting on a fax machine somewhere. As a result, his mother has to repeat the information over and over again. While she is doing that, time is being wasted, and sometimes much more than just time is lost.

Today, information can travel around the globe in a second, but it is still difficult for a patient's health records to make it across the street. Bill S-5 seeks to remedy that issue. We are talking here about what I would describe as the cost of working in silos, which can be explained in numbers, and those numbers speak for themselves. Four out of five patients want to be able to access their health care records digitally online. However, only 39% are able to do that, and often they can access only some of the information. In 2023, 42% of Canadians reported gaps in the coordination of their care because of systems that do not communicate with one another. Behind those numbers are tests that had to be redone, delayed diagnoses and doctors who are searching for information instead of providing care. There are also families that carry their own health records around in an envelope or even a plastic bag—I have seen it happen—because the systems do not communicate or share data.

Consider the people who provide care. Our doctors, nurses and pharmacists already work under tremendous pressure. Every hour spent filling out forms, waiting for a fax—yes, I did say a fax—or calling another clinic is an hour less spent with a patient. That is really the important thing. That is the service that we want to provide to our citizens. In a system low on resources, unnecessary paperwork is not just a detail; it is health care time wasted.

I would also call this compartmentalization an “opportunity cost”. It is a collective cost. It prevents us from fully understanding which policies work and which performance indicators are best for the work at hand. It prevents us from knowing where shortfalls exist, where to look for the best impact indicator, or how to locate the best efficiency indicator, simply because the systems do not communicate; they exist in silos, with less integration. When systems operate in silos, information is not only less integrated, but the lack of interoperability prevents us from attaining the global perspective we need to measure them properly. Without seeing a situation clearly, it cannot be corrected. Without a global view, improvement is impossible. What cannot be measured is difficult to quantify or even to improve.
Of course, inequalities still remain. Bill S‑5 does two simple but essential things.

First, it requires interoperability. Health information technology vendors will need to ensure that the systems they sell, license or supply as a service can talk to each other and communicate according to common Canada-wide standards, including information security standards.

Second, it prohibits data blocking. A vendor will no longer be able to lock a patient's information to keep its clients captive. Health data belongs to a patient's continuum of care, not to a vendor's business model.

Let us consider a simple example. When people switch phone providers, they get to keep their phone number. No one would consider that revolutionary today. It is taken for granted. It is simply the way things work. Why, then, should we accept that a person's medical history remains trapped in a particular software platform or IT solution? If we demand number portability for our phone service, then we certainly can, and should, demand the same for the health of our families.

I have spent a good deal of my career in IT governance and in business and corporate architecture. To be honest, technology is rarely the problem. More often than not, the problem and the challenge are cultural, including the absence of common rules. People build islands and then act surprised when there are no bridges connecting them. Bill S-5 represents an obligation and an opportunity to build those bridges.

Building bridges involves creating connections. However, connecting systems does not mean we want to expose our data. Some people will ask where Bill S‑5 stands on privacy. The answer is clear: It makes no amendment to any federal, provincial or territorial privacy law. The current rules on the collection, use and disclosure of data continue to apply as they always have. Only authorized users will have access to records. Bill S‑5 does not mandate the sharing of data. It allows for the secure transfer of information where such transfers are already permitted by law.

To reiterate, connecting systems does not mean data will be exposed. On the contrary, data will be better protected. Experts also see data integration as a way to enhance data security. When data is distributed, or even scattered, across multiple siloed systems, redundancy can result in inaccurate information being shared without the knowledge of the individual concerned.
We need to stop relying on a patchwork of systems that, in Quebec and elsewhere, are unfortunately quite outdated. The government is not trying to take control; it is proposing a partnership.

I want to speak directly to my colleagues from Quebec: Health care falls under provincial and territorial jurisdiction, and this bill respects that. It acts as a safety net where similar legislative measures do not exist. Quebec already has a well-developed interoperability regime, and common standards will be clarified in consultation with the provinces and territories.

We are not starting from scratch on this. Federal, provincial and territorial governments are already working together to develop a pan-Canadian interoperability road map, and Bill S‑5 does not seek to supplant that. Its purpose is to support, assist and accelerate the process.

There is also a real economic benefit. Adopting common standards reduces barriers to entry and enables Canadian digital health companies to grow, innovate and compete. Greater competition can foster more modern and potentially less costly solutions for our public health systems.

As for my Conservative colleagues, I know they share our commitment to improving the quality of data in order to make better-informed decisions. Bill S-5 is an essential step toward that objective. Let us be clear: The bill does not require anyone to adopt a single system, nor does it replace the tools that are already in use. It requires them to communicate and exchange information with one another. That approach is simpler, more flexible and more respectful of what each province has already built.

For me, this is a matter of fairness, first and foremost. When information does not follow the patient, it is always the same people who bear the consequences: seniors who are seeing multiple specialists; families living in rural and remote communities; and newcomers, including many in my own community. For a family in a rural or remote community, an electronic prescription, a referral to a specialist sent in a matter of seconds or a remote consultation with the correct medical records to hand can save them hours of driving, days of waiting and a great deal of worry.

In closing, let me go back to the mother from Montreal North who went to the emergency room in the middle of the night. Thanks to Bill S‑5, she will no longer have to be the system's memory. The doctor will have the information they need and her son will receive safer, faster and better coordinated care. Data saves lives and so does integration.

The Senate has carefully studied this bill. In the House, all the parties are saying that they want modern care. We need to ensure that we have the means to achieve our ambitions. Let us work together to pass Bill S‑5 quickly.
Madam Speaker, my colleague gave a good description of how the Liberals have allowed our health care system to fall behind.

Medical associations have been calling for these changes for 10 years. In 2022, Canada's Competition Bureau also highlighted the problems associated with electronic health records. However, the Liberals let Bill C‑72 die on the Order Paper when they called the election last year.
I am glad they are finally taking action, but why did they wait so long?
Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for her very pertinent question. I am also very enthusiastic about this bill and am delighted to hear that she supports it.
To answer her question, I would simply say that we no longer want medical records to be sent by fax. We want to modernize. We share the same objectives.

As for the delays, whether they were caused by an election or by other circumstances, we share her frustration and want to see this work advance. As I said earlier, there are several provincial or territorial laws and regulations. As my colleague mentioned, Bill S-5 seeks to speed up the process. That is our government's intention.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Maggie Chi (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Health, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, what really resonated with me is what my colleague and friend said about breaking down silos and creating the condition for connected care. That is exactly what this bill is aiming to do.

My colleague mentioned that in Quebec, there is already a system in place for that, so I want to ask him to describe the benefits he is already seeing in his community and the benefits he wishes to see once we have a connected system across the country.
Madam Speaker, I would like to begin by thanking the parliamentary secretary for her question and for her work both in government and in her wonderful riding.

The first thing I can say about Quebec is that it has already proven itself. It has done its job. Bill S‑5 takes nothing away from Quebec. As I said earlier, its purpose is to assist, support and accelerate the work.

Here is an example: A mother in my riding, Bourassa, goes in with an envelope or a bag containing information that she cannot make sense of. Imagine what it must be like for a doctor to go through that information compared to looking at a file that is available directly to them. Obviously, reading it that way is not the same; the jargon is not the same. We want to make that information accessible. The goal is to save time and provide more direct services to people, to patients, because most of the time should be spent with them, and that is where the greatest impact can be made.

Madam Speaker, I think there is a reasonable expectation among Canadians that their health data should move with them. I am from Saskatchewan. If I had a health incident here in Ontario, I would want to know that it would be very easy for my health data to be readily available to whoever is providing the service that I needed in that particular moment.

I think it is important that it be up to the individual, in a sense, to decide where that data is available, so I wonder if the member has any ideas, with the bill, on how to make the individual, not so much a company and maybe not even a regional authority, the ultimate person to say that, yes, they want their health data to be available, either across the country or in certain provinces.
Madam Speaker, what I am hearing is that we share the same objectives. That is really very important.

Health data belong to the patient's own continuum of care. They should not belong to a vendor or to anyone else. This is what we are trying to do, and it is very important that my colleagues opposite know about it. If health care professionals have less paperwork to do, then they will have more time to spend caring for their patients. That is very important.

There may be criticisms from certain organizations. That is normal. It is part of our job to listen to them, but this should not in any way interfere with measures that we want to put in place. This is the solution that we have all agreed on to give everyone access to this data. This is really about integrating health data.
Madam Speaker, I will be splitting my time.

This bill is very easy for the people of Nanaimo—Ladysmith to associate with. To be diagnosed with a chronic illness in Nanaimo—Ladysmith really is to find out how transportation works in British Columbia, because we inevitably need to receive treatment not only in Nanaimo but also in Victoria, in Vancouver or sometimes in other places on the island. We know very well what the consequences are of medical information not being available where we receive our medical care. Those consequences include misdiagnoses, non-diagnoses, wrong medication and lower quality of care as a result.

The reason we need to receive health care all over the island and the mainland, and in some cases why we need to go to other places in our community, is that the Nanaimo Regional General Hospital, which is the main hospital in Nanaimo and the area, has about 345 hospital beds. However, I cannot remember a day when the number of patients in the hospital, when I have been there either visiting someone or for another reason, has been below 400.

This means that we travel for health care, and we know what happens when our medical records are not available. We understand the problems that come with needing to stop, find information and have it faxed over from one place to another. In B.C., in fact, we have more than 40 different electronic medical record systems, which are used across health authorities, specialists and family practices. We understand the consequences when those systems do not talk to each other.
The BC College of Family Physicians reports that more than 78% of doctors use between two and five systems. Believe it or not, that is actually by design, and it puts our lives in danger.

What this bill deals with is a phenomenon known in the health care world as “data blocking”. The minister admitted and said in her speech this morning that 92% of doctors in Canada have said that a lack of access to patient medical records hampers their ability to provide care. Health Canada has reported that only 29% of primary care providers share patient information electronically outside of their practice. That is one of the reasons the Canadian Medical Association and other medical health organizations have been calling for a decade or more for electronic medical records to be available where and when health care providers need them.

Dr. Margot Burnell, who is a previous Canadian Medical Association president, has described this as doctors facing “an uphill battle trying to provide timely patient care when they are routinely dealing with health systems that cannot communicate with each other”. That makes this bill a very long time coming. In fact, it is not the government's first attempt to bring this forward. Bill C-72 died on the Order Paper in the last Parliament because the Liberals decided that it was more important for them to go to an election.

We ask two questions on this side of the House. The first question is, what took the government so long? Why has it taken this long to bring in a bill that Canadians so badly need and that has been called for by patient advocates, by medical professionals and by patients? The other question is, why did it take the government 18 months to introduce this bill in the House when this bill so clearly needs to be implemented to save lives?

The next question we need to ask about a bill like this when it is being brought forward by the government is, what do we need to do to make sure it will get this right? We cannot afford another software debacle or failure in this particular case. We cannot afford for Canadians' medical records to become unavailable or get scrambled the way we have seen with so many other programs the government has tried to implement in the software space. Whether it is PrescribeIT, Cúram, or some of the other problems that we have had, we cannot afford to see that happen in this space.

In that context, it is distressing to have learned from the Senate's testimony here, and I believe my colleague recounted this earlier, that the government is considering hiring Canada Health InfoWay to administer this particular program. That is a situation where, given the management issues and health care issues with that organization, specifically those related to health care software in the past, Canadians may have some very reasonable concerns.

A second issue that I really believe we need to deal with at committee is a number of definitional concerns. The idea of contextual interoperability can mean different things in different circumstances. We must ensure that the data that travels in between systems, when the software interoperability is implemented, is seamless, is not another data dump, is readable on the other end and is usable.

Similarly, we need to ensure that there are clear definitions for terms such as “data blocking”, “good enforcement mechanisms”, and “real remedies for failure”. The Competition Bureau pointed out in 2022, which is another reason why we are asking why this is taking so long, that electronic medical record vendors were, in fact, blocking data deliberately. This bill is now targeting those problems, including vendor lock-in, data blocking and the unreadable data dumps I just discussed, so it is very important that the bill expand the information-blocking penalties to include hospital networks and authorities that sit outside of these systems and may further hamper interoperability.

The Senate committee on this bill recognized that vendors are only one part of a wider health data system and recommended that the government consider extending responsibility as I have described. I would recommend that the House committee that examines this bill take a look at that gap, because software can only make the record available. Someone still has to complete the referral, the transfer, and get it to the clinician who is taking over care.

Privacy is also something that needs a very precise answer with respect to this bill. Section 5 of the bill says that the interoperability duty does not require access, use or exchange where privacy law prohibits it, but clause 6's data-blocking prohibition has no equivalent expressed privacy law exception. I would note here that the Office of the Privacy Commissioner supports interoperability, but recommends that the ban be subject to privacy law. Therefore, the committee should examine and close that gap where appropriate so that a vendor is not treated as blocking information for refusing an exchange the law, in fact, forbids.
There is also a need to ensure that compliance costs are not so high as to prevent entry by new providers.

What I would say in closing, is that Bill S-5 would not build the tower that Nanaimo needs. It would not add the staff beds or the cath lab we need north of the Malahat. I will continue to advocate for those things both here in Ottawa and with provincial decision-makers in Victoria. However, this is a good start. I hope we will see the committee do good things with this bill and that it will come back to the House in a format we can support.

Mr. Speaker, I want to commend our colleague for her speech. She obviously demonstrated her deep experience and knowledge of how a modern health care system should work, including in her community. It is very clear from what she has said that she really believes in the value of health data to provide better services to Canadians in her community in particular.
Does she have practical experience with respect to the ways in which access to data can improve quality of care and perhaps even save lives?

Mr. Speaker, as the member knows, one of the things that happens in our offices on a regular basis is that people contact us with the experiences they have had with the health care system. As MPs, it is very frustrating for us, because we want to help, but health care delivery is something that is up to the provinces.

Like my colleague, I have heard many stories of parents taking kids to hospitals and finding out that nobody can remember what the medication is and the records are not available. There are also circumstances where seniors who may have dementia or other issues are taken to the hospital by care providers and are not able to provide a full medical health record. Hopefully, this is something this bill would work to address using a federal power in the background.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to recognize that health information technology is all about the patient. For many years, we talked about information from patients and how it contributes to the betterment of health conditions. This legislation would actually save lives. It would improve the conditions.

I am wondering if the member can provide her thoughts on the principle of the legislation. I understand there are some concerns with it, but does she support the principle of the legislation to the degree that she would vote in favour of it going to committee?

Mr. Speaker, I think I explained in some detail in my speech why I do support the objectives of this legislation and why it is particularly important in communities like ours, where the federal government has not provided enough health care infrastructure and health care support to be able to have access to those records when we have to travel between cities to receive care. On the principle side of things, I wonder what took the government so long. In terms of the operation, it is really important that, in committee, we make sure to get the provisions right so we do not have another Liberal health software boondoggle on our hands.

Mr. Speaker, again, I am going to recognize that what we are talking about is doctors, hospitals, institutions and pharmacists, all of which have records. Some provinces are much further advanced than other provinces. I think of the province of Ontario or of Quebec compared to my home province. Having legislation of this nature is ultimately in the best interest of all patients in all regions of the country.
I would like to get the member's thoughts on that issue.

Mr. Speaker, I think we all know that sound travels more slowly than light, so sometimes it takes Ottawa longer to hear the needs of British Columbians. We are looking forward to seeing a time when those records are portable. I cannot say it more clearly than that. Let us get this right, though. Let us get it right, because it would save lives.
Mr. Speaker, today, I rise on behalf of the great people of Edmonton Southeast to discuss Bill S-5, the connected care for Canadians act.

No Canadian needs reminding of the challenges facing our health care system. On this side of the House, we believe Canadians deserve timely, world-class health care when they need it, regardless of their financial circumstances, yet too many Canadians are waiting for a family doctor, a specialist appointment or a procedure that would allow them to return to work and live without pain. Canadians need better care. In many cases, their lives depend on it. While provinces and territories are responsible for delivering health care, the federal government has a responsibility to work constructively with them to improve access and support better outcomes.

Bill S-5 presents an opportunity to address one part of this challenge, the difficulty of sharing health information between the professionals responsible for a patient's care. The principle of this legislation is common sense. However, much more work is needed to ensure that this bill would deliver meaningful improvements for patients.

In Alberta, we know that a gap in communication can have serious consequences. In 2012, Greg Price died at just 31 years of age. A subsequent inquiry found that poor communication between providers and breaks in the continuity of care contributed to his death. His family has since worked to ensure that others learn from their tragic experience.

More recently, tragedy struck closer to home. Last December, Prashant Sreekumar, a 44-year-old father of three, died at Grey Nuns Community Hospital in Edmonton Southeast after he waited nearly eight hours to see a doctor for chest pain. These cases involved different circumstances, and we should be careful not to suggest that one piece of legislation could have prevented everything that went wrong, but these stories demonstrate why this issue is important.

When patients are referred to specialists, they should know whether their referral has been received and who is responsible for following up. When important test results become available, those results must reach the right professionals and therefore be acted upon. A patient dealing with a serious illness should not have to chase records and coordinate communication between medical offices. That responsibility should not fall on a family already worried about the health of someone they love.

Bill S-5 would require health information technology vendors to ensure their systems can communicate with one another. It would also prohibit data blocking, subject to regulations. Put simply, a patient's information should be able to follow them securely through their care. A commercial interest in keeping customers tied to one software system should not prevent the appropriate sharing of information needed to treat a patient. It is a practical goal that Conservatives support.

According to the Canadian Institute for Health Information, in 2024, only 68% of hip replacement and 61% of knee replacements were completed within the recommended six-month benchmark. Median waits for MRI scans were also 15 days longer than they were in 2019. These delays have consequences. For a person waiting for knee replacement, it may mean months of difficulty in walking, working or caring for their family. For someone waiting for a scan, it can mean prolonged uncertainty about a potentially serious condition.

Better information sharing can help prevent unnecessary repeat tests and the delay caused by missing records, but connecting computer systems will not on its own add more doctors or create additional surgical capacity. Canadians need a broader effort to improve access. The government must explain how this legislation will contribute to that work and how its results will be measured.

We must also consider the people delivering care. Doctors enter medicine to help patients, yet too much of their working time is consumed by unnecessary administrative tasks. A joint survey by the Canadian Medical Association and the Canadian Federation of Independent Business estimated that physicians in Canada spend nearly 20 million hours each year on unnecessary administrative work. Disconnected records are only one part of that burden, but that is a part we should address. When clinic staff repeatedly request the same records or a physician must enter information already held in another system, valuable time is lost. That time could be used to see patients.

The question is whether Bill S-5 would make that work easier. Would referrals become simpler to track? Would doctors spend less time searching for results? Would small clinics receive the training and support needed to adopt new systems? We cannot promise less paperwork while creating another complicated process for doctors to manage. Frontline professionals must be involved in developing these requirements.

Furthermore, Canadians must have confidence that their personal health information is protected. Health records contains some of the most sensitive details of a person's life, including their mental health history, prescriptions and diagnoses. Patients share that information because they trust their health care providers. That trust must be maintained.

Protecting confidential information must not be confused with improperly withholding it for commercial reasons. During the Senate committee review, stakeholders recommended baseline security requirements for vendors, including encryption, strong authentication and records of who accesses information. These recommendations deserve serious consideration. Doctors should not be expected to become cybersecurity experts to determine whether a vendor's product is adequately protected. Vendors must have clear responsibilities for maintaining safeguards, and patients need clear answers about how their information can be used and what happens if it is compromised.

Finally, much of this legislation would depend on regulations developed after it were passed. These regulations would address standards, enforcement and the legislation's application within provinces and territories, which may also require careful examination. Provinces, health care professionals and patients deserve clarity about what would be required, what it would cost and who would be accountable.

Conservatives believe in health care that delivers for its patients, but ultimately what Canadians need are shorter wait times, reliable follow-ups, seamless information transfers, and doctors who have more time to practise medicine rather than working on endless paperwork.

Mr. Speaker, this important bill would be a big step forward for the medical system throughout Canada. It seems that doctors still send faxes, which is basically the equivalent of stapling a piece of paper to the back of a dinosaur. It is kind of crazy how backward the health system can be in Canada.

Among the IT interoperability, prohibiting data blocking, protecting access to health information and supporting virtual care, I wonder if there are any specific provisions in the bill that the member opposite sees as being the most helpful for the constituents in his riding.

Mr. Speaker, one thing I appreciate about the bill is that it is not too lengthy, but that does not mean it answers all the questions. We want to send it to committee for review so additional loopholes can be looked at. As recommended by the Senate review committee, more work can be done on it so clarity can be found, the paperwork can be reduced and the process can be streamlined.
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise on behalf of Windsor West.

Given boondoggles such as the $300-million PrescribeIT scandal that we have faced, how much confidence does my colleague have that this legislation would be able to deliver anything of value to the Canadian taxpayer?

Mr. Speaker, that is a really serious question. Given the track record of the government over the last 11 years, a lot of boondoggles have happened that failed to deliver any results needed or promised by the government. However, that does not mean we should not look at the positive side of this bill.

The death of Greg Price is a reminder for the government that, after 14 years, we are still figuring out how we can streamline the process so miscommunication cannot happen and tragedies like his cannot happen again, or can be controlled. I believe we still need to look at the bill from a positive angle, and all the positive suggestions should also be welcomed by the government.

Mr. Speaker, the member for Edmonton Southeast mentioned in his great speech that the Canadian Medical Association estimates that some 20 million hours are spent on administrative work. I agree with the member that excessive administrative time is often wasted and should probably be spent in other ways. I am curious as to whether the member can comment on how many of those 20 million hours could potentially be reduced through Bill S-5.

Mr. Speaker, that is a more technical question that more statistical data could answer if the bill is adopted and royal assent is provided. However, before it gets to that stage, we still need to review how we could make this bill better so all these delays and the jargon could be avoided and streamlining could be established.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I am really encouraged by a number of the words the member has put on the record. I want to pick up on the point about saving lives. The legislation would do more than just save lives. It would also improve many people's current health conditions. Could the member expand on that point too?

Mr. Speaker, it is part of the bigger challenge. It is one step towards it. All the professionals' having access to a patient's records is the right step towards streamlining the medical process and the delays that are in the process.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Brendan Hanley (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern and Arctic Affairs, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I will be sharing my time with the member for Québec Centre.
I am pleased to speak today to Bill S-5, the connected care for Canadians act, and its role in supporting a more connected health system.

Bill S-5 may seem rather technical, and indeed it is. However, I cannot emphasize enough how important this bill is for patients, physicians and indeed all cadres of health care professionals, for caregivers and for the people responsible for the planning and administering of our health care systems.

What is the bill about? Well, Bill S-5 would advance connected care by mandating the adoption of common data standards for health information technologies used across Canada. It would also prohibit data blocking, the practice of restricting access to health information for authorized users such as providers and patients, when privacy laws would otherwise permit it.
In other words, Bill S-5 will allow for the secure sharing of health information between patients and their health care professionals at the time and place that it is needed.

Data that is reliable, accurate and accessible saves lives, and the standards established by this bill would help make that possible. Research shows that patients who have access to their health information are better able to participate in treatment decisions, identify potential errors and manage chronic conditions more effectively. Improved access to health information would also support the more than four million Canadians who serve as informal caregivers in Canada. Today these individuals often devote countless hours to tracking down test results, coordinating records and repeating medical histories on behalf of their loved ones, often while balancing their own work, family and responsibilities.

When patients and their caregivers do not have access to their complete medical records, they finds ways to compensate. They rely on memory, keep physical records, take screen shots and repeat their medical history to every health care provider that they see. Canadians do this because the system does not do it for them. These are creative and ingenious solutions, but they are also time-consuming and stressful and they can lead to misdiagnosis, delays in care or worse.

Thirteen per cent of Canadians say their care was negatively affected due to poor information sharing between providers. The consequences can be profound, even tragic. Indeed, according to a recent physician survey conducted by the Canadian Medical Association, 92% of physicians reported that disconnected health systems, such as the inability to share patient records, test results and clinical notes, affected their ability to provide care. Two-thirds of those physicians say this happens often, highlighting the extent to which the lack of interoperability shapes day-to-day clinical practice. When providers do not have access to a patient's complete health history, they are forced to make decisions without the full clinical picture. This increases the risk of delayed care, misdiagnosis, adverse drug interactions and unsafe treatments.

Bill S-5 would enable a seamless and secure exchange of patient health information to support better collaboration among health care providers. For example, a family physician could securely share a patient summary with a specialist, helping support more timely assessments and better continuity of care. The bill would also strengthen team-based primary care, where timely information sharing is foundational to the way care is delivered. Similarly, for Canadians living with complex or chronic conditions and seeing multiple providers across multiple points of care, connected systems are a necessity. This is indeed true for Yukoners, who in many cases are in touch with providers across different jurisdictions.

Harms resulting from disconnected care are especially high for people travelling in Canada, whether from northern, rural and remote communities, across provincial and territorial borders for treatment, or simply for work or vacation. For example, an elderly individual became ill while visiting family in another province. Although antiviral treatment was recommended, it could not be provided, because the lab result required to confirm eligibility for treatment was trapped in the patient's provincial digital health system.

One service provider explained that, at a hospital in a border region, patients admitted from a neighbouring province are often seriously ill. However, because the provincial health systems are not connected, patients typically arrive with photocopied and incomplete medical records.

When systems cannot communicate, the result can be duplicated tests, delays in care, unnecessary costs, and frustration for patients and families. Bill S-5 would help bridge these gaps by mandating the standards that enable information sharing across the health care system. Importantly, disconnected data puts health care providers in the position of having to make clinical decisions with incomplete information. Bill S-5 would help to address this by enabling health care providers to access their patients' complete health care information in order to provide safe, high-quality care.
The purpose of the bill is to improve patient safety. However, patients are not the only ones who stand to benefit. Bill S‑5 also offers significant benefits to our valued health care professionals.

Interoperable health systems can help reduce administrative burden associated with charting, forms, sick notes and tracking down test results. Today, valuable time is spent manually entering data and copying information from one system to another, instead of spending time with patients. Artificial intelligence is already supporting providers by reducing repetitive administrative tasks and improving access to information, and its use will only expand.

However, these tools depend on reliable and connected data systems. Bill S-5 would help establish the secure data foundation needed to support that progress. For example, studies have found that physicians spend an average of 86 minutes a day searching for patient data due to a lack of interoperability. Now, 20 million physician hours are wasted annually on unnecessary administrative tasks. This unsustainable level of administrative work can lead to burnout, fatigue and low job satisfaction. Results from the CMA's 2025 national physician health survey showed that 46% of physicians and residents report high-level burnout.

Providers also mentioned the personal distress associated with the fear of making clinical decisions based on incomplete information. This affects their mental health, self-confidence, and ability to provide safe care.

Dr. Ewan Affleck, a physician who has spent most of his career in the north and is a leading Canadian expert in digital health information, likens running a health system without connected data to flying blind, which, in his own experience, has cost patients their lives.

To address this crisis, we must transition to working with digital health information within systems that can connect with one another. This will ensure consistent data transfer and reduce errors, which will help health care professionals provide high-quality care and, ultimately, improve patient safety.

Bill S-5 would also support the broader use of digital tools that help patients connect with their providers, including secure platforms for booking appointments, requesting prescription refills and communicating with their care team.

Transformation of any system requires investment. Whatever the cost it takes, the cost of inaction is likely to be far greater than the cost to do this work. As it is, we are already paying a staggering price for disconnected health data, estimated up to $9.4 billion annually. Beyond the financial cost, the consequences I have talked about today can hardly be measured in dollars but in patient safety, quality of care and the well-being of the health care providers who support them.

Bill S-5 is a technical bill but its purpose is straightforward: to connect data to prevent patient harm. Canadians turn to the health care system seeking care and relief. I would encourage my fellow members to join me in supporting the bill so that all Canadians can receive safe health care that is informed by accurate data and is accessible wherever and whenever decisions are made.

Mr. Speaker, I completely agree that data sharing is going to prevent harm. I am curious about the data sovereignty aspect of this. What has the government proposed to ensure that Canadians' health care data remains sovereign and protected through the legislation?

Mr. Speaker, this is really all about supporting data sovereignty and interconnectivity at the same time that we support existing privacy protection. Authorized access remains governed by applicable privacy legislation. The bill is really about making information available when it is legally permitted to be shared and not expanding access beyond existing privacy rules. It is really helping to get that balance right, which is really all about data sovereignty.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague's speech clearly reflected the concerns of an excellent physician from Yukon. We had the opportunity to serve together on the Standing Committee on Health.

The bill gives the minister the discretion to impose her intentions by order in council. When the pan-Canadian interoperability road map was announced, Quebec indicated that it would not be moving in that direction, while remaining open to the possibility of sharing information.

In keeping with what the Minister of Health said this morning about being determined to respect Quebec's jurisdiction, would my colleague be open to adding a preamble specifying that Quebec remains in control of its health policies?
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question, and I acknowledge the work we have previously done together on the Standing Committee on Health.

It is important to recognize that the territories and provinces remain responsible for delivering health care. Bill S-5 does not change anything. It sets common standards enabling different systems to communicate with one another. The goal is not to impose federal control, but rather to ensure that health care professionals have access to the information they need to safely care for patients.

Mr. Speaker, I have the benefit of being a member of Parliament in an urban riding, where I do hear about concerns around health data. Could the member talk a bit more about the Yukon, which represents a lot of rural and more disconnected communities?
What kind of impact would Bill S-5 have for members of his community in the Yukon?

Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned throughout my speech, Bill S-5 is particularly relevant for more remote and northern rural settings, because so much of the health care depends on the interconnectivity of communities to referral centres. For example, Whitehorse hospital is the referral centre for the territory. It receives a lot of patients and a lot of calls from around the communities, but we also access care in British Columbia, in Alberta and sometimes in other jurisdictions. I cannot tell the House how many times I hear, either personally through my former career or from colleagues, about how the lack of interchangeability of data has affected patient care. I am really looking forward to the implementation of this bill and the subsequent actual interoperability of health systems.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and speak to the House on Bill S‑5, the connected care for Canadians act, and on the collaborative approach that we intend to use to implement it.

I would like to remind the House that the bill's objective is to establish a connected health care system, in other words, a system that provides fast, easy, reliable and secure access to health information for the people who need it.

To ensure fast, secure access, Bill S‑5 requires health information technology vendors to adopt technical and data-related standards and establish clear rules that prevent data blocking. By prohibiting harmful data-blocking practices, this bill will pave the way for health data networking, which offers considerable benefits for patients and professionals, not to mention its social, economic and, obviously, health benefits.

Data saves lives, and it also has the power to transform our health care system. However, our current health care system remains siloed, fragmenting care and putting patients at risk. As a result, 13% of Canadians say that the quality of their care has been compromised by a lack of communication between providers, and 8% report poorer health outcomes because their care team could not access the health information they needed. This situation obviously puts patients' lives and health at risk.

This becomes even more problematic when patients need to seek care in other provinces or territories. Take, for example, patients who rely on cross-border care, such as a truck driver with a chronic illness whose work takes him across provincial borders, a student at an educational institution outside their home province or even just a person who lives in either Gatineau or Ottawa and wants to receive treatment in one province or the other.

Canadians can experience real harm when their health care providers do not have timely access to the information that they need. A lack of connected data exposes patients to increased risks, including misdiagnosis, medication errors, delays in treatment and unsafe procedures. Health care providers regularly express frustration at being unable to access lab reports and results when they need them. Reliable access to this type of information is essential across the country so that health care providers are fully aware of a patient's medical situation when making urgent and often delicate clinical decisions.

This bill also supports research and innovation, which, as we know, lead to new treatments and which will obviously stimulate economic growth in a sector with a very bright future. That is why interoperability is not just about technology. It is a strategic issue that will make the health care system fairer, improve access and enhance its quality and viability.

As part of our efforts to improve access to health data and the sharing and use of such data, the Canadian government is working with the provinces, territories and key stakeholders to move forward and to implement pan-Canadian interoperability. Significant progress has been made to date.

The federal, provincial and territorial governments are working together, and have been for quite some time now, to implement a shared road map. Progress has already been made in Nova Scotia with the One Person One Record initiative and in New Brunswick with MyHealthNB. These collaborative efforts have improved patients' access to their health information, among other things.

However, the progress that has been made at the national level has been variable and inconsistent, and voluntary approaches have their limits. That is why it is essential to pass a law to help the provinces and territories, where appropriate, to harmonize the enforcement of standards and prevent data blocking so that everyone can benefit from health data interoperability.

To fully realize the benefits of interoperability, Bill S‑5 will be implemented and operationalized through regulations that will require health information technology vendors to meet a set of data sharing standards; prevent data blocking, which is the practice of preventing authorized users like patients and health care providers from accessing health data when they need it; and establish a system of administrative monetary penalties to ensure compliance.

These regulations will be developed in close co-operation with provinces, territories, indigenous partners, health care system stakeholders, vendors and patients to support a practical and co-ordinated implementation approach that takes Canadians' needs into account and supports interoperability across the country.

In developing this legislation, we looked at examples from other countries with similar approaches. The lessons learned, connections made and discussions carried out with the United States and some members of the European Union focused on the importance of adopting consistent standards and prohibiting data blocking. Based on the experience of these countries, voluntary approaches alone are insufficient to achieve widespread and effective interoperability, underscoring the need for clear legislative and regulatory requirements for these technologies and these companies.

The law will also serve as a safety net in provinces and territories that do not have similar legislation in place. Provinces and territories will have ample time to harmonize their own laws with the objectives of the federal framework, if necessary and if they deem it appropriate.

In closing, one important lesson to be learned from the health care system as a whole in 2026 is clear: Digital systems that are disconnected from one another pose a threat to the health and safety of all Canadians.

I believe that once implemented, Bill S-5 will save lives, improve the quality of care, reduce health care costs, and, more generally, make the work of health care professionals easier across the country.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague mentioned a piece on Canadian innovation. I would like his comments on how we are going to ensure through this legislation that we do not add red tape and barriers to smaller entrepreneurs, inadvertently creating a market where only the big players can play and smaller innovators cannot compete.

Mr. Speaker, that is an excellent question. Data blocking is bad for at least two groups of partners we really need to support and invest in in our health care sector. First, it is bad for researchers who complain, including in Quebec, about data inaccessibility that prevents the development of new technology and connections across health care professionals. It is obviously very bad for patients. Second, it is bad for small businesses that would like to develop software and technologies to compete with bigger businesses. If there is no interoperability, the data controlled by bigger businesses cannot be accessed by smaller businesses, which prevents smaller businesses from competing in this area.

Mr. Speaker, we are talking about connecting sensitive data from coast to coast to coast. My colleague concluded his remarks by saying that if the systems were disconnected, it would pose a threat to patients' health.

How did his government ensure the necessary cybersecurity measures were in place to prevent an attack on an interconnected system, a cyber-attack like the one we saw in July, in which autonomous artificial intelligence agents attacked Hugging Face without human intervention?
Mr. Speaker, my colleague is right to emphasize the importance of security in data sharing. His remarks were very eloquent.

We also need to recognize the importance of making the data accessible across Canada. For example, I could get sick on a trip to Edmonton. If the doctor who cares for me in Edmonton is unable to access important personal data to save my life, that is a problem for me.

I could be a student in Gatineau who lives in Ottawa. I could get sick in Gatineau and may have to be moved to a hospital in Ottawa to be able to access my medical data so that the doctor can treat me. That is a waste of time, and it could also put my health at risk.
Connectivity to support nationwide data sharing is also very important.
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague for his great speech.

I know he has previously served as health minister, and I am rather curious to know whether, when he held that position, he had any discussions with provincial and territorial ministers to gauge the level of interest in this interoperability.
Could he also talk about how this interoperability might improve the quality of health care services in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to point out that my colleague herself has also served as health minister and that she contributed to moving this program forward. I tried, to the best of my ability, to follow her example and continue to push it ahead. Indeed, the bill was nearly finished when I was in the post. Things have changed since then.
The good news is that the new Minister of Health is very committed to moving it forward, and rightly so.

The provinces and territories have consistently emphasized the importance of working with the Canadian government because big tech operates across several provinces at once. It is easier, as a country, with the provinces and the Canadian government working together, to put enough pressure on those companies to ensure they do not block the data that is important to patients.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Dan Albas (Okanagan Lake West—South Kelowna, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the member for his intervention today, particularly given that in 2022, when he was minister of health, there was an agreement between John Horgan and Justin Trudeau for health-sharing information. I asked the then minister for some information about privacy, and his office did send a response. I could read it one way, or I could flip it around and read it a different way, so it was good political communication.
Why do we still have the problem in this country that health records cannot be shared between provinces securely?

Mr. Speaker, since I have to be very brief, I will thank the member for his continuous advocacy. He knows there has been progress over the years, but he also knows really well that we need more progress in order to support all provinces and territories, regardless of where Canadians live, in their ability to access and benefit from the health data that is so important to them.

Mr. Speaker, I think there is broad agreement in this place about the problem this bill is trying to address. Canadians should be able to access their own health information, and when they seek care, the people treating them should be able to get the information they need securely and with the appropriate privacy protections.

I support interoperability. In fact, I have spoken about this in the House before. In the previous Parliament, the former member for Cypress Hills—Grasslands brought forward Bill C-294. It dealt with the Copyright Act and interoperability, and it eventually became law. I congratulate that member, and I spoke in favour of it at the time.

The example I used in that debate was pretty straightforward. It was about a farmer who could own a tractor or combine and buy an implement made by a different manufacturer. It could hook up just fine. Mechanically, there would be no reason it should not work, but technological protection measures could prevent the two pieces of equipment from communicating with each other.

I said at the time, “real competition pits products and services against one another, rewarding innovation and productivity, not copyright and exclusivity.” I also said that the right to interoperability was critical for consumers. I stand by that. I still believe it today. However, health care is obviously different and considerably more complicated.

I want to be very clear: I believe in the importance of interoperability. Canadians should be able to access their personal medical information, and health care professionals should be able to get the information they need to care for their patients safely and with respect for privacy.

However, we need to make a distinction: Making software interoperable and making our health care system truly interoperable are two different things. I have some concerns in this regard about this bill.

Bill S-5 is principally about health information technology vendors. It would require the technology covered by the legislation to be interoperable according to established requirements, and it would prohibit data blocking by vendors. Those sound like very reasonable objectives to me. If a vendor is deliberately preventing health information from moving simply to keep a customer locked into its ecosystem, there is a legitimate role for Parliament, but I think we need to be careful about what happens next.

Canada does not just have one health system. We have provincial health care systems, and within those systems, there are health authorities, hospitals, laboratories, primary care providers and other organizations that have brought in different technologies at different times under different contracts to do different things. Some of those systems are relatively new; some are not. Some communicate reasonably well, and some require people to find workarounds just to move fairly basic information. If there were one health care system, one purchaser and one set of specifications, establishing common technical requirements might be simpler, but there is not.

I do not think the answer is to turn the federal government into the health care technology purchaser for the entire country, although I am sure there are some members on the opposite side who would enjoy that. Health care is principally administered and delivered by the provinces, like it or not. The federal government needs to respect that.

I will be fair about the legislation. There are provisions in the bill that recognize that reality. The federal requirements would not simply apply uniformly, regardless of what a province or territory is already doing. The bill would provide a mechanism that takes into account whether a province or territory has a substantially similar or stronger requirement.

I think that is completely sensible, but it also points to a larger problem. The federal government does not run the health care system. I hope we can all agree on that. Some Canadians might reasonably respond that they are not entirely convinced the provinces are running it either. We have seen in Nova Scotia and, more recently, in my home province of British Columbia that the Conservatives of those provinces actively ran for and won majority governments despite the old logic that Conservatives cannot speak to health care issues and only run away.

In my home province, there are wait times at the ER, that is if it is actually open. I heard from the daughter of 90-year-old woman that her mother had been kept in the hallway of the Kelowna General Hospital ER for days. She was literally unable to sleep with all the incoming patients, and the first responders and health care professionals trying to do their job while her mother was waiting for a bed.

Constitutionally and practically, the provinces administer and deliver health care regardless of how badly. They are dealing with hospitals, health authorities, physicians and procurement decisions, and much of the information is already in place. Therefore, I think this House should ask a fairly basic question: Why should we assume that the federal government knows best when it comes to procuring and implementing complex information technology when its own record does not exactly inspire confidence?

Let me give an example. We all remember ArriveCAN. The Auditor General of Canada could not even determine exactly what the application cost because the government's financial records and controls were so poor. She estimated the cost at approximately $59.5 million. She found that federal organizers repeatedly failed to follow good management practices in contracting, development and implementation, and concluded that the application did not deliver the best value for the taxpayer dollars spent. That deserves some reflection.

The federal government is now entering into another debate involving sophisticated information technology and procurement, yet in the case of ArriveCAN, or arrive scam depending on who we talk to, the Auditor General of Canada could not even establish the precise cost of the government's own application because the records were inadequate. That is not an ideological argument, but the Auditor General's finding.

Then we come to PrescribeIT. This example is arguably even more relevant because it was a health information technology project. The objective was straightforward. It is 2026; why are we still sending prescriptions around by fax? The goal of PrescribeIT was to move prescriptions electronically from prescribers to pharmacies. According to public reporting, more than $250 million was spent on PrescribeIT since 2017, yet fewer than 5% of Canadian prescriptions were being transmitted through the system. The centrally operated service ended this year after Canada Health Infoway concluded that national adoption had not been reached to the scale necessary for long-term sustainability. The organization has moved toward an open national e-prescribing standard instead. Let us think about that for a moment. The problem was not that no one could figure out how to make an electronic prescription. They could. The difficult part was getting a complicated health care system to use it. Adoption mattered. Existing information systems mattered. Costs, I would hope, mattered. Provincial participation absolutely mattered. The day-to-day practices of doctors and pharmacists mattered. Implementation mattered. ArriveCAN could teach us something about federal procurement. PrescribeIT should teach us something about health care technology implementation. Both should give the Liberal government a warning to show a little humility.

I am not saying the federal government has no role here. It does. Preventing genuine data blocking can be a legitimate federal role. Working with provinces on common technical standards makes sense. Removing legitimate federal barriers makes sense. The federal government can certainly demand results when it is spending taxpayer money. However, the Liberals on the government benches should be very careful about assuming that because they can pass a law about interoperability, they therefore know how to procure, integrate and operate health information systems better than the people delivering the care. Writing requirements in Ottawa is considerably easier than making technology work on the ground, and Canadians have paid enough money over the years to understand the difference.

I have been thinking of all of this because of two conversations I had on my Finding Solutions podcast. One was with Dr. Stuart Edmonds of the Canadian Cancer Society. We were talking about clinical trials and why they matter to cancer patients. I think most Canadians understand generally what a clinical trial is, but it looks rather different when we think about it from the perspective of somebody who has cancer and may be running out of treatment options. There may be a clinical trial available for that person, but somebody has to know that patient exists. They have to know what kind of cancer that person has. They have to know what treatments have already been tried. They may need pathology results, diagnostic information or other testing. Then they have to determine whether that patient might qualify for the trial. At that point, interoperability stops being a debate about software and becomes a question of whether the right information can get to the right people when it matters. With cancer, I do not think I have to tell members, time matters.

I had another conversation on finding solutions with Louise Binder, a long-time patient advocate working with the Save Your Skin Foundation. We talked about the postal code lottery in cancer care. We talked about clinical trials, access to new medicines, families travelling to receive treatment and what that all means for someone who is already dealing with a serious illness. We discussed this legislation on interoperable health information and the importance of a care team being able to see the full picture of the patient. That, to me, is the most persuasive case for what the government is trying to accomplish.

A cancer patient should not have to become the human interface between computer systems that cannot communicate. If someone from my communities in the Okanagan has to go to Vancouver for specialized treatment, that person should not have to reconstruct their medical history every time they encounter another part of the health care system. If someone has to travel to another province for care, that gets even harder. The relevant health information should not simply disappear because people cross the provincial boundary. The technology should work for the patient. The patient should not have to work for the technology to work.

I want to come back to the patient, because this law should exist for them. If I am a cancer patient, I do not care which company developed the software used in my hospital. I do not care what government bought the system. I want to know whether my doctor has the information he needs to treat me. That is all. If I need to go to another region or another province to obtain care, I want important information to follow me.
I therefore support interoperability. That said, passing an interoperability act and creating a truly interoperable health care system are two different things.

The government itself says that only 29% of health care providers share electronic information securely and seamlessly outside their offices. Obviously, that is not good enough, but that statistic also raises an uncomfortable question. We have been talking about digital health in Canada for years. We have spent money, billions of dollars. We have developed strategies. We have established organizations. We have announced initiatives. We have negotiated funding agreements. Where are the results?

This is not an argument against doing more. It is an argument for understanding why what we have already done has not produced the results Canadians reasonably expected. It comes down to this old political trap. There is a problem, something must be done and this is something. Therefore, we must do this. That does not mean Bill S-5 is inherently bad legislation. It means Parliament should not confuse legislative activity with health care results. Passing a bill is relatively easy. Writing regulations can be done. Holding a press conference can certainly be done. We know because we see it almost every day with the government.

However, the difficult work comes after that. How does this work with the systems provinces already purchased? What happens to older systems? How much will it cost to make them compatible? What happens when standards change? What happens when one institution is capable of exchanging the information, but another is not? What happens when the barrier is not the vendor? What happens when the problem is an existing contract, an institutional practice, a procurement decision made 10 years ago or simply an old system that is too expensive to replace? Those are not reasons to abandon interoperability. They are reasons to be honest about what this legislation can and cannot accomplish.

The federal government has a role to play, but having a role to play does not mean playing all the roles. The provinces administer their health care systems. They know their facilities. They make their own procurement decisions. They are responsible for delivering care. Ottawa can remove certain obstacles. The federal government can work with the provinces to establish common standards. It can prevent unwarranted data blocking. When it spends taxpayers' money, it can certainly demand results. However, a national standard cannot replace co-operation. Federal legislation alone cannot solve all the problems that exist in our health care systems.

There is another contrast that I think is worth considering. The federal government already knows how to sit down with provinces and reach agreements on specific health outcomes. The federal government has agreements with British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and the Yukon, covering a range of diabetes medications and contraception. Those are agreements with provinces and territories, yet there are only four. It seems to me that the government is pivoting away from the kind of approach that costs money and instead trying to find another problem to solve.

Interoperability, as I said, is a problem, but is that the best use of everyone's time? We need to start asking whether or not the Liberal government is seeking results or if it is just seeking to have announcements. I think the same approach should guide interoperability. What do I actually want to know about this bill?
First, would it stop vendors from blocking information that would legitimately be available? If it does, good.

Second, would these standards actually work with systems that provinces and health care providers already have? Telling everyone that tomorrow's technology must comply does not necessarily fix the equipment and the software that were purchased five or 10 years ago.
Third, how would the government work with provinces, not consult them so that someone can put a check mark beside consultation, but actually work with them?

Finally, what would the patient notice? Can they access their information? Can their doctor get the information they need? If I live in the Okanagan and go to Vancouver for treatment, can the professionals treating me see the relevant records? If I end up in an emergency room somewhere else in the country, what happens then? If I have cancer and possibly qualify for a clinical trial, will the information needed to identify that opportunity actually be available? Those are the questions I care about.

Frankly, I am less interested in whether a technology vendor can tell the federal government that it has complied with the regulation. I just want to know whether the thing actually works. Do not come back to Parliament in two years and tell us how many meetings were held. Do not tell us how many vendors submitted compliance paperwork. Do not tell us how many pages of regulations were published. Tell us what happened to the patient.

That is how we should measure success. Can patients access that information? Can doctors? If a patient moves away, can their information follow them? If a treatment or clinical trial is available, can the necessary information be accessed in a timely fashion?
Results are what matters. I do not just want to know if software is interoperable on paper. I want to know if the system works in real life.

I would just mention an incident that I had an occasion to ask a former minister of health about. In 2022, the prime minister at the time, the premier of my province, John Horgan, and the health minister, who is still a member today, reached an agreement on health care information sharing. Billions of dollars were announced. Now, that was four years ago and what has changed? Zip.

What I am saying to the government here is that it can make announcements and spend money, but that does not necessarily mean the job gets done. It should start to listen to the people who know the systems, start to put them in charge of the job and make sure that it is seen not only as an announceable, but a deliverable, and make sure the government is behind that.

After speaking with people such as Dr. Stuart Edmonds and Louise Binder, I see a case for this bill in health care very clearly, but we have learned enough from previous digital health projects and, frankly, from federal IT procurement more generally, to know that passing legislation is the easy part. Making it work is the hard part.
Let us make sure that doctors are not relying on faxes. Let us make sure that the government relies on facts. Let us not confuse passing the law with solving the problem.

Patients do not need another announcement about interoperability; they need a system that works. When a physician has to make an important decision, they should have access to the right information at the right time. Patients should not have to act as a go-between for two computer systems that cannot communicate with one another. That is the outcome we should be working toward.
Ultimately, this is not about databases. This is about people. I ask the government to really focus on the people more than the data and not to focus on the announcements, but on the actual results.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I genuinely believe that Bill S-5, and what the Minister of Health talked about when she introduced the legislation, is all about the patients. It is all about delivering for patients. It recognizes that health information technology has to play a critical role.

I agree with the member that there has to be a high sense of co-operation. Passing the legislation would not necessarily make it happen on its own. We would need to have the provinces and territories buy in. We have seen that some provinces are further ahead than others.

Would the member not agree that no matter what level of government we talk about, if everyone agrees to the principle of putting the patient first, we should be able to have a better system that would serve those patients?

Mr. Speaker, I talked a little about the agreement that John Horgan, Justin Trudeau and the former minister concluded. It was for over $26 billion, over a 10-year period, to solve the very basic problem of not being able to access health records in another province. I asked the former minister what was still blocking that. It is not for a lack of money or a lack of consensus. It is implementation.

The member can say, “We're all about interoperability. We're all about data privacy and sharing of information.” That is great. I can say bravo. Good on them. However, if it does not happen, if that minister is pulling a lever that goes nowhere, it is all talk. That is a point that the Liberal government could probably learn from.

Mr. Speaker, before I ask my question, I want to wish my good friend Dr. Sandeep Sharma, one of the top plastic surgeons in India and past president of the Indian Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons, a happy birthday in advance.

We have seen this movie before. PrescribeIT was supposed to modernize prescription management, but the service ultimately had to shut down. The Minister of Health has consistently and steadfastly avoided questions on PrescribeIT.

Would my colleague agree that before the government embarks on another ambitious digital health initiative, Canadians deserve to know what went wrong, what the cost of that boondoggle was and why the legislation would work this time around?

Mr. Speaker, I really appreciate the member and his intervention. I think it comes down to one thing. It is really easy to pass legislation that forces other entities, in this case companies, usually very large organizations, to comply with particular standards. Again, whether they actually do it or not, they can send in the paperwork required and say they meet all of the requirements under the interoperability provisions of Bill S-5. That is there.

However, it is different when the rule-maker now has to be the person to deliver. That seems to be where the Liberal government continues to slide. It is like a vacuum that money, good intentions, announcements, meetings, everything gets thrown into, but nothing ever seems to come out. That is what I think Conservatives are opposed to.
I want to thank my colleague for his speech, which I listened to with great interest.
I would like to commend my colleague, who spoke in both official languages.

I want to talk a little about data blocking and ask the member opposite whether he believes the banning of data blocking is a good thing. We have seen some very serious instances, in his province and in mine, of companies refusing to let the data be used and refusing to let it exit the electronic systems because they are hanging onto it to monetize it. I wonder if the member thinks it is a good thing that the Government of Canada would put an end to that with Bill S-5.
Mr. Speaker, if monetizing Canadians' information was important to the government, it would be doing it right across the board.

When I walk, Apple owns my health data. When I spend, my bank owns that particular data. That is the problem here, that the government only tries to pick and choose when it believes there is something politically popular. As I said, in the case of this particular bill, it seems the government wants to do something on health care, so it has landed on something that is germane and, I think, everyone agrees with. Another member of Parliament brought up the issue of interoperability in the agricultural sector.

I think what we need to do more than anything is what the Australians considered, which is the equivalent of a royal commission, where they did intense hearings. I have read through some of their books. They are so far ahead when it comes to the issues of data, monetization, personal privacy and the efficiencies that can be given when consumers are empowered with their own information. There is so much that can be done. I hope the member pushes the government to do more on those things.

Mr. Speaker, if this bill is about putting patients first, why does the government not establish clear consequences and penalties when health care technology companies fail to protect or properly share Canadians' medical information?
