Mr. Speaker, that is a tough but fair question, and one for which I must show respect to the member. I affectionately call him the sheriff because of his previous career in law enforcement, during which he served his community ably.

I would simply say that we can have a rule, but if we do not have consequences, then people are not going to respect the law. The sheriff is absolutely right. There needs to be more. This is why we should get it to committee, and it is why that member, I hope, will be pushing for those penalties to be clarified.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to pick up on one of the member's comments on the whole idea of technology, because I really do agree with it. We have to ensure that technology works for people and not the reverse, in terms of having access. I will get the opportunity to expand upon that shortly, but I wanted to amplify just how important it is, in recognizing Bill S-5, that the primary focus is on patients in using technology.
The member seems to imply that he supports the legislation in principle and wants to see it go to committee. Does he believe it is something that could be passed before Christmas?

Mr. Speaker, I would encourage the member to speak to the hon. Minister of Transport, who in addition to being a part-time minister of that portfolio is also the government House leader. He would probably have a better read on where things are going.

All joking aside, I did not get to address this in my speech, but if we look at Europe, if we look at the United States, that is where most of these companies come from, and really, that is where the big money is spent. I do not know whether Canada would see significant compliance from those companies. I certainly hope those companies would look to do this. I just hope, though, it would not slow the adoption of new technologies as they come out, because, again, differing standards in different regions create a de facto trade barrier whether the government wants to admit it or not. I am hopeful that this bill would be helpful, but let us just say it is not unconditionally positive in all respects.
Mr. Speaker, I will be sharing my time today with the member for Winnipeg North.

When I was a health system and academic leader, we used to talk about having two jobs in health care. First was taking care of the patient of today. To do that work, obviously, we need access to the health data across a patient's journey, no matter where they are in the health care system. We also talked about having a second patient, the patient of tomorrow, and that is the work of supporting research, quality improvement and health system innovation.

Bill S-5 is a critical piece of legislation that would allow us to care for both the patient of today and the patient of tomorrow, and that is why I am proud to rise in the House today to speak in support of it.

All over Canada today, people are going to visit their family doctors. They are going to be talking about their mental health. They are going to be talking about their diabetes and their blood pressure control. They are going to be talking about their cancer journeys. They are going to be getting immunizations, prescriptions and requisitions for medical imaging. They might be getting a referral to a specialist. They might be referred for counselling or for physiotherapy. In pretty much every one of those family doctor's offices today, they are going to find their family doctor sitting and typing away on a computer, generating tasks for the physician or the health care worker and for the patient.

If a referral is made, the doctor is going to be typing away, generating forms inside that computer, and if that patient then goes to see a specialist, they are going to find the specialist sitting at their desk taking notes on a computer. If they end up in an emergency situation and have to go to the hospital, all the notes, the test results and the imaging results are going to be stored in an electronic record.

In my community of downtown Toronto, those places, the family doctor's office, the hospital, the emergency department and the specialist's office, might be just a few subway stops away from each other. Sometimes they are even in the same building, so one could forgive a patient for assuming those computers are talking to each other. However, it turns out that all too often, that is not the case. People could be forgiven for asking why, in a set of single-payer health systems across the country in any given province or territory, the data generated in the hospital, the data generated in the doctor's office and the data generated in the home care interface are sitting in separate silos, not talking to each other.

Bill S-5 seeks to remedy that. By requiring the vendors of the electronic systems we use in our health systems every day to meet interoperability standards and putting an end to data blocking, wherein vendors hold onto the data of Canadians under the mistaken view that they own the data about the health of our people, as opposed to the patient and the health system as a public good, we would be putting in place the necessary infrastructure for a modern health care system across the country.

It used to be that in order for electronic systems to talk to each other in a health care system, they had to actually be on the same system. I am pleased that this is no longer the case. We do not need all of Canada to be using a single electronic health record for data to flow in the ways that patients need, because technology has leapfrogged that requirement. When vendors meet those interoperability standards referred to in this bill, the data would be able to move in order for us to take better care of people. The hospital and the clinic would be able to securely share information that is relevant to the care of the patient.
To emphasize the importance of this bill, one need only quote the preamble:

Quote.QuotePara: the health information of Canadians is not easily accessible to them or to their health care professionals, which puts the safety of Canadians at risk;

Content.ParaText: There is broad consensus among stakeholders that the interoperability between health technologies and health information systems, as well as a prohibition of data blocking, are necessary to ensure patient health and safety, improve health outcomes and promote equitable care for Canadians.

For patients to make informed decisions about their own health, they must have easy, comprehensive and secure access to their health information. Their health care professionals and researchers must also have access to it.
Why does this bill matter? Why do we need health records to be interoperable, and why do we need health data to be treated as a public good?

I want to speak to primary use and secondary use and begin by talking about the delivery of clinical care and access to one's own records. We have covered well in the House today in this debate the necessity of interoperability of health records for patient safety in terms of clinicians being able to access critical information when a person comes in for care, so I want to focus my remarks on the two other critical aspects. First is the ability of Canadians to access their own health records. Second is the ability to use the data for research, quality improvement and system oversight.

The pan-Canadian OurCare consultations, led by Dr. Tara Kiran and an incredible national team of researchers and experts in public engagement and primary care, had conversations with hundreds of people living across Canada to understand what Canadians wanted from a better primary care system. In their conversations, a core refrain arose again and again: People in Canada are frustrated that they do not have access to their own medical information. People shared how not having access to their own medical records made it challenging to get the care they need when they had an emergency, when they moved to a different province, when their doctor moved or retired, when they did not have a doctor or when they were just trying to advocate for themselves or for their loved ones.

Through the OurCare consultations, people in Canada spoke clearly and consistently. They want access to their own health records online in a format they can share with clinicians and loved ones and where they can have confidence that the information will be kept private and secure, which is not a very radical or unusual idea. Countries around the world have already given people access to their own health records through an app, like the Nordic countries, for example, but also Estonia, Spain, Portugal, France, England and Australia, just to name a few.

As we look to build national infrastructure and to become more self-reliant as a country and as we look to create the conditions for our country to thrive in the years to come, we need to invest in the most foundational of assets: the health of our people. Bill S-5 would open the door for people being able to access their own health records by ensuring that their data would be liberated from the vendors who may be holding on to it.

That brings me to secondary use and the patient of tomorrow. This is an aspect of data interoperability we should not neglect, because beyond the care of individual people, we need health data to do quality improvement, to do groundbreaking research, to engage in health system oversight and to develop artificial intelligence and apply it to the biggest problems facing the health of Canadians.

This is what we call secondary use of data, because health data is the raw material for improving care. Research and quality improvement teams use data to track people's health outcomes over time, to measure the impact of our interventions and to ask important questions that will lead to the next generation of breakthroughs.

Health data also contains the stories of important inequities and outcomes across the country. It helps us to understand whether people living in rural communities, people experiencing homelessness, indigenous people, Black Canadians and other groups are getting the care they deserve. This information can then drive our investments and programs as a government, but to understand the story, we need the data. Our superb Canadian researchers and health system leaders cannot do their jobs without it, and if it is being blocked sitting inside a vendor's records, we are going to be in trouble.

Finally, I want to say a few words about artificial intelligence. We are obviously at a new frontier. If we want to use AI to reduce wait times in emergency departments or wait times for specialist care, and if we want to use AI to improve the quality of care being provided to seniors in long-term care, to cancer patients in our cancer centres or to children in our family doctors' offices, we are going to need data and the data will need to be linked in order for us to do it.

Bill S-5 would regulate vendors. It would require them to play ball in ensuring that data can be shared across our health systems. Once the data is unblocked and interoperable, a lot of work still remains to be done. This bill would not replace the work ahead on sovereignty, commercialization, data export approaches and indigenous data sovereignty, all of which have been flagged by our colleagues in the Senate, but it would lay the foundation for all those things. Bill S-5 would lay the foundation for us to care for the patient of today and tomorrow. I am proud to support it.
Mr. Speaker, I can sense the passion in my colleague's voice. I want to thank her for her over two decades' worth of service as a family physician.
She knows first-hand where the system breaks down. If she could fix one particular thing in this bill, what would it be and how would it help regular Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, in my colleague's riding today, as in mine, there are family physicians like my colleagues who are spending an inordinate amount of time chasing results, trying to figure out what happened to their patient when they were admitted to the hospital and what changes were made to their medications, and calling the pharmacy to try to figure out what occurred. This bill would lay a foundation. It would open the door for the kind of information data flow that is truly necessary to fix these problems. A lot of work would have to happen after that. The bill would not magically fix everything, but if we do not pass it, we will not have the infrastructure necessary to address these important issues.
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for her service for two decades. She knows exactly about one patient, one data.

Can my colleague tell us how the bill would reduce barriers to care? Also, we heard that there is workforce pressure. How would it be more helpful for the patient and reduce the burden of administrative work?

Mr. Speaker, I think we all know that the barriers for health care workers in the system today are considerable. There is a lot that artificial intelligence, for example, can do to improve the productivity of our health systems and reduce administrative burdens on our health care providers, whether they are a home care worker in a home, a PSW in long-term care or a nurse practitioner in primary care. AI can help all those people spend their time taking care of patients instead of running around trying to access information. It can reduce the administrative burden, whether it is from filling out forms or getting appointments for patients. However, all of that requires that the data be accessible, that it be linked and interoperable and that it not be blocked by the vendors of electronic medical records and electronic health records. That is why this bill would make a difference for the workers in our health systems across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I agree wholeheartedly that data transfer between departments and interchangeability are extremely important to help reduce harm in Canada. One thing the member mentioned in her speech is that the bill would lay the foundation for data transferability within Canada, but it would not complete the conversation on data sovereignty. How can we lay the foundation for data transfer but not at the same time lay the foundation for data sovereignty? If we are not doing that, are we not be putting health data in Canada at risk?

Mr. Speaker, it will be critical, in order to do this work, for the data to flow. The data needs to be linked so that across different parts of the health care system, we can follow a patient's journey over time. Once that occurs at the technical level, we have to figure out how we will govern the data, how we will make sure that privacy is protected and how we will ensure that the data is available to the people who need to use it and have permission to use it, but not misused by others, whether that would happen through the regulations coming out of this bill or, more likely, at the level of the health systems as people work through this over time. Right now, people across Canada doing health care leadership cannot even begin those conversations because they cannot access the data because it is being blocked. This is a necessary step on the journey to health system transformation across Canada.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise and speak to Bill S-5 today. If we take a look at information nowadays, it has never been easier to access. It has become critically important that when we take a look at our health care system, we look at ways in which we can improve upon it.

I want to reflect on some of the days, going as far back as when I was the health care critic in the province of Manitoba, when I was meeting with patients and stakeholders. Even back then, they were talking about information gathered on behalf of clients or patients and how that information is retained and ultimately shared.

I remember that when I had to change my family doctor, as my first one made the decision to retire, I was given a yellow envelope to bring to my new doctor. A year ago or so, when I was with my family doctor inside the checkup room, he was sitting at a computer, which I could watch. It was truly amazing how he was able to connect my health care needs through the computer. I did not have to get a prescription issued from the doctor or a piece of paper. Rather, he told me that I could go to X place and that my prescription would be ready.

When I take a look at what Bill S-5 is all about, it is all about patients, whether directly or indirectly. That is why I would like to think that all members of the House will see the value of supporting the legislation.

I have listened to members opposite all morning talk about the concerns they have, and I am not going to marginalize their concerns. I suspect that all members have some concerns as we move into this area. It is a very challenging area; there is no doubt about it. Someone mentioned that while we could bring in legislation, it would not guarantee that the system is going to work and the patient is going to benefit. There are jurisdictional issues. To individuals who are genuinely concerned about the issue of which level of government is responsible for what, I will say that instead of that being the primary concern, the primary concern should be the patient.

If we view this through that lens, I believe we will see more co-operation taking place among institutions, private companies, non-profit companies and the different levels of government, if we are prepared to do what the minister has made very clear. In her statement, she talked about working with provincial and territorial jurisdictions and indigenous communities.

At the end of the day, information does matter. What takes place in our doctors' offices, our hospitals, our care facilities and our pharmacies really does matter, as does a person's ability to go into a facility, whatever type of facility it might be, and have a sense that a health care provider has access to the information that is so very important for that patient. If that were to be done right, where we get collaboration and get all systems onside moving in one direction, with the priority being the patient, we would see less duplication.

People would understand the differences in medications that might be being taken at one end versus at the other end. Some testing may not have to take place, or in some cases testing would take place, such as an x-ray, a lab test or whatever it might be. The different types of medications an individual takes throughout the year would be known. These are all important pieces of information. In working collaboratively with other jurisdictions, I would argue, as I said at the outset, and putting the lens on the patient, it is the patient who would benefit with the passage of Bill S-5.

I had the opportunity to ask members opposite some questions regarding the principle of the legislation. I am encouraged by the Minister of Health and the government's agenda to get this legislation through with fantastic support from the Senate of Canada. I am pleased with the general approach of the opposition, as the principle of the legislation appears to have been accepted. That being said, I suspect there might be a number of issues, based on what I have heard, that would come up at the committee stage.

I am sure there would be representation at the committee stage about issues related to things such as data blocking, which has been talked about a great deal. Data blocking is done far too often. Because of a vested interest, information is being retained by one vendor for reasons I will not go into today, but much of it would be driven by the dollar. Data blocking would be directly dealt with in this legislation, which is a very good thing.

Then there are interoperable issues. For example, in the province of Manitoba, there might be a care facility using a different technology system from what is being used at the Health Sciences Centre. Because of that, it is the patient who loses the most. That is one of the reasons the compatibility of technologies is so important in the legislation. The data would be able to be transferred. We hear a great deal about data, records and so forth, and it is important for us to recognize that with regard to data and technology, the government is very concerned with ensuring that privacy is respected. As we know, Canadians are very concerned about the issue of privacy, and understandably so.

Some provinces are further advanced than others, and I recognize that, but as we roll this out, what would end up happening is that the quality of health care services would improve for all Canadians. The health care worker, be it a nurse or a doctor, would have better opportunity to provide bedside care or to provide consultation, as a direct result of moving forward with Bill S-5. That is not to mention, as some have already pointed out, that it would also save lives.

Someone asked why it is taking us as long as it is. I think it is important to recognize that we have a very substantial legislative agenda. In the last 18 months, we have been pushing forward on a series of legislative initiatives. This bill is an important piece to it, because our health care matters in Canada. Canadians want us—
Questions and comments, the hon. member for Kitchener Centre.

Mr. Speaker, one thing in particular the member opposite said that I would like to concentrate on is that we have to look at this through the lens of the patient. I wholeheartedly agree with that, and the lens I am going to look through is data security. If this is implemented across Canada in partnership of course with the provinces, how would we ensure that, first, it would still be the patient who would decide whether the data is going to be transferred, and, second, how would that data be protected?

Mr. Speaker, the member, in posing the questions, highlighted something I had indicated. If everyone would do exactly what she did with respect to her question, which is to put the patient first and look at it through that lens, I suspect that the debate would be well served not only on the floor of the House of Commons but also in committee. I can assure the member that it does not matter what side of the House one looks at. I believe every member wants to ensure the privacy and protection of data. There is no doubt whatsoever in my mind on that.

Mr. Speaker, the member for Winnipeg North has often oversimplified things in the past, but I found it especially interesting today when he said that people should care more about patients than about jurisdictions.

If my colleague were consistent and really cared about patients, he would not accept that his party is making cuts to health transfers, and he would not accept this disgraceful situation where, year after year, the federal government underfunds health care. Right now, the federal government is barely covering 22% of health care costs. If the member really cares about patients, then he should try to convince his government to be less stingy when it comes to health care funding.

Mr. Speaker, there is a long story with respect to health care transfers. We could go back many decades to when the provinces and the federal government made the decision that they wanted some change in tax points to the provinces in favour of having direct cash going to them. I was never a big fan of that. I believe that the federal government needs to not only have a strong, healthy Canada Health Act but also to maintain a basic level of health transfers. That is something the government, under the Prime Minister, has committed to do.

In addition to that, I would recognize that the Prime Minister came up with a $5-billion fund to build Canada's capital health infrastructure. I look forward to those health care dollars' being spent across the country.

Mr. Speaker, I just learned that the member for Winnipeg North is a former Manitoba health critic. His comments on a stronger collaboration are well noted. However, I wonder if my colleague can elaborate a bit more on data blocking and vested interests. Why is data blocking important?

Mr. Speaker, the simple reason is that often data blocking is not done in the interests of the patient but in the interests of some vendor that has a vested interest, and often that vested interest is driven by money. Whether it is the Prime Minister or any member of the Liberal caucus, what we are saying is that we need to put the patient first. If we put the patient first, we will have a better, stronger and healthier health care system.
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise on behalf of Kitchener Centre to speak to this really important issue.

I think we can all agree that every Canadian should be able to access quality health care when they need it, without waiting and regardless of where they live and what they earn. Unfortunately, that is not the reality of our current health care system. Canadians are struggling to find a family doctor. They are waiting months if not years to see specialists. They join long wait lists for surgeries and imaging. Emergency rooms are overcrowded, and patients spend hours waiting even to be assessed. For too many Canadians, the challenge is simply accessing health care. While we can all agree that our health care system is worth protecting, it cannot mean defending something that is failing too many Canadians.

Canadian taxpayers spend an enormous amount of money on their own health care. Taxpayers will spend $57 billion in 2026-27, and Canadians are still left waiting for proper care for their investment. Do members know that Canada ranks last among 10 similar countries with respect to timely access to health care? Only one in four Canadians gets an appointment with a doctor or nurse the day they need it. Most Canadians wait two months or longer to see a specialist.

We have to ask ourselves how we can make our system work better. It is not just about how much money we put into health care. It is about its effectiveness. How do we support health care professionals, and how do we improve the outcomes for all Canadians?

Let us imagine that somebody from Kitchener decides to travel across this beautiful country to Alberta. Maybe they are visiting family, enjoying a family vacation or travelling for work. Then, unexpectedly, they have a heart attack. They are taken to the ER, and the doctors treating them need to know their medical history, such as what medications they are taking, if they have any allergies, if they have had any previous surgeries or if there are any underlying issues or conditions that could affect their treatment. The patient is lucky enough to have a family doctor in Ontario, but their medical records are not in the same system as Alberta's, and the hospital cannot access them.

What happens now? The patient literally cannot provide their health information if they have had a heart attack. They cannot give their history. They cannot give their allergies or the pertinent information the doctors may need in that exact moment. The doctors now are spending time trying to access the patient's information instead of immediately caring for them. Tests may be needed or repeated, and information is not available. All this is happening while the individual is not getting the care they need. Would it not make more sense if the patient's medical information could just follow them so surgeons would immediately be able to operate on them, potentially saving lives?

A colleague just shared a story with me. A man and his wife were travelling across the country, and they got in a car accident. Because of that car accident, the gentleman needed immediate surgery, and his wife was unconscious. Right on the roadside, penicillin was administered to the man during the operation, but unfortunately he was allergic to the penicillin and passed away. Data transfer can literally save lives in this country.

We have already invested in medical records across this country. More than 95% of physicians use electronic medical records today, but that is not the same as having a connected system. A doctor might have a patient's entire medical history on their computer, but if the doctor treating them next door does not have that same information, we have a problem. Only 29% of primary care providers make patient information available outside their own practice. Only a quarter of practitioners make that information available outside that practice. This leaves 75% of the population without records that can be immediately accessed so patients can get immediate care in the times they need it.

This costs Canadian taxpayers an extra $9.4 billion a year. Let us think about that. Billions of dollars are being lost because the information that already exists on a system somewhere is not being accessed by someone right next door. Patients are undergoing repeat tests. Health care professionals are spending extra time tracking down records. Important information is being missed when patients move between providers.

Doctors, nurses, pharmacists and other health care professionals should be spending their time caring for patients, and that is it. They should not be spending their time trying to access information that already exists on another system. It is a complete waste of, first, the physician's time and, second, the immediate access to care for patients who immediately need it. Not having to chase down medical records or repeat work that has already been done would only help the care of patients here in Canada. We should be giving physicians the tools they need to do their jobs, not making their jobs more difficult by repeatedly investigating the care that a particular person may need.

There is a tremendous opportunity with the bill, but there are a lot of questions behind the scenes. We do need to make sure that the details are right with this piece of legislation, because Canadians need to be able to access their own data, and we do need actual improvements for Canadians. This cannot just be another measure where we are saying that we are going to be doing something in Parliament but not actually working with the provinces and territories to make sure that it is implemented across Canada.
We have questions that we need to ask, and as we move forward, we will ensure that we ask these questions in committee.

Provinces and territories are responsible for their own health care systems. As the federal government, we need to respect the role of the provinces. We should be working with them to make sure that health information can be shared across provinces in a way that all provinces agree with. We have to ensure that we are not going to be encroaching on provincial territory when we are trying to implement a system to access care across systems. This is a key important piece of this legislation that we need to look at.

We need to understand how the bill would work with the systems that are already in place and make sure provinces still have a say in how these changes are made. We know that different practitioners use different systems, so what does that mean for the current systems that practitioners are already using? Are they going to be able to keep these systems or are they going to need to move to a different system? None of these questions have any answers to them yet, and these are the things we are going to look at.
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to recognize the 55th anniversary of Boeing Winnipeg, located in my riding of Winnipeg West.

Established in 1971 with just 57 employees building Boeing 747 components, Boeing Winnipeg has grown through five major expansions into Canada's largest aerospace composite manufacturing facility. Today, nearly 1,500 skilled workers operate across its 700,000 square foot facility, producing critical components for Boeing commercial aircraft, including the 787 Dreamliner, as well as the P-8 Poseidon, Canada's next multi-mission aircraft.

With an extensive local supplier network and a recent $36-million investment supporting research, development and robotics, alongside its contributions to STEM education and veterans' opportunities, Boeing Winnipeg remains an important anchor of Manitoba's aerospace sector.
Please join me in congratulating Boeing Winnipeg and, most importantly, its dedicated workforce, on 55 years of innovation, excellence and contributions to our community and economy.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Clifford Small (Coast of Bays—Central—Notre Dame, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, families and seniors across Coast of Bays—Central—Notre Dame are working hard and doing their best to live within their means, yet they are struggling to make ends meet.

The Liberal Prime Minister promised Canadians affordability, but the reality is that we have higher costs and growing financial pressure on households. In Newfoundland and Labrador, food security affects more than one in four residents. Food bank usage across our province has increased by 44% since 2019. These are not just statistics. These numbers represent real people making impossible choices between groceries, heating their homes and putting fuel in their vehicles.

As Liberals prepare to table their budget, Canadians deserve action, not more spending and debt. The government needs to cut waste and restore fiscal responsibility, instead of spending and making more debt. The government needs to eliminate all taxes on gas and diesel. It is high time that the Prime Minister lives up to the expectations of those who voted for him—
The hon. member for Hochelaga—Rosemont-Est.
Mr. Speaker, I want to take members on a trip down memory lane.

In 1926, seven visionary and determined women founded BPW Montréal, a business and professional women's network. For the past 100 years, BPW Montréal has played an important role in advancing gender equality and promoting women's professional development.

To the many CEOs and dedicated board members who have served the organization over the past century, congratulations on this remarkable milestone. While some are no longer with us and are watching over us today, I am certain they would be immensely proud of all that has been accomplished.
To the tireless, the passionate, the go-getters: Your contributions have left an indelible mark on the organization as we celebrate it today.
My colleagues and I have great admiration for all that has been achieved, and we fully appreciate the strength and collective power of women.
I wish BPW Montréal a very happy centenary.

Mr. Speaker, as we begin Veterans' Week and we approach Remembrance Day, I had the privilege of co-hosting a reception this afternoon for the Royal Canadian Air Force Foundation under the leadership of Jeremy Diamond.

When Canadians think of veterans, minds can often drift to historical black and white photos. We remain deeply appreciative of the freedoms that they fought for, but there are also heroes who walk among us today. They are our neighbours, parents of young children and colleagues that we work with, and they bore heavy burdens in modern conflicts like Afghanistan, the Gulf, and many other missions.

By supporting modern veterans and inspiring tomorrow's aviation leaders, the Royal Canadian Air Force Foundation bridges our history with our future through STEM scholarships, with recipients joining us today, including Anjana Ramaswamy, Clare Balkissoon, Arabella Allen, Nehsy Poinen, Declan McCloskey, Virajdeep Rattan, Lucy Levy and Vincent Bujold-Roux.
Let us stand united behind our veterans, past and present, and remember that a life of service is the only life worth living.
Mr. Speaker, I rise to mourn Eric Bauza, Scarborough's very own Emmy Award-winning voice actor.

Eric attended St. John Henry Newman Catholic High School in my riding of Scarborough Southwest, and from those hallways he went on to become the voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and many other beloved characters. A proud Filipino Canadian, Eric broke barriers in an industry where very few look like him, inspiring young people across our communities. During the pandemic, he joined our virtual New Year's celebration, bringing laughter and joy when we needed it the most.
I want to quote Eric's parting message from his high school yearbook: “Well, b4 I go, I'd like 2 say thanx 2 every1 who thought I was funny, & if I ever do b-come famous, party at my house!”
I call on the members of the House to join me in offering our deepest condolences to Eric's family and loved ones. Eric's legacy lives on through the laughter that he gave to this world.
Mr. Speaker, as we begin Veterans' Week, I rise to pay tribute to World War II veteran Margaret Heinmiller.

Marg passed away this week at the age of 101. Born in Berkshire, England, she came to Canada at the age of four, and when World War II broke out, she was determined to serve. She joined the Royal Canadian Navy, the senior service, as she was quick to tell us, and almost joined the air force. Like so many of her great generation, when Marg's service in uniform ended, her service to the community continued. She was the first woman to join the Listowel Legion in 1947 and was the first woman president of the Palmerston Legion.
Even at 101 years old, Marg was quick with a witty joke, often delivered while on one of her daily walks down Main Street in Palmerston. Our hearts are with Marg's family and loved ones.
On behalf of a grateful nation, Bravo Zulu, Marg. I thank you for your service.

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessTitle: Service de police de la Ville de Montréal

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, since June, certain facts have been coming to light about the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal. A team at station 39 was disbanded, allegations of racist acts were made, and evidence of domestic violence provided by a victim was allegedly destroyed.
On Monday, we learned that the police force had fired seven police officers. That response was necessary. However, for the riding of Bourassa, it is neither a finish line nor the end of the matter.

I am telling the police force that it needs to meet the moment. Montrealers are entitled to transparency and public accountability. I am thinking about the people who were affected, the families who were afraid and the police officers who had the integrity to break the silence.
I want to remind all of those people that they are not alone. In Canada, safety is not a privilege, dignity is not negotiable, and a person's background should not determine how they are treated.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of the 6,000 auto workers in Windsor-Essex at the Windsor assembly plant. Next week, these workers will be laid off by Stellantis, marking the fourth shutdown before Christmas.

The Liberal government has handed more than $6 billion to Stellantis, yet these workers are still without work. The government is also spending billions in foreign aid abroad and opening our market to state-subsidized Chinese EVs that compete with our own vehicles.

The Prime Minister promised a deal with the U.S. by 2025. Instead, families in Essex are losing faith because they are losing their jobs. No deal means no jobs. These workers are not asking for government handouts. They are asking to work and provide for their families.

The Liberal budget should put Canadian workers first, reduce foreign aid spending, stop opening our market to state-subsidized Chinese vehicles and take action to prevent Canada's auto industry from being hollowed out. Essex workers have paid the price for the government's failures for far too long.
Mr. Speaker, today I want to talk about a strong, larger-than-life man who has become a legend in the Canadian Armed Forces: Chief Warrant Officer Marco Côté.

This guy from back home began his military career in 1988 with Le Régiment du Saguenay. In 1999, he was selected to join Canada's elite special operations unit, where he served for more than 20 years.

Following the events of September 11, 2001, he was deployed to Afghanistan and was awarded the highest U.S. military honour, the Presidential Unit Citation. In 2003, he completed sniper training, and in 2010, he became the warrant officer in charge of the sniper team. In 2017, he was promoted to chief warrant officer and became the regimental sergeant major of the Canadian Special Operations Regiment.

It would take too long to list all the awards he has earned, but I can say that Marco Côté is an exceptional leader, capable of the greatest sacrifices and endowed with a talent and courage that would put Rambo and Chuck Norris to shame.
Mr. Côté, we are all very proud of you.
Mr. Speaker, it is a great honour to rise to honour the life of Patricia May Martyn, who passed away recently at the age of 86.

Married for 66 years to her best friend, Harold, together they raised four children, Paul, Linda, Anne and Karen. Karen, of course, is our former colleague, Karen Vecchio, who served the House so ably and with such great talent and dedication from 2015 through 2025.

Adored by her children, of course, her grandchildren and many great-grandchildren, Patricia May Martyn was an outstanding Canadian, someone who loved her community and her family. She is someone who will be deeply missed.
Our country is a great place, a great country for so many reasons, but it is unsung heroes like Patricia May who made it so. It is an honour to speak about her today. May she rest in peace.

Mr. Speaker, lobster season opens November 10 in southwest New Brunswick. Fishing families along the Bay of Fundy are ready to work, but many are worried about making ends meet. Before setting day, diesel is already up 50% in a year. It is made worse by the Liberals' clean fuel tax that adds 19¢ a litre to diesel and 15¢ a litre to gasoline. Every boat carries hundreds of lobster traps; they have now been hit with a Canadian tariff.

Our fishermen are literally paying their own government in Ottawa just to go to work. These men and women work hard, follow the rules and pay their taxes. They are the backbone of coastal communities. They work as hard as ever, pay more and fall further behind.

This is a story across Canada, worsened by 11 years of massive deficit spending. It is a government that spends well beyond its means and passes the costs to Canadians. The budget must cut taxes, stop inflationary money printing and end its wasteful spending. Canadians deserve nothing less.

Mr. Speaker, it is official. The Canadian Baseball League's top executive in 2026 is Hamilton's Eric Spearin. Fans packed into Bernie Arbour Stadium in Hamilton Mountain all season long to watch the Hamilton Cardinals play with a talent-packed roster. The Cardinals are among the city's oldest sports teams, but their last championship game was in 1978. For a long stretch, the team struggled until Eric Spearin became owner in 2022. His vision brought the team a real winning culture and, for the first time, the Cardinals were on top heading into the championship series.

The team's impact goes much deeper than winning ball games in Hamilton. When 80 children were suddenly left without a way to get to the Salvation Army summer camp, Eric Spearin dispatched the Cardinals team bus to make sure no one missed out. We are grateful and proud.
Congratulations to the Cardinals.

Mr. Speaker, after more than a decade of inflationary Liberal policies, Canadians are concerned with the direction our country is going. News of Canada's inflation rate rising is sad confirmation they have every reason to be. While the Prime Minister promised affordability, Canadians are watching the cost of housing, groceries, fuel, insurance, utilities and everyday living rise to increasingly unsustainable levels. Even though they are working full time at good-paying jobs, they are still struggling to afford necessities. Recent reports of increased food bank usage and people skipping meals because they cannot afford groceries are further confirmation of this sad reality.

The Prime Minister is out of touch, his spending is out of control and Canadians are out of money. In today's budget, Conservatives are calling on the Liberals to cut wasteful inflationary spending, keep their promised debt anchors and save Canadians money by reducing the cost of gas, groceries—
The hon. member for Vaudreuil.
Mr. Speaker, this Saturday, I will have the pleasure of marking the 10th anniversary of Mille et une huîtres, an oyster dinner fundraiser organized by the Fondation Paul-Leboeuf.

For 10 years now, this event has been bringing our community together to give children and adults with special needs a chance to enjoy adapted and inclusive camp experiences at the Centre Notre-Dame-de-Fatima. Thanks to the generosity of the attendees over the past decade, more than 20,000 camp days have been offered, supporting 1,398 campers with special needs and their families.

I would like to thank Steven Grenier, Guillaume Roberge, France Pomminville, and the entire team and board of directors for their hard work year after year, not to mention all the donors whose generous contributions continue to support this important work in our community of Vaudreuil.
May this extraordinary camp continue to thrive for years and decades to come.

Mr. Speaker, the budget will be tabled in less than two hours, and we, the Conservatives, want Canadians to have more money in their pockets. That is why we are proposing to eliminate gas taxes, which have a real impact on the cost of food and other goods, to reduce wasteful and inflationary spending and to save Canadians money at the pumps, at the grocery store and everywhere else.

For businesses, we want what they want: less bureaucracy. Incidentally, I commend the representative of the Association hôtelière de la région de Québec who came to Ottawa to highlight the hotel industry's contribution to Quebec's economic growth. Six hundred million dollars in spinoffs is good, but too much bureaucracy is not.

Although the Prime Minister, the prominent banker, promised affordability, everything has become more expensive since he took over. For the sake of all Canadians, we are hoping for a responsible budget.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Judy A. Sgro (Humber River—Black Creek, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I rise today to recognize an extraordinary member of our community, Danny Montesano, who will soon be honoured with the Ordine al Merito award by the National Congress of Italian-Canadians.

I have known Danny for decades and have seen first-hand his kindness, generosity and dedication to helping those around him. A respected business leader and successful entrepreneur, he has never lost sight of the importance of giving back. Through his long-standing record of charitable donations, including generous support for local hospitals and many other causes, Danny has made a meaningful difference in the lives of countless families across the community.

This recognition by the national congress is a testament to a lifetime of hard work, leadership and service. I extend my heartfelt congratulations from my family to his. To Danny, on this well-deserved honour, bravo.
I thank him for all that he does for our community.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, one in three Canadians are skipping meals because groceries are too expensive. The number one job of the budget is to save Canadians money.
Will this Prime Minister get rid of all of his 20¢-per-litre taxes on diesel and gasoline to help Canadians save money at the pump and at the grocery store?
With one in three Canadians skipping meals because they cannot afford groceries under this Prime Minister, job one for the budget is to save Canadians money.
Will he get rid of his 20¢-a-litre tax on gas, to save Canadians at the pump and at the grocery store?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, in a few hours, we will unveil the budget so that Canadians can become masters of our destiny, and therefore masters of their own destiny, through affordability, opportunities and, above all, sovereignty, so that we can live our lives as we choose.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister cooked the books on immigration. He either lost count of, or lost altogether, 300,000 people in this country. Last year, the Liberals announced a cut in levels, only to bring in two backdoor programs to sneak in thousands more. Therefore, the population is again growing and levels are again at historic pre-Trudeau levels, or higher than pre-Trudeau levels.
Will the Prime Minister cook the books again today to hide the number of people he is bringing in to profit big corporations with lower wages and higher rents?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition needs a little work on his maths. The population growth in Canada was the lowest rate in decades. This government has taken back control of immigration. The number of asylum seekers is down by 70%; temporary foreign workers, down by 60%; foreign students, down by 80%; and permanent residents, down by 100,000. In a few hours, they will see the next phase of that immigration platform.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, that is cooking the books. When they compare themselves to insanity, it is insanity. He is comparing the numbers to the Trudeau-era levels.

Let us compare them to the Conservative government. The asylum claimants backlog is up from 10,000 to 259,000, a 2,500% increase. The number of temporary foreign workers is up to 166,000 from 71,000, a 130% increase. The number of temporary residents is up 300% and he has 700,000 people here on work permits, even though there are thousands of youth who cannot find jobs.
Will he stop cooking the books, and put Canadians first?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I am not comparing myself to insanity. I am comparing myself to conspiracy.
We have taken back control of immigration. The number of non-permanent residents has slowed from over 7% to just above 5%. We believe in this country. We are building Canada strong.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the numbers I cited are from his government, so he must be in on it then. He cooked the books on immigration. He cooked the books on debt. He will stand up now and give fake and phony statistics on debt and deficit, but that is because he is dividing his expenditures onto not one, not two, but three different credit cards, using accounting rules that no one else in the world uses. If a company did it, they would be criminally charged for defrauding their shareholders.
The Parliamentary Budget Officer says that the Prime Minister will add $700 billion of new debt over the next five years. How much will Canadians pay?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we will see in a few hours how to manage the government's finances and the country's finances. We will see a government that is taking control of spending, that has slowed it from over 8% to less than 2%. We will see a government that is balancing the operational budget. We will see a government that knows how to invest in the future of this country because that is what Canadians want.
I understand the Leader of the Opposition, who has only ever torn things down, does not understand how to build things up at this time.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I will confess that I have no idea how to build up $733 billion of new debt, which is what he is planning to do, and it is going to the Liberal club.

The Prime Minister has attempted to distract using the Trump card to justify the 2.3 billion tax dollars he has given to Telesat, the company of his friend Dan Goldberg, but the excuse does not work, because Telesat is giving a billion of those dollars to Elon Musk's SpaceX for launch capabilities.
Has the Prime Minister ever discussed Telesat with his public servants, his ministers or his staff, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I have not been involved in any decisions related to contracts with Telesat or the financing of Telesat. Those decisions began with the Conservative government in 2007. They ran through the public procurement process.
The final decision was made by the Secretary of State for Defence Procurement. I had no knowledge of those decisions. I did not participate in those decisions. I am proud of Canada, however.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, how he chooses his words so very carefully. Earlier on, his government claimed he did not have any discussions about Telesat, and now he has deleted that word, just as he deleted mention of his friend and that company from a later edition of his book.

The company got the contract in August of this year, a decade after the Conservatives left office. Here is the question for the Prime Minister: Did he ever discuss Telesat with any public servant, any staff member or any minister, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I was not involved in any decisions related to that company—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
It is getting too loud.
The right hon. Prime Minister, from the start.

Mr. Speaker, I was not involved in any decisions related to that company, but if the Leader of the Opposition would like to learn something, he might want to read the national security strategy. He might want to recognize that one of the key determinants of this country's sovereignty, which this budget is going to help deliver, is control of space. We will build Canada strong in space.
Mr. Speaker, the National Women's Liberal Commission—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
I would ask the hon. member for Beloeil—Chambly to repeat his question from the top. We had to wait until the noise died down enough to hear him.
The hon. member for Beloeil—Chambly.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party's National Women's Liberal Commission submitted a brief that is strongly opposed to Bill C‑39. This group is the official women's wing of the Liberal Party of Canada. Among other things, they condemn the excessive and permanent powers that weaken environmental protections and consultations with indigenous peoples.
Will the Prime Minister listen to them, or will he claim that he alone makes all the decisions?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, what Quebeckers and Canadians want is to build this country with high standards. We will do that, and we can do that with Bill C‑39: one project, one review, one year, one stronger country.

Mr. Speaker, Magali Picard of the Fédération des travailleurs et travailleuses du Québec, the FTQ, has also spoken out against Bill C‑39. Ms. Picard criticized the Prime Minister for the provisions limiting the right to strike. She announced that the FTQ will challenge Bill C‑39 in court because it is unconstitutional and is the most restrictive anti-worker law in the G7. The Prime Minister previously asked Magali Picard to advise him on Canada-U.S. relations. I, for one, wish him good luck.
Will he listen to Ms. Picard, or will he ask her to pipe down?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I have a great deal of respect for Ms. Picard. I listen to all of Ms. Picard's advice. I listen to what she has to say about the bargaining process between workers and corporations. The best agreements are reached at the bargaining table. That is the objective of the amendments to Bill C‑39. We will maintain high standards when it comes to unions and bargaining.

Mr. Speaker, the chief of the Assembly of First Nations, Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, has criticized Bill C-39, saying that it violates the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. We are hearing the same thing from the Native Women's Association of Canada, which has also expressed concerns about the environmental impacts of the bill and the potential repercussions for women. Except for the government members, no one really agrees with Bill C-39.
Will the Prime Minister also tell indigenous peoples to keep quiet?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, last week, I had a big meeting with all of the first nations chiefs and most of the provincial and territorial premiers. We had discussions about the need for projects here in Canada and about the importance of having real participation from indigenous and first nations partners, and that was with the agreement of Ms. Woodhouse Nepinak.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I asked the Prime Minister if he had ever talked to a minister, staff member or public servant about Telesat. He got very nervous. He refused to answer the question, and he talked in generalities about his budget—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
I would ask the member to start over.
It looks like they are all getting very nervous over there, Mr. Speaker.

Let us look at the reality. It is illegal under the Conflict of Interest Act, section 9, for the Prime Minister to in any way discuss matters that could favour the interests of a friend. Dan Goldberg is his friend of 20 years. The company got a $2.3-billion taxpayer-funded contract in August of this year, and contracts have exploded under the Prime Minister.
Again, did the Prime Minister ever discuss Telesat with a public servant, a minister or a staff member? Did he ever discuss Telesat, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as the leader well knows, because he is subject to the same rules, Canada has world-leading rules in terms of ethics, disclosure and compliance. Of course, we will always at all times comply with the legal provisions of the Conflict of Interest Act and other applicable laws. We have the most stringent rules in the world, and obviously every member on this side of the House spends a great deal of time devoted to complying with those regulations.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michael Chong (Wellington—Halton Hills North, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the government needs a serious fiscal anchor, less debt and a path to balanced budgets. That is what Kevin Lynch, former finance deputy minister and clerk—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
There's competing shouting from this side to that side and back. Let us keep the level of noise down so that we can hear the questions and answers. It is on both sides.
The hon. member for Wellington—Halton Hills North, from the beginning, please.

Mr. Speaker, the government needs a serious fiscal anchor, less debt and a path to a balanced budget. That is what Kevin Lynch, former deputy minister of finance and clerk, said today. It is what economist Chris Ragan said yesterday. It is what former finance official Don Drummond has been saying for months. The PBO has said that the interest on the national debt has doubled since 2021 to $60 billion a year, more than health care or defence.
Will the Prime Minister deliver a credible fiscal anchor in today's budget to reduce the debt and skyrocketing interest payments?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Wayne Long (Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, while the leader cannot master his own caucus, in a few hours we are going to table budget 2026, “Masters of our destiny”. We are going to build Canada. We are going to bring down barriers to investment. We are going to double non-U.S. exports. We are going to invest in major projects, in housing and in infrastructure. We will also do what they never do. We are going to make sure we look after the most vulnerable.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michael Chong (Wellington—Halton Hills North, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, borrowing costs are rising, growth is stagnating and risks are tilted to the downside. Canada's fiscal buffers are depleting, leaving us unable to deal with the next major crisis that the Prime Minister's own national security strategy says could be coming.

The government's fiscal anchors have done little to rein in government spending and borrowing, so will the Prime Minister ensure a credible fiscal anchor in his budget, and more importantly, will he ensure a full accounting in the budget so we do not have to learn about things at some future investment conference?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Wayne Long (Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, despite the fake rage, we have a plan to build our economy. The fundamentals of our economy are extremely strong: the best net debt to GDP in the G7, one of the strongest fiscal positions in the G7, wages outpacing inflation and a AAA credit rating.
Despite them wishing it is not so, we have a plan to build Canada strong. We are going to invest in our country and our economy.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals are masters of illusion. They say, “Look over here at the operating budget, but do not look over there, where we are taking on unprecedented levels of debt.” They say, “Look at the operating budget, but do not look over here, where we are hiding billions of dollars in Crown corporations.” They say, “Keep looking over here at the operating budget, not at the billions of dollars being relabelled into capital investments.”
Who is going to pay for all this debt and how?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives are so committed to their pessimistic world view that they cannot see past the paper that was handed to them in their lobby to read off these QP questions that are repetitive every single day and punching down the Canadian economy.

We are here to promote Canada. We are here to invest in Canada. That is exactly what our government is doing, supporting people with affordability measures, growing the industries of tomorrow and creating jobs for tens of thousands of Canadians. That is what we were elected to do. We will not apologize for being positive about the prospects of this country.
Mr. Speaker, there was a lot of shouting, but if you noticed, there was still no answer.

The Liberals are masters of fiscal illusion. They are hiding behind the net debt-to-GDP ratio so they can borrow even more. What they do not tell us is that that calculation subtracts Canadians' pensions, money that Canadians worked decades to save for retirement. That money is not for the finance minister to spend or borrow against.
When will they stop using Canadians' pensions to justify the amount of debt they are leaving for our children and our grandchildren?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is well known everywhere but the Conservative caucus that Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7. That is not an exaggeration. That is the IMF, a world rating agency. We have a AAA credit rating. We had the strongest second quarter growth in the G7. We have the lowest net debt-to-GDP ratio by far.

We are not compromising that fiscal position in strength. We are leveraging it to the hilt to get the best results for Canadians, to get returns for Canadians. Those dividends will be jobs for the future and higher-rising incomes.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians cannot afford another inflationary Liberal budget. Under the Liberals, millions of Canadians are lined up at food banks. According to a report from the Daily Bread Food Bank, 38% of food bank users are employed. That means even a paycheque no longer guarantees a full fridge under the government. While Canadians are working harder to get ahead, they keep falling further behind.
Will the Prime Minister end this inflationary spending in today's budget, or will Canadians keep paying the price?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Rebecca Chartrand (Minister of Northern and Arctic Affairs and Minister responsible for the Canadian Northern Economic Development Agency, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Manitoba is a powerhouse for aerospace, the third-largest in Canada, and the member opposite keeps voting against every measure to support it. Magellan and StandardAero are creating good jobs in Manitoba. We just invested $8.8 million in the University of Manitoba to support research and create jobs. These are all measures we are taking to support the work to grow the economy in Manitoba, and the member opposite keeps voting against them.
Mr. Speaker, in two hours, the prominent banker that is the Prime Minister will table his budget.
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
I will interrupt the member for a moment to call the House to order.
I invite the hon. member to start again so that we can hear what he has to say.

Mr. Speaker, in two hours, the Prime Minister will table yet another budget and become Canada's undisputed champion of deficits. That is less than two hours away. He will ensure that all Canadians are forced to pay more interest on the debt.
That is money that will not go toward supporting families. It is money that Canadians will send to the government instead of spending it on groceries, housing or everyday necessities.
Can the Prime Minister at least guarantee that his budget will reduce the deficits and cut costs, so that Canadians can finally save some money?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for the compliment he paid to the Prime Minister. He called him a prominent banker.
Canada has one of the strongest fiscal positions in the G7, the second-lowest net debt-to—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
Order.
Normally, it is the opposition that makes it impossible to hear the answers, but in this case, it is MPs from the minister's own party.
I will ask the minister to continue, although not from the beginning.
Mr. Speaker, I note that, in his question, he referred to taking money away from families.

They are experts at taking money away from families. For example, in his riding, Mégantic—L'Érable, $100 million is distributed to 24,000 children through the Canada child benefit. This has reduced child poverty by nearly 40%.
He voted against providing an average of $3,500 per child.

Mr. Speaker, while Quebeckers are struggling with the cost of living, the greedy oil companies continue to rake in record profits from the war in Iran. In nine months, Suncor made nearly $10 billion. That is more than it made in its best year ever. Its refining margin shot up 260%, which means that, yes, it is ordinary people who have been paying the price. The greedy oil companies are getting richer than ever at Quebeckers' expense.
Will the government finally cut off their supply of public funds in the budget?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we will continue to invest in clean and renewable energy, as we did with the then premier of Quebec and the Premier of Newfoundland and Labrador by investing in Churchill Falls. We will continue to invest in heat pumps for households. We will continue to invest in wind and solar energy. In short, we will continue to invest in technologies that will ease the burden that fossil fuels place on the backs of Canadian consumers.
Mr. Speaker, at the rate they are going, heat pumps will end up running on gas.

Oil companies are posting record profits again this year because of the war in Iran. Meanwhile, the Liberals want Canadians to foot the $40-billion-plus bill for a pipeline out west. We are already forking out tens of billions of dollars in fossil fuel subsidies, and now we are learning that the upcoming budget will overhaul exploration deductions for oil and gas companies. I would bet an old two-dollar bill that the goal is not to reduce those deductions.
When will the Liberals stop making Canadians pay to help the greedy oil industry?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, let us talk about energy investments that benefit Quebec and Canadian consumers.
We are providing $6 billion in refundable tax credits to move the Churchill Falls project forward and secure a supply of renewable green energy for future generations of Quebeckers.
Let us talk about energy investments and Quebec consumers. We are very much looking forward to this debate.

Mr. Speaker, last year, the Liberals set the immigration levels and then promptly added a couple of side programs to inflate their numbers nearly 40% higher, a classic Liberal smoke-and-mirrors confusion campaign. Even worse, they blew through their targets. Instead of 385,000 temporary residents, they have issued permits for 950,000. They planned for 60,000 temporary foreign workers, but they have issued permits for 120,000. Today, the government will issue a new immigration levels plan with more smoke and mirrors.
Does the immigration minister really think Canadians do not see when she cooks the books?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Lena Metlege Diab (Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister and I have said a number of times, we will not budge from sustainable levels.

We have acted on the mandate that Canadians gave us to restore sustainability and durability to the immigration system, and the results are clear. The temporary resident population has dropped. We have stabilized levels, and as a result Canadians are seeing lower prices. I very much look forward to tabling our government's immigration levels plan later today.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians do not believe that. That is why they are asking for lower immigration levels. The government likes to pretend the numbers are coming down, but they are comparing them to the highest levels in Canadian history, created by the Minister of Justice over here.

What really matters? On housing, our housing starts are decreasing. The levels plan will not consider where those people will live. On jobs, unemployment is rising, especially for our youth. The levels plan will not consider where they work. The current plan is adding a city the size of Saskatoon every year.
Where will these people live, work and find a doctor?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Lena Metlege Diab (Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we have made reforms to the immigration system to restore sustainability, stability and balance. These reforms are working.

As the Prime Minister said and as I have said, we will not budge from sustainable levels. While the Conservatives are focused on division, our government is focused on building a strong Canada and a sustainable immigration system. Again, I look forward, very shortly, to tabling our next immigration levels plan.

Mr. Speaker, grape growers and wineries in my riding are anxious about their future. Many have completed their harvest not knowing if the wine sector support program will be renewed for this or future vintages. Worse, they fear changes could force wineries to reduce Canadian wine production, purchase fewer Canadian grapes and cancel contracts with local farmers.
Today is the federal budget. Will the government commit to extending the wine sector support program to provide the certainty our grape growers and wineries so badly need?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Daniel Gobeil (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture and Agri-Food, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I invite my colleague to take a look at today's budget.

Our government will always be there to support all producers in value-added sectors in order to have the strongest economy in both rural and urban areas, to develop the economy and to produce quality Canadian products.

Mr. Speaker, after 11 years of Liberal government, food affordability continues to get worse. A recent Salvation Army report found that one in three Canadians is skipping meals. In Niagara Falls, visits to Project Share increased by 23.7%, while visits to Newark Neighbours in Niagara-on-the-Lake have doubled since 2022.
Will the Liberal government's budget deliver tax cuts to help Canadians who are struggling right now?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Leslie Church (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretaries of State for Labour, for Seniors, and for Children and Youth, and to the Minister of Jobs and Families (Persons with Disabilities), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the very first day that the government formed, we delivered a tax cut for 22 million Canadians, and affordability has been at the top of our agenda ever since.

We are going to continue making progress when that member gets to see the federal budget later this afternoon. We are going to be committed to the programs that we have created and brought forward, things like our national school food program and our groceries and essentials benefit. These are programs that are helping put food on tables and ensure that Canadians have the support they need in their lives.

Mr. Speaker, my team and I recently volunteered at the North York Harvest Food Bank. We witnessed first-hand the growing hardship facing Canadian families. One in four food bank clients is a child, and 53% of clients have skipped meals to afford other necessities. The Salvation Army reports that 31% of Canadians are skipping or reducing meals, because they simply cannot afford groceries.

Will the Liberal government finally get its spending under control and cut taxes, instead of forcing struggling families to pay the price for another unaffordable budget as its programs are not working?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Adam van Koeverden (Secretary of State (Sport), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I think my colleague knows this, but the number one way to help out Canadians with affordability is to ensure that they have a safe and affordable home to live in. That is why our government has thousands of shovels in the ground.

We have a budget today that will build more affordable homes for all Canadians, homes like the Lou Fruitman Reena Residence in that member's riding, in Vaughan, where 138 of her constituents live. Despite her opposition to supportive housing, we are getting the job done.

Her Conservative leader has a record on building housing; he built six when he was the minister of housing. Not only that, he stands in front of people's homes, embarrasses them and shames them. The Conservatives have a bad record on housing—
The hon. member for Davenport.

Mr. Speaker, we are focused on strengthening Canada's sovereignty so that Canadians can continue to live as they choose and be free to determine their own future. True sovereignty requires greater strategic autonomy, built on a secure and growing economy, and a disciplined foreign policy rooted in our national interests. We are moving quickly.
Can the Minister of Foreign Affairs take a moment to update Canadians on recent developments and how they are advancing Canada's sovereignty and strategic autonomy?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Anita Anand (Minister of Foreign Affairs, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this has been a landmark week in Canadian foreign policy. From releasing the national security strategy to the Canada-EU Summit to the G20 and the Commonwealth, we are forging relationships around the world, securing over 20 security, defence and trade agreements in the last year alone. We are deepening our national resilience. We are strengthening our strategic autonomy and, through budget 2026, we are masters of our own destiny.

Mr. Speaker, Telesat received a $2.3-billion contract from the government. The CEO of Telesat just happens to be a close personal friend of the Prime Minister. Section 9 of the Conflict of Interest Act states that a public office holder shall not influence a decision to further the interests of a friend.
Did the Prime Minister discuss, and I emphasize the word discuss, this $2.3-billion contract with his staff or anyone in government, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as the member well knows, Canada has among the most stringent ethics guidelines and laws in the world. These measures and these rules are followed rigorously by all members on this side of the House and, indeed, I assume, all members of the House and all senior officials. The Conflict of Interest Act and other measures are constantly followed and constantly updated. We will continue to follow them.
Mr. Speaker, that was a yes-or-no question. The Prime Minister has a blatant conflict of interest in relation to his friend, the CEO of Telesat, which received a $2.3-billion contract.
Again, did the Prime Minister discuss any aspect of this contract with his staff or anyone in government, and why did he not issue a public declaration of recusal as required by law?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister, like, I assume, all members of the House, rigorously follows all of the various kinds of ethics requirements that are in place.
Mr. Speaker, hello, everyone. It is nice to be here with all of us—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
That is eating into the member's time.
The member may continue.

Mr. Speaker, the AI minister, the Prime Minister and the Telesat CEO are all buddies. They sent their kids to the same elite private school. They are in the same book and running club. They even ran a marathon together. The AI minister took the correct steps of adding Dan Goldberg to his ethics screen.
Why will the Prime Minister not do the same?
If the AI minister can do it, why can the Prime Minister not do it?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, no one in the House will ever match that member for describing his friendships to the world.

Mr. Speaker, we see another example of the Liberals deflecting and dodging a very important question about $2.3 billion of taxpayer money.
