What we are pointing out is that the AI minister took the correct steps of adding Telesat CEO Dan Goldberg to his ethics screen. The question is why the Prime Minister cannot do the same.

Their personal friend Dan Goldberg has been personally enriched by a government contract and Canadians deserve to know why the Prime Minister will not acknowledge his friendship in his conflict of interest ethics screen.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as that member knows, Canada has among the most stringent ethics requirements in the world. Those requirements are followed rigorously by the Prime Minister and all members on this side of the House at all times.
Mr. Speaker, Telesat has over $3 billion in debt that is coming due soon. The company itself is saying that it does not think it will be able to pay its creditors.

Hold on a minute. They have a card up their sleeve. Mr. Goldberg, the CEO of Telesat, is a good friend of the Prime Minister. What is the result? The government just awarded Telesat the largest contract in the company's history. This contract is worth $2.3 billion, and there was no competitive bidding process.
Can the Prime Minister explain how a company led by one of his buddies can obtain billions of dollars from Canadians without any competition?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Canada has some of the highest standards, rules and laws when it comes to ethics. The Prime Minister follows them rigorously, as do all members on this side of the House and, I assume, all members in the House.

Mr. Speaker, there are other facts to consider. We know that the CEO of Telesat is a long-time friend of the Prime Minister. He attended the Prime Minister's swearing-in and went to visit him in England. They even run marathons together. How nice for them.

The Minister of Artificial Intelligence is also a buddy of Mr. Goldberg's, but he had to recuse himself from matters involving Telesat to avoid a conflict of interest. Apparently, the Prime Minister is under no obligation to do the same.

Can the Prime Minister guarantee that he never participated, directly or indirectly, in the discussions that led to a $2.3-billion contract being awarded to one of his buddies? If he did, that would be illegal.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Canada has among the strictest ethics standards, rules and laws in the world. We adhere to them rigorously, and we always will.

Mr. Speaker, Telesat was not legally bankrupt, but it was facing severe financial distress, insolvency warnings and an immediate risk of defaulting on its massive debt obligations. The Prime Minister's buddy Dan Goldberg, the CEO of Telesat, received 2.3 billion Canadian tax dollars just as $1.71 billion U.S., or roughly $2.3 billion Canadian, in debt was coming due on December 6. Is it a coincidence? Perhaps.

To the Prime Minister, does “masters of our own destiny” apply only to his club of well-connected Liberal insiders taking care of themselves while those not in the clubs, such as hard-working families, seniors and single-income moms, pay the price?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Canada has the most stringent standards, laws, disclosure requirements and regulations in the whole world.
Canada will always have extremely high, if not the highest, standards of ethical behaviour for public officials. That will continue to be the case, and we will continue to live by those standards.
Mr. Speaker, I have two questions.

Can the Prime Minister explain why hard-working, taxpaying Canadian families, seniors and single-income moms gave $2.3 billion to his CEO friend and Liberal Party fundraiser at Telesat with a big government contract just as a nearly identical amount of debt was approaching maturity?

I would also love to have the Prime Minister answer this one. Can he also explain what safeguards were put in place to ensure that these tax dollars are not being used to relieve the company of his lifelong buddy, a well-connected Liberal insider and fundraiser for the Prime Minister, of its financial pressures near insolvency?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Canada has among the highest ethics—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
The hon. government House leader has the floor.
Mr. Speaker, Canada has among the highest ethics standards in the world. Those will continue to be maintained and vigorously adhered to.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is completely lacking in transparency. At the Major Projects Office, employees work for the government but are paid by private companies that could benefit from decisions that are, shall we say, favourable to them.

Who pays whom? Who decides what? Who keeps an eye on all these people? Who benefits? Above all, who is lining their pockets? The Liberals refuse to answer simple questions like those. Then they ask Canadians to trust them.
What is the Prime Minister hiding from us?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Dominic LeBlanc (President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade, Intergovernmental Affairs, Internal Trade, and One Canadian Economy, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I understand why our colleague is spouting phrases like “lining their pockets”. He is desperately hoping to make it onto the evening news tonight. He should think twice before using words that he knows full well are not true.
He referenced the Major Projects Office. Yes, employees from the private sector are seconded to work at the Major Projects Office.
This program has been around for over 50 years. It is transparent and rigorous, and the rules are always followed.

Marie producer Algoma Steel in polar steel, and it is going to begin pouring the steel in 2027. This comes at a critical time, as the unjust, unfair tariffs from the Americans have virtually shut down the market.
Can the Secretary of State for Defence Procurement please update the House on how the steelworkers in the Soo are going to benefit and how they are going to contribute to Canada's Arctic sovereignty?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Stephen Fuhr (Secretary of State (Defence Procurement), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the member from Sault Ste. Marie for his strong advocacy for all the hard-working steelworkers in his community.

I do not know if the House knows this, but Canada is one of only a handful of nations that can design and build a heavy and medium-sized icebreaker. That is something we should all be very proud of. Our steel companies, like Algoma Steel, will now provide the steel we need to build these ships, strengthen our supply chains and keep more of our procurement dollars here in Canada.

Yesterday, the Minister of Energy dismissed questions about potential corporate conflicts as “conspiracy theories”, but what is suspicious is the refusal to disclose which corporate interests pay government employees and which projects they assess. With both public and private financing involved, Canadians deserve transparency, not secrecy.
If there is nothing to hide, why will the minister not just name the companies?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the exchange program has been in place for over a decade. It has been used by governments on both sides to build this country strong. The Major Projects Office is creating jobs, thousands and thousands of jobs, in Alberta, in British Columbia and all across this country. Rather than talk down the office that is creating those jobs, why do the Conservatives not help celebrate the hard-working men and women who are working in that office to build Canada strong?

Mr. Speaker, that answer is exactly why the Liberals should clear this up, because the public interest must be protected in an office that advises on projects potentially worth $200 billion. However, the Liberals will not name the companies that help pay MPO staff, so Canadians cannot tell whose interests come first in government decisions worth billions of dollars. “National interest” is not an excuse to hide private interests when staff may assess projects that involve their employers and competitors.
Will the minister table the company names, salary arrangements and recusal records so Canadians can know exactly whose interests are protected?

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the interests that are protected are those of Canadians by these hard-working men and women. Some of them come from the private sector, two-thirds come from the federal public sector, and some of them are loaned from other orders of government.

I had a conversation with the colleague who just asked the question at a committee this week. We undertook to provide the committee with all available information on this practice. We look forward to doing exactly that.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, first of all, let me express my condolences to the family impacted by this horrific crime, but let me also say that since taking government last April, our government has brought in transformational legislation on criminal justice. We will continue to ensure the safety and security of Canadians by bringing forward additional measures to support—

One question cropped up again and again during our discussions: today's unpredictability, which is making investment, production and diversification decisions all the more complicated.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague from Beauport—Limoilou for his question and for his leadership within Quebec City's business community.

Our government focuses on the things within its control, which includes improving our productivity, resilience and sovereignty. Among other things, this means the productivity mega deduction, which is available to businesses of all sizes across the country.

We have not had an instance of extortion like we have seen in previous years. That is because our government has made the changes that are necessary and has also removed people who were not supposed to be in the country, and that is why we are seeing the good results we are seeing when it comes to extortion.

Will the government change course and deliver meaningful investments in non-market housing, affordable groceries and better health care in today's budget?

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, in just over an hour, the finance minister will deliver budget 2026 in the House. I know we are all very excited, including the member opposite, who I know cares about a number of issues that are affecting Canadians.

The hon. member for Edmonton Strathcona.

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed consideration of the motion that Bill S-5, An Act respecting the interoperability of health information technology and to prohibit data blocking by health information technology vendors, be read the second time and referred to a committee.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I would like to reiterate that there is tremendous opportunity behind this bill to ensure that we would have data transfer of our health information, but at the same time, we have quite a few questions we need answered to ensure that we would remain sovereign, would be protecting our innovation and that it would still be within the jurisdiction of our provinces. We need to make sure these details are right, because Canadians need actual improvements. They do not need announcements or grand gestures. They need real improvement to a system in which our data is not being transferred between jurisdictions.

Provinces and territories are responsible for making their own health care systems. As a federal government, we need to respect the role of the provinces in this discussion. We should be working with them to make sure their health information can be shared across other provinces but that we would not be creating more red tape in doing so and that provinces would actually have their say on how this needs to operate.

We need to understand how the bill would work with the systems that are already in place and to make sure provinces would still have a say in how these changes would be implemented. If one province is using one system and another province is using another system, we have to ensure that there would be compatibility between the two and that they have a say, instead of arbitrarily saying that there is another provider to use and everybody has to make the adjustment to a new system This would cost the taxpayer entirely too much money as we try to implement this across Canada.

The other thing we need to talk about is making sure we would not make it harder for small businesses and start-ups to compete in this industry. We do not want so many rules and regulations, so much red tape, that the biggest companies would be the only ones able to develop the softwares that would be used for the data collection and transfer as we move forward. Our innovators and entrepreneurs have great ideas and amazing solutions, but they need a fair chance to compete. We should be encouraging more competition and innovation, not creating barriers that protect the biggest players and keep the little guys out.

The third thing we need to talk about is privacy and security. Canadians share some of their most personal information with the health care system, and they need to know that this information is protected. Imagine someone with a communicable disease who does not want everyone to know about it. Some hacker gets in, and then all of a sudden everyone knows about something the person has held very private, kept to themselves. We need to ensure that this information would not get out to the general public. We need to make it easier for doctors and hospitals to share important records and information, but at the same time ensure that they would be the only ones that could access them. They have to be protected, sovereign and secure.

Better information sharing is important, absolutely, but it would not fix every problem in our health care system. It would not put more family doctors in communities that desperately need them. It would not shorten the wait times for hip replacements or get someone into the emergency room faster. These challenges still need to be addressed, but this does matter. We need to make sure that the changes would lead to actual results for Canadians. This is one of the things on which we would hold the government to account should the legislation go through the steps and pass: that the government implement something and truly make a change for Canadians, not just another grand gesture with Liberals' saying they did something, but then nothing ever came of it.

Another important discussion we need to have is about data sovereignty. As we connect more of our health care systems, we need to think about who controls Canadians' data and health information. Where would the information be stored, who would have access to that information and which country's laws would apply to our Canadian health care data? This is extremely important. We cannot be dependent on foreign companies to operate the technology that our health care systems rely on, because then we could need to answer to the U.S. CLOUD Act or other provisions that would allow the U.S. to take control of our Canadian citizens' health care data.

We have to ensure that we remain sovereign, take a very sovereign approach to our Canadian data and protect the most vulnerable information of our citizens. There is absolutely nothing wrong with embracing new technology or working with companies that have offered the technology and can share that information, but we cannot put ourselves in a position where we would lose control over these systems or no longer be able to protect that information at the same time.

Canada needs to build its own expertise, strengthen our digital infrastructure and make sure we have the ability to protect our information under Canadian laws. This is the key part. Our data has to be protected under Canadian laws, especially when it comes to our health care data. Being sovereign in today's world means more than just where a company is operated or being on Canadian soil. It also matters where the data is being stored and what server is being used. Is it the cloud? Is it on the premises? How is this information being stored to protect Canadian data?

We should be embracing innovation and should be looking for ways to make our health care system more efficient and better connected, absolutely, but we must do this by having control over our own data, not by compromising Canadians' health data. Privacy, security and control matter in this conversation, and we have to make sure we discuss it.

Bill S-5 is an opportunity to make progress on an issue that is holding our health care system back. That does not mean we open our data to non-protections to move forward with data transfers. It does not mean that we will not have questions to bring forth as this policy moves forward.

When it comes down to it, Canadians are not worried, really, about which software their hospital uses or how systems communicate. What they want to know is that when they need medical care, their doctor has the information they need, they can get their services fast and their personal information will be protected. That is what Canadians care about. That is what this bill should be about, not just better information sharing, but better care, better access and better outcomes for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I want to commend my colleague from Kitchener on her great speech. I wonder if there is anything specific she hears from her constituents, with some examples perhaps, about frustrations with accessing their health care data. Is there something that she really feels could be added to this bill to improve their daily lives?

Mr. Speaker, we get emails all the time about how people go to one practitioner and then have to go to the hospital and re-explain their entire medical history. Then they go back to their practitioner to get a referral and go to the specialist with the referral, and they end up on the operating table if need be. They have to share their information across all those different avenues. That is happening all the time. I get emails all the time from constituents who ask why they cannot do it once to make sure they mark the right leg and move forward.
Yes, I think this is going to help in specific situations like that.

Mr. Speaker, the bill would give the government the power to establish administrative monetary penalties for health IT vendors that do not comply. I wonder what would stop these penalties from simply being another cost of doing business. How can we ensure that the penalties are strong enough to actually deter data blocking?

Mr. Speaker, these are the questions we will have to bring up at committee, absolutely. How are we going to prevent data blocking? What regulations are going to be put in place? How would we ensure that it would not just be the conglomerates that are able to play in this game anymore? We have to make sure the start-ups, the innovation and the free market can still compete in this area at the same time as we hold regulators accountable to make sure they are sharing that information.
Mr. Speaker, as we can see, my hon. colleague is an expert in the field, being an engineer.

My concern is this: How do we protect victims of violence to ensure that their perpetrators do not have access to this information? What controls do we have to ensure that this information is kept secret?

Mr. Speaker, this is one of the sensitive topics that we absolutely need to address when this bill moves forward, because there are going to be perpetrators out there who want to access personal health information, as in the trafficking world. We have to make sure that we are able to protect that data, that the data remains sovereign and that it is up to an individual to share that data. How is the government going to make sure that all those things are in place as it moves this bill forward?
Mr. Speaker, I will be brief.

Health is a jurisdiction that belongs to Quebec and the provinces. We fail to see how this bill can truly establish data interoperability while also respecting Quebec's jurisdictions. The Bloc Québécois is issuing this fairly serious warning given that we have not yet received sufficient guarantees.
Has my colleague also noted the risks involved in failing to properly connect the pieces across the provinces, Quebec and the federal government?
Mr. Speaker, it was the member opposite who mentioned that if we look at this through the lens of the client, the patient, we will be able to come to a consensus on how it needs to work.

Absolutely, this falls under provincial jurisdiction, and we have to make sure that we are maintaining that jurisdiction as we move forward. However, the conversation would become easier between the provinces if we looked at it through the mindset of the patient. That is where we really need to focus in this legislation.
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my colleague's explanation. She is an expert in this field.
What would the member say is the most important thing here? If and when this bill goes to committee, what would be the most important thing that would need to be addressed or changed in this bill?
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague for the gravitas for my expertise.

There are some key elements here that we need to discuss. Number one, would we stifle innovation and free market through it? Number two, would the data be protected? Number three, would it be up to the individual to even share their data in the first place? These are three questions that I have, and as we move forward, I will be continually asking them.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the member could comment on how we can ensure that interoperability will not come at the expense of privacy and that the government commits to involving the Privacy Commissioner in developing the regulations and security standards under this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, it is extremely important that we protect data as we move forward with this legislation. It is going to be up to the government to answer the question of how data would be protected and what regulations it would put in place. It is the number one thing we need to focus on to make sure that our data is secure so that someone cannot just hack in and get access to our most critical information, our personal critical information, and so that our data remains sovereign and falls under Canadian law, not under a foreign jurisdiction or a foreign country's law.
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for her in-depth explanations.

Has data sovereignty been an issue in other countries? I am sure we are following and are quite a bit behind some other countries on this issue. Does my colleague know of any other countries that had problems with their data being hacked or their health system being hacked when they were proceeding with interoperability?

Mr. Speaker, I am not 100% sure of other countries that have had their data hacked, but we do hear in the news all the time about different companies that have been hacked. Even AI has been, so there is a real risk there and an opportunity for this information to be hacked. As my other colleague brought up earlier, it could even be a perpetrator who wants information from someone, so they hack into the system and specifically target one individual.

There are lots of scenarios we can talk about. We have to really make sure that our data is secure as we move forward with this bill. At the same time, we need to move forward with this legislation. We need to have conversations surrounding it, and we have to make sure we get it right for the interests of Canadians and health care across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, as drafted, clause 7 of the bill puts Quebec and the provinces under federal control, although such responsibility is by no means within the federal government's purview. Health is the exclusive jurisdiction of Quebec and the provinces.
Does my colleague support amending clause 7 to recognize Quebec's jurisdictions?
Mr. Speaker, this needs to remain under provincial jurisdiction. Nothing needs to change there, but I think the provinces need to work together to make sure that data can be interchanged.

It is extremely important to reduce harm and save lives. As I mentioned in my speech, I know of someone who was given penicillin by accident and died because their information was not transferred from province to province. They had gotten into a car accident. The provinces need to work together to ensure we have a transfer of data, but I absolutely do not think this should be removed from provincial jurisdiction.
Mr. Speaker, I rise today on behalf of the residents of Similkameen—South Okanagan—West Kootenay to speak to Bill S-5. I am always honoured to speak in the House for my communities.

Bill S-5 is an act respecting the interoperability of health information technology and to prohibit data blocking by health information technology vendors. I am pleased to speak to this legislation as a member of the Standing Committee on Health. It has been a great honour, in my time in the House, to provide oversight of our health care system. Canadians are proud of our health care system, and for good reason. However, most Canadians and most members in this House agree that it needs improvement.

There are many issues, too many for me to even list here, that we are addressing in our committee. To name one, the Canada health transfer has risen substantially, yet access remains poor. In fact, the Canada health transfer increased from $37.2 billion in 2017-18 to $57.4 billion in 2026-27, a 55% increase in nominal terms. Despite this increase, Canadians are still waiting longer for several priority surgeries and diagnostic tests than before the pandemic. Canada continues to rank poorly, internationally, for timely access.

Younger Canadians face particularly poor access to primary care. In 2023, more than one in four Canadians aged 18 to 34 did not have a regular health care provider. One in five Canadians aged 35 to 49 lacked a regular health care provider. We have a gateway system in our health care, and it did work for quite a long while. However, it does not work unless Canadians have a health care provider or a family doctor. Canada ranks last among 10 peer countries examined for timely access to care and, of course, the lack of that initial provider is one of the reasons.

In 2025, the C.D. Howe Institute analysis ranked Canada 10th out of 10 countries for timeliness. Again, I know everyone in this House who has had to wait in line or bring a loved one to a hospital for any kind of testing would not question that data. Only 86% of Canadians reported having a regular doctor or place of care, and just 25% can see a doctor or nurse the same day. In the communities that I represent in Similkameen—South Okanagan—West Kootenay, it is not 86% that have a doctor. I know a lot of these stats are different for rural communities like mine that have a severe lack of family doctors and specialists. Thousands in Similkameen—South Okanagan—West Kootenay right now have no family doctor.

Forty-seven per cent of Canadians waited two months or longer for a specialist, and 59% waited two months or longer for an elective surgery. In 2024-25 at least 23,000 patients died in Canada while on wait-lists for surgeries or diagnostic scans. We have to wonder if that number is even accurate because there are a lot of people who might not be included who died of other issues they were having while waiting. It is hard to know if it is even much more than that; I am sure it is.

Emergency rooms are under significant pressure. In 2024, 1.2 million emergency department visits, or 7.7% of all reported visits, ended with the patient leaving before being seen and assessed by a physician.

Canadians are spending longer in emergency departments. In 2024, half of emergency patients waited just under two hours for an initial physician assessment, while one in 10 waited more than five hours. Of course, some of this can be attributed to what we are talking about today and the issues that Bill S-5 is trying to solve. One in 10 patients waited more than 14 hours in an emergency department overall. That is a 28% increase from 2018.

Hospital capacity is contributing to extreme delays for patients who need to be admitted. In fact, in 2024-25, one in 10 admitted patients waited more than 36 hours for an in-patient bed after the decision to admit them had been made. That is a 45% increase from 2018.

Surgical and diagnostic waits remain worse than before the pandemic. In 2024, only 68% of hip replacement patients received surgery within the 26-week benchmark. That is down from 75% in 2019. Only 61% of knee replacement patients met the benchmark, down from 70%.

The most important thing is there are people behind the statistics. There are people who are extremely active, who want to stay active, who do not want to go into a home and do not want to be a burden to their families. They cannot get that hip surgery in a timely manner. They cannot get that knee surgery. They want to continue to play tennis, to play pickleball, to go running, to go walking on trails, and they cannot because they are in extreme pain for months. It is really not fair.

Let us go to MRI waits, which are 15 days longer right now than they were in 2019, while waits for CT scans are taking three days longer. The Standing Committee on Health is studying these wait times currently. Knowledge is power and the more we know exactly what is going wrong compared to other countries, the more we will be able to resolve this problem.

Waits for specialist care and treatment remain lengthy. The Fraser Institute 2025 physician survey reported a median 28-week wait for referral by a family doctor to receipt of treatment. Again, I believe those numbers are even higher in rural areas that have an even greater shortage of specialists. Canada spends heavily on health care and continues to struggle with access and capacity. Among the 31 high-income countries with universal health coverage, Canada ranked third-highest for health spending as a share of GDP, but 27th of 30 for the availability of doctors, 27th of 31 for MRI machines and 28th of 31 for CAT scan machines.

These are things that Bill S-5 would address. Being able to communicate is one of the issues, obviously, with Canadian health care, and that is why I do support much of what is in this bill. It attempts to improve our system by making our health care data accessible beyond our own home province. We are travelling more within the country now. We are buying Canadian, we are travelling Canadian, and we are vacationing Canadian.

We need to be able to cross provincial boundaries, into any province, and if there is any kind of situation where we need to see a health care provider, which of course happens all the time, we need them to have our information available, to know, as my colleague mentioned, whether we are allergic to any kind of medication or need some operation, and to know what is happening at home with our home doctor. If we cross provincial boundaries at this point, there is no information available most of the time.

We are exploring our great country. We are hiking the Rockies north of the border or we are heading for Montreal instead of Palm Beach now. As more Canadians are exploring the country, they will need to interact with other provincial health care systems. Re-injuring an existing injury or refilling a prescription has become more common. People across our country move between family doctors, community clinics, hospitals and diagnostic labs, yet in far too many cases, their medical history fails to follow them. Systems remain trapped behind digital walls and information remains fragmented. We cannot allow provincial silos to limit our medical services in Canada.

Obviously, this runs counter to the spirit of the Canada Health Act and to our health accords. Again, there are people behind all these statistics. The number one thing is that we need to keep the Canadian people healthy.

I represent one of the country's eldest regions. Our communities are also full of young families, alongside many recent retirees and long-time residents. Generations of wisdom are always on display, and we are fortunate that so many Canadians from every province choose to make Similkameen—South Okanagan—West Kootenay their new home in their golden years, but as they bring their cherished mementos, they can also bring complex medical histories, long-term prescriptions, diagnostic scans and test results.

Seniors should not be made solely responsible for ensuring that their medical history is properly updated with local health care professionals, not in a country where our health care is supposed to be universal.

I can give two examples in my region that illustrate this need. Penticton Regional Hospital recently lost its entire staff of neurologists, even though our region is home to more seniors than anywhere else in the country and it is one of the eldest regions in our country. Neurology is a vital service to ensure seniors' aging brain and nervous system changes are properly screened, cared for and managed. The loss of these neurologists will mean more seniors will have to travel further for screenings and speak with neurologists many hundreds of kilometres away about the care they received in Penticton. If they need to go to another health authority for specialized screening, it is not always guaranteed that they would be able to see the testing history from their former hospital. We all know that this is true, because sometimes we can drive from one pharmacy on one side of town to another pharmacy on the other side of town, and they have no idea what prescription we are on.

If these seniors go to another province, and I have spoken with residents who have seen specialists in Alberta, their data is not available. Similarly, the emergency room in the town of Oliver, has seen sudden, random closures repeatedly over the past few years, more than 40 times, or almost once a week in a calendar year.

I would like to take this time to thank the former mayor of Oliver for his service over the past eight years and for sitting as a witness before the Standing Committee on Health to talk to members of Parliament about what it is like for a small community to have their emergency room close randomly, sporadically, multiple times a year. It is more than 40 times a year. I thank Martin Johansson for the service he has given to our communities and for putting those first.

Let us remember that, when a small community like Oliver's emergency room closes randomly, it has a domino effect throughout the whole region, because not only is it an emergency that needs to be attended to, but the other hospitals these people have to go to will get extremely backed up.
I have received so much mail about the health care system, so much mail and so many calls about how broken the system is.
I am going to read a short letter from one of my constituents, Marie-Louise, who says the following:
“I am writing to express my concern about the lack of timely medical care in the Emergency Hospital in Penticton.
“In the Similkameen—South Okanagan this sad situation is not new....
“Unfortunately, long delays in seeing a doctor can leave all patients, and especially parents of babies and young children, frightened, helpless and anxious.”
When a person goes to the hospital's ER, prompt attention from a doctor is expected and needed. Marie-Louise continues:

“This happened to our family on Monday of a long weekend. We had our three-month-old baby granddaughter go to the emergency room. The doctor came in to see the baby 3 hours later, and she came after the shift switch. Meanwhile the baby had arrived 3 hours earlier and apparently the emergency room was fairly quiet on that early morning.
“These delays in seeing the doctor in due time are not new.
“These delays are not acceptable....”
This is especially true with a three-month-old baby.

I want members to think about the stories of Canadians who check in at one ER in one province and are dismissed, only to end up in the care of another hospital in another province with a checkered history at best of what prior tests were done or of any prior observations by doctors.

In its current form, Bill S-5 is intended to address the concern that many electronic health records and health IT systems cannot easily communicate with each other because of data blocking. Data blocking is when health IT vendors restrict access or the exchange of health data to protect market shares or extract licensing fees. This is not acceptable. We cannot allow big tech to act as an armed bandit when it comes to accessing health care records. Other jurisdictions have moved to prohibit this practice, and I am glad we have the opportunity to do that right here.

Getting health data right is not something for computers. It is for patients. It is for the people. It is for Canadians. This means fewer duplicative tests and fewer bad diagnoses made with incomplete information. It must mean making Canada's 13 different health care data systems able to connect to one another and not be at the mercy of health tech companies setting costly and artificial restrictions on Canadians' most sensitive information. In other words, legislation must be a win-win for those working in health care and those who need health care.

I do want to say, as a member of the health care committee who helped lead the investigation into the PrescribeIT scandal, I can say with some expertise that allowing Infoway to handle the regulations for shared health care records would be a costly and futile disaster for taxpayers, patients and doctors. Even our health minister has agreed that this agency needs an audit as soon as possible. We are waiting for that audit. Infoway should not be put in charge of this new program. Basically, I would like to say I believe the minister knows it is not fit for that—
I will have to interrupt the hon. member as the time for her speech has elapsed.
The hon. member for Shefford.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague herself raised the issue of health transfers. In a few minutes—we can hear the buzz in the House—the budget will be presented. We know that Quebec's request, made earlier this week, has two priorities. Quebec's new finance minister has asked for the current health transfer agreement to be renewed. It is set to expire next spring. Minister Marceau is also asking that the agreement include a minimum annual growth rate of 5%.
What does my colleague think of this entirely legitimate request from Quebec, given that health care falls within its jurisdiction?

Mr. Speaker, it is very important that health care in this country, in every province, has the appropriate funding, yet we have to make sure that money is well spent. If we do not have our health information going between provinces, or even within provinces, our health care will only get worse.

I believe that we can throw as much money as we want at all the provinces to improve their health care, but if the money is not spent appropriately, it is of no use. Right now, the communication is blocked. That is why we need a bill like Bill S-5. I am looking forward to it going to committee so we can scrutinize it even further.

Mr. Speaker, during the member's remarks, she reflected on the challenges that many rural Canadians face in accessing health care services that the average Canadian in a large urban area would take for granted.
Could the member comment more on the challenges that rural Canadians face in equity with respect to health care?

Mr. Speaker, I know much of my colleague's riding is rural, so his constituents have many of the same issues that rural communities have across the country. They cannot access a family doctor. They cannot access specialists.

A good example is the Penticton hospital, which is a regional hospital. It services thousands of people and, by the way, it services thousands of seniors, many of whom have neurological issues. All three neurologists at the hospital quit or stepped down, so we do not have a neurologist in our regional hospital. I do not think that would happen in an urban centre. We are going to be in a lot of trouble if that is not corrected. That is just an example of a problem faced in rural Canada right now with health care.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank and congratulate my colleague on her excellent speech. I think she highlighted our broad support for the bill, and the goals and objectives of the bill, while still making it very clear that there are a number of clarity points that we will be discussing with the government at committee when the bill moves to that stage.

I wonder if my colleague would provide a bit more clarity and detail on her experience with the Health Infoway scandal. I know we are awaiting the results of the audit, but I would like to hear some more thoughts from her on that.
Mr. Speaker, I really appreciate that the Prime Minister is sitting in the House. Oh, I do not think I am allowed to say that.

I really appreciate that most of the Liberal Party is here, so we can go over, again, the scandal of PrescribeIT and Infoway, as $300 million has been lost into thin air. We do not know why because the health minister refuses to come speak to the committee about it. Also, the health minister has even said that Infoway needs to have an audit and does not want to secure its regular funding until there is an audit. There is no way that an organization like Infoway can run the program that is described in Bill S-5. I appreciate the fact that most of the Liberal Party is in the House right now and will address, hopefully soon, the problems with Infoway and PrescribeIT.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise on behalf of the people of Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola, and I am going to take this last opportunity to hope that the budget includes funding for things in Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola like the rebuilding and fast-tracking of the Red Bridge. The Liberals can groan all they want about the funding of the Red Bridge, but I will fight every single day for that funding, or for a new Barriere fire hall. It is always wonderful to ask for these types of things. The Liberals may groan, but I am here to fight for my constituents and common-sense measures.
My colleague talked about the PrescribeIT scandal. The minister has not appeared at committee. What does it say to Canadians when a minister refuses to go to committee?

Mr. Speaker, I think there are a lot of things that Canadians are looking for in their health care system, but what they are really looking for is trust. They want to be able to trust everyone in the House. They want to be able to trust the system. If they cannot depend on a program, for example, PrescribeIT, which wasted $300 million, run by Infoway, how can they trust any new program that comes forward from the Liberals?

We need to, as a House, rebuild the trust of the entire Canadian people and put in new programs like those described in Bill S-5. We need to first rebuild the trust that has been lost by the public, which has read and learned about what has happened with the scandal of PrescribeIT and Infoway.
It being 4 p.m., the House will now proceed to the consideration of Ways and Means Motion No. 12 concerning the budget presentation.

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessQualifier: Financial Statement of Minister of Finance

PersonSpeaking.Affiliation: Hon. François-Philippe Champagne (Minister of Finance and National Revenue, Lib.)

Content.ParaText: moved: That this House approve in general the budgetary policy of the government.

He said: Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 83(1), I would like to table, in both official languages, the budget documents for 2026, including the notices of ways and means motions. The details of the measures are contained in these documents.
Pursuant to Standing Order 83(2), I am requesting that an order of the day be designated for consideration of these motions.
Mr. Speaker, it is budget day, and I will try to make this speech only half as long as last year's, but with the same level of ambition and optimism, while bringing good news to Canadians.
The moment in front of us is serious. Canadians know it. Our new government knows it. The moment demands an ambitious plan to be masters of our own destiny, maîtres chez nous.

Canadians know that we are living through extraordinary times. The rules we counted on no longer seem to hold. The global trading system that brought stability for decades is being rewritten. Wars and geopolitical competition are reshaping supply chains. Artificial intelligence is transforming our economies at breakneck speed.

For many Canadians, this uncertainty affects them daily. It means wondering whether their job or their children's jobs will be secure, whether their business can survive another shock, and whether they will be able to afford a home, raise a family or build the life they have worked so hard for. However, Canadians have met moments like this before, and as the Prime Minister reminded the nation and the world, “Nostalgia is not a strategy.” As Canadians, we know how to turn global volatility into national opportunity.

Let us remember that we are a nation of builders. We built railways from coast to coast and a seaway connecting our industries to the rest of the world. We founded leading universities, research centres, businesses and public institutions—pillars of knowledge and drivers of prosperity. We leveraged Canadian ingenuity to fight for freedom during both world wars and to explore outer space.

We built a country in which generation after generation could aspire to something better, and every time the world changed, Canadians adapted. We do not retreat. We lead with purpose, determination and ambition because we are Canadians.
In the face of adversity, we are seizing opportunities and working together to rebuild stronger.

I sincerely believe that in a few years, Canadians will see this moment as another turning point in our history. Our ambition is clear: accelerate growth through an investment supercycle; make life more affordable for Canadians; and defend our sovereignty while celebrating our rich cultural heritage.

One thing is clear: Our country is more united than ever in the face of these challenges. As Lester B. Pearson said in the House on November 28, 1967, “The future of Canada, Mr. Speaker, will be decided in Canada, by Canadians.”
I even thought for a moment that the Conservatives would applaud for this part.

This is the essence of who we are as a people. This is the essence of being masters of our destiny, maîtres chez nous. We have the strength to build, the discipline to deliver and the values to take care of each other.

Canada enters this defining moment in history with every reason to be confident. We have one of the most highly educated workforces in the world. We have the energy and the critical minerals the world needs. We are a leader in key industries such as artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, nuclear energy, mining, agriculture, agri-food and advanced manufacturing. We have preferential market access to 1.5 billion consumers, and we will soon double that number and reach three billion consumers. This is the Canada of the 21st century. We also have the strongest fiscal position in the G7, with the lowest net debt-to-GDP ratio, and we are projected to have the second-fastest-growing economy in the G7 in 2027.
However, our greatest strength, as the Prime Minister said, is something that cannot be found on a balance sheet: trust. Trust is what defines Canada in an uncertain world.
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!

Hon. François-Philippe Champagne: Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives can laugh as much as they want, but Canadians know it. They know that what defines Canada is its values. The fact is that the world wants to engage with Canada, so they had better listen, because there is more good news.

To inspire trust, we need a solid foundation. Through fiscal discipline, budget 2026 keeps us on track to meet both fiscal anchors by balancing day-to-day operating spending with revenue by 2027-28, a full year ahead of schedule, and by keeping the deficit-to-GDP ratio on the declining path, while unlocking Canada's full growth potential.
I even see in the members' eyes and in their hearts how pleased they are.
We are seeing what happens around the world when governments lose their fiscal room to manoeuvre. Choices become harder.
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
Hon. François-Philippe Champagne: Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives are so excited about the budget that they are already commenting, but they should wait a bit, because there is more good news.

In Canada, our fiscal strength is giving us the freedom to live our life as we choose, to be masters of our destiny. With solid revenue growth and a shift toward capital investment and clear strategies, we are in a position to transform our economy toward stronger growth and productivity.

Budget 2026 is the next step in our ambitious plan to help businesses of all sizes invest and grow, to help Canadians get ahead and to build a stronger, sovereign Canada. Let me start with the first pillar: economic growth. Investing in our future means having an ambitious growth agenda. We need the mines, the transmission lines, the ports and the trade corridors, the nuclear reactors, the electricity dams, the AI infrastructure and the factories to power our future.

First and foremost, we need Canadian workers and Canadian companies building them, and we need to build faster. That is why our government will propose amendments to the Impact Assessment Act to bring greater legal certainty and predictability to projects, consistent with a “one project, one decision, one year” process, while maintaining environmental protections and upholding indigenous rights.

Last year, budget 2025 laid out a generational plan to build a stronger Canada. The plan is working and is already paying dividends. We are already moving major projects forward, with 28 nation-building initiatives that have been referred to the Major Projects Office, including projects in energy, critical minerals and transportation, and with budget 2026, we are building on that progress.

For too long, a lack of access to growth capital has held Canadian companies back. Too often, Canadian talent and Canadian ideas have had to look elsewhere to scale. Budget 2026 changes that with the most comprehensive revamp of business incentives in generations. At the heart of it is the new productivity mega deduction, which will boost Canada's investment supercycle. Businesses, both large and small, will be able to immediately deduct the full cost of most new investments. That is a game-changer for small businesses across our nation. Over the next 10 years, this should expand Canada's productive capacity by adding about $22 billion a year to GDP and supporting up to 80,000 jobs. This is a game-changer. This is how we boost the investment supercycle.

The productivity mega deduction is available to a manufacturer buying more efficient machinery, such as the shoemaker Pajar, whom I visited in Montreal yesterday; a farmer purchasing newer silos and a combine harvester; or a mine adopting new technology to reach deposits. Let me be clear. We are making it easier for businesses to choose Canada, and we are also making Canada the global partner of choice. This country is going to grow like never before.
Again I can see in the members' faces and hearts how happy they are going to be next week to tell their constituents all this good news.

We are not stopping there. With the Canada growth incentive, we are backing Canadian innovators and start-ups so they can grow their business here at home in Canada, allowing builders and key employees to keep more of the benefits when a business succeeds.

With the enhanced small business rollover, we are making it easier for successful entrepreneurs to reinvest in the next generation of Canadian businesses. By expanding the scientific research and experimental development program to support commercialization, we are helping Canadian ideas become reality.

By pursuing a balanced immigration policy, we are attracting the talent that our growing industries need, supporting communities and families and retaining the Canadian tradition of welcoming people fleeing conflict, while ensuring that we keep immigration levels at a sustainable level.
This is Canada. Through the most ambitious efforts in decades to simplify Canada's tax system, we are making it easier to invest, to grow and to do business in Canada.
Not every Canadian business is in a position to invest today. Many have been hard hit with unjustified U.S. tariffs. I think tonight about the steelworkers in Hamilton.
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
Hon. François-Philippe Champagne: Mr. Speaker, instead of shouting, they should probably listen to this.

I am thinking about the aluminum workers in Saguenay, the forestry workers in British Columbia and the auto workers in Windsor and Oshawa who are affected and understandably worried. Canada's new government has one simple message for them today: We will be there for them with whatever it takes and for as long as it takes. This is our commitment to their family and their community.

To date, we have provided $44 billion to help our workers and businesses protect jobs, retool and find new markets. Colleagues have been doing great work to help our workers, our industries and our sectors. The measures in the budget will help them further, to adapt and compete for the long term.

Our message to Canadian businesses is simple: We are behind them. Are they going through a difficult time? We will be at their side for as long as it takes. Do they have a great idea? They can bring it to life here, in our communities, in Canada. Are they ready to grow? We are here to support them. Are they a successful entrepreneur? We want them to reinvest in the next generation of small and medium Canadian businesses.
I come from a family of entrepreneurs, and this budget is designed to help young people succeed in the new economy.

I am also from Shawinigan, a town that was at the cutting edge of economic development more than 125 years ago. Shawinigan showed Canada what is possible when energy meets ambition. Our ancestors harnessed the power of the Saint-Maurice River to build entire industries, create thousands of jobs and foster the economic prosperity of their region and province—and of our country.

The same ambition guides our electrification strategy today, because the countries with abundant electricity will be the leaders of the 21st century. As we electrify our economy, demand for electricity will increase. Canada has a head start: Our grid is already 80% clean, and our electricity is among the most affordable in the G7.

We are working with provinces, territories and indigenous partners to double Canada's grid capacity by 2050. We will connect provincial grids. We will build thousands of kilometres of transmission lines. We will develop the nuclear energy sector. We will build Canadian, buy Canadian and create good jobs for Canadians.
This is what it means to be masters of our destiny.

These measures, as the Prime Minister said, also prove that we do not have to choose between the economy and the environment. The two go hand in hand. Our climate plan is built on four priorities: build more clean and affordable power, make it easier for Canadians to switch to electricity, transform how we use energy so we waste less and do more, and innovate and invest in Canadian clean tech right across this great country.
Canada has had to think big in the past. It is time to think big once again, because we want to be masters of our destiny.

Economic growth gives us the means. Our plan is to turn that growth into greater opportunity, greater security and a better life for all. I know that Canadians are watching. It is to deliver on what matters most: giving Canadians the opportunity for a better life. That means lowering the cost of living, making it more affordable to buy a home and ensuring that no Canadian is forced to sleep on the street because they do not have a place to call home. I even see the leader being very much interested in that.

That is what the second pillar of budget 2026 addresses: making life more affordable for Canadians. Budget 2026 provides over $22 billion over five years in new measures to ease the day-to-day financial pressures on Canadians. This winter, the new 2027 Canada groceries and essentials benefit supplement will give more than 12 million Canadians a 50% boost to their benefit, which is $4.1 billion in extra help with groceries and essentials in 2027.

We are investing more than $610 million to strengthen and expand the nutrition north program, helping lower the cost of food, supporting local harvesting and distribution, and reaching more communities across the north. We are launching the build Canada workers benefit to support 1.9 million workers, including 180,000 additional recipients, because hard work should always pay. We are also making the Canada caregiver credit fully refundable. That means more than $1,000 a year in support for 585,000 caregivers, including 180,000 who will get it for the first time. This is what I call making Canada stronger.

This builds on the help we have already delivered in recent months to Canadians. We have suspended the federal fuel excise tax through January, reducing Canadians' bills at the pump by up to 10¢ per litre on gasoline and four cents per litre on diesel. We are helping more than a million households retrofit their homes and lower their energy bills, saving a Canadian family an average of $1,400 every year afterward. We are also helping first-time homebuyers with the cost of a new home, saving them up to $50,000.
By making life more affordable for Canadians and taking care of each other, we are masters of our destiny.
The measures presented in budget 2026 could lift hundreds of thousands of people out of poverty in 2027.

The new Canada groceries and essentials benefit supplement alone could lift 120,000 people out of poverty. I sincerely hope that all the members of this House will vote in favour of this budget so that we can show our unanimous support for the Canadians who need it most.

With budget 2026, we are helping Canadians today and giving them a bridge to a better future by building more housing, by producing more renewable energy, by increasing competition and by building an economy where salaries and opportunities continue to grow.

However, this also means facing a harsh reality. Tonight, sadly, thousands of Canadians will sleep in shelters or on the street, with none of the security or stability that adequate housing provides. We can do better. We must do better. We will do better.

With budget 2026, we are putting Canada on a path to end homelessness within 10 years. We will renew the Reaching Home program and the veteran homelessness program. We will work with provinces, territories and indigenous partners to link housing with mental health, addiction and community care services. Through Build Canada Homes, we will build more affordable housing.

The investments we make today will define our society tomorrow, a society where every Canadian has a safe and affordable home where they can thrive and make their dreams come true. To truly be masters of our destiny, we must make sure our prosperity benefits everyone.

Finally, being masters of our destiny is about a safe and sovereign Canada, one where we celebrate who we are. Canada is an extraordinary country. We span three oceans, six time zones, two official languages and thousands of communities with different traditions and stories to tell. We have built something together, something beautiful, something inspiring. We have grown to be a strong and successful nation, one greater than the sum of its parts. That is worth protecting, and it is worth celebrating.

In 2027, Canada will mark its 160th anniversary. It will be a moment for Canadians to come together to celebrate our communities, to discover more of our country and to pass on what we love about Canada to the next generation. This is why budget 2026 will invest in the places and experiences that bring Canadians together, the community spaces where neighbours meet and newcomers find their footing, the festivals where communities celebrate their traditions and the museums, parks and historic sites where Canadians discover their country. We will also revitalize the arenas and rinks where generations of Canadians have learned to skate, play and dream. This is Canada at its best.

We will do more. We will renew the Canada strong pass for another year so that more families can discover their country, and we will make our national museums permanently free year-round for young Canadians so that young Canadians can discover our museums and history and dream. A strong country is one where people feel connected to it and to each other, and that connection comes from the stories we tell.

However, today, a large part of what Canadians watch, read, and listen to comes from outside Canada. Canadian creators are among the best in the world, attracting the attention of increasingly connected consumers. Our writers, musicians, filmmakers, journalists and artists are carrying Canada's voice to the four corners of the country. This is why we want to give them the best chances of succeeding at home.

Budget 2026 will make it easier to discover and borrow books by Canadian authors through a new national digital collection. We will support the publishers, local journalists and cultural institutions that bring our stories to life. We will develop a new tax credit for Canadian creators, which will provide a tax relief of up to $45,000 on income derived from original works. This is our way of giving a shot in the arm to all artists across the country. Let us celebrate together.

The unity of our vast country also depends on the ability of Canadians to travel and gather together. Our railways, roads, ferries and bridges have always represented more than just infrastructure. They connect families. They connect communities. They connect and unite our vast country. This is why we are investing in railways and ferries across the country to bring communities together.

Building a strong and united Canada also means continuing the important work of reconciliation. It means ensuring that indigenous communities across our nation have the same foundations that every community needs to thrive: safe housing, clean water, good schools, reliable infrastructure, stable and culturally responsive policing services and the ability to shape their own future. It means advancing reconciliation with more than $50 billion in stable and predictable funding over 10 years for indigenous people in this country.

It means we are providing stable and predictable funding, but we are also including a dedicated amount for first nations off-reserve, Inuit and Métis, and modern treaty and self-governing partners to invest in affordable, supportive and transitional housing, because being masters of our destiny must mean having the tools to shape a better future together.

Yes, sovereignty also means being able to defend the country we are so proud to call home. At a time when the world is more dangerous and divided, Canada is rebuilding its armed forces. We are investing in the capabilities we need to defend our country, particularly in our north and in the Arctic, and we are strengthening our defence industry here at home so that Canada makes more of what our forces, and our allies, need to do the job. We are taking greater responsibility for our own security, just as we are for our economic future, because sovereignty ultimately comes down to the same idea: having the confidence, the capacity and the freedom to live our lives as we choose, to be masters of our destiny.

As we speak about the men and women who serve our country, I want to pause to reflect on the tragedy in Wainwright. I want to draw attention to those who lost their lives and to those who were injured and are recovering. I think I can speak on behalf of all members of the House in saying that our thoughts are with them, their families and the entire community. We will honour their courage by providing $25 million to further support members of the Canadian Armed Forces, their families and local communities affected by this tragedy. We will also provide $3 million directly to the Wainwright Military Family Resource Centre. We are thinking about them.

Finally, my thoughts are with the people at the heart of budget 2026. My thoughts are with Michèle Lafontaine from J'ai mon appart' in Shawinigan, who is with her son Félix on Parliament Hill today. She works with vulnerable adults every day so they can have a place to call their own.

I also think of Rachel Reid, Louise Penny, Barbara Fradkin and Fred Pellerin, some of Canada's writers and storytellers who remind us that sovereignty also means having the confidence and the means to tell our own stories. I think of all the workers who, day to day, are building Canada strong. We have some great examples of those hard-working Canadians on the very first page of the budget. To all of them, to those watching at home and to Canadian workers across our great country, this budget is about them and what we can build together. I think they deserve a big round of applause.

More than three decades ago, another finance minister came before Parliament at another moment of profound economic change. His message was that Canada has to confront the the world as it is, not as it wished it to be. This is one of those times for our nation. The world around us is changing. We must change to lead with purpose and ambition.
We must have confidence in what Canada can become. We must build at an unprecedented speed and scale. We must take care of one another. We must defend our sovereignty.
With budget 2026, we will build the strongest economy in the G7. We will make life more affordable for Canadians, and we will defend our sovereignty while celebrating who we are.
This is the essence of being masters of our destiny. Let us seize the moment, let us be ambitious, and let us build Canada strong together.
Long live Canada!

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michael Chong (Wellington—Halton Hills North, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this budget would be better titled “masters of increasing debt and interest payments”. The budget fails to establish a credible fiscal anchor to reduce the debt and balance the budget. The national debt on the government's own plans is increasing over the next five-year horizon, interest costs are starting to take off, and there is no plan to balance the budget.

All this borrowing is making life more unaffordable for individuals, families and companies because it is increasing the cost of capital. We have all seen the five- and 10-year bond yields over the last several years increase, increasing the costs of mortgages, car loans and lines of credit. It is also reducing the flexibility of the federal government to deal with a major crisis that the Prime Minister's own national security strategy says is coming, including a potential war.

Finally, all this borrowing is not showing up in the numbers. Business capital formation has declined in five of the last six quarters, unemployment remains a full per cent above pre-pandemic highs, and GDP is flatlining, estimated to be less than 1% this year.
Would the minister comment?

Mr. Speaker, let me try to help the member because I appreciate that he only had a few hours to read the budget. We had a lower deficit last year, we have a lower deficit this year, and we will have a lower deficit during the fiscal period. That is number one.

Number two, we are bringing direct program expenses from 8% in the last decade to 2%. We are kick-starting an investment supercycle, we are investing $400 billion in capital investment over the framework, we are putting forward $22 billion to make life more affordable for Canadians, and the Canadian economy is going to be $4 trillion by the end of this decade. We are going to build Canada strong. Canadians understand that.
On this side of the house, we understand that every day is a good day to fight for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, this budget does not reimburse Quebec for the costs it has incurred in taking in asylum seekers, which represents approximately $700 million. Ottawa has been dragging its feet on this issue since 2024.

Ottawa is also staying the course with its plan to reduce the annual escalator on health transfers from 5% to 3% starting in 2028, even though Quebec is calling for an increase in health care funding. Quebec cannot afford a federal budget cut in health care.

On the one hand, Ottawa is reducing Quebec's fiscal room by $1 billion a year through its mega deduction. On the other hand, it is reducing its financial contribution to health care. Ottawa is undermining Quebec's financial independence. Ottawa is investing heavily in the symbolism of its “Canada strong” agenda as a way of pushing back against Quebec nationalism, yet it has no money to repay what it owes Quebec.
Why did the government not listen to or consult Quebec?

Mr. Speaker, I have a great deal of respect for my colleague. I have known him for a very long time. However, I can say that, on this side of the House, with more than 40 members from Quebec, we have a strong voice for Quebec.
I listened to Quebeckers. That is why we are investing in our artists, in our culture and in our SMEs, which from the backbone of Quebec's economy. That is why we renewed funding for mental health.

Instead of criticizing, my colleague should join us and applaud what we have done to help all Canadians. This will benefit Quebeckers. The Bloc Québécois even talked about the Canada groceries and essentials benefit. We are here for Canadians, and we have enhanced that benefit.
We will always be here for Quebeckers.

Mr. Speaker, Christmas came early for CEOs, thanks to the Liberal government. This budget puts corporate interests over those of struggling Canadians. There is $36 billion for a business mega deduction but only half of that for affordability measures. Liberals are allocating one in five tax dollars to military spending today, increasing to a staggering one in four dollars in 2030. They have $55 billion for a pipeline the private sector will not touch but not one extra dime for pharmacare, dental care or child care, and they admit they will not even come close to meeting their own housing targets.
Will the finance minister explain why he is choosing the interests of big business over the welfare of working Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, we are choosing Canadians. What the member failed to mention is that we are investing up to $30 billion on measures to help with ending homelessness in this country. This is a national endeavour. We are going to work with provinces, territories and municipalities.

Instead of complaining about what we are doing, why do they not join us and help us to end homelessness in this country? This is one of the greatest endeavours this House has ever taken, and it is under this new government and this Prime Minister that we are doing that. I hope he is going to remember that.

Mr. Speaker, how can Canadians be masters of their own destiny when they lack even the means to fill their refrigerators? This budget tells us that the government is going to get $30 billion in new revenues from Canadians, with absolutely nothing for the middle class. Deficits will reach $62 billion in 2026‑27, $62 billion in 2027‑28, $57 billion in 2028‑29, $53 billion in 2029‑30, and $52 billion in 2030‑31.
The debt is going to soar to astronomical levels. Interest is going to reach an all-time high. Who is going to pay for it all? Canadians are going to pay, especially the middle class.
Why did you leave out the middle class?
I would remind the member that questions must be addressed through the Chair.
The hon. Minister of Finance.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians watching at home are probably wondering whether the hon. member has read the right budget. The 2026 budget we have just presented contains $22 billion in measures to make life more affordable for Canadians, on top of the $100 billion in affordability measures already in place.

On this side of the House, we know that more needs to be done on housing, and that is exactly what we are doing. We recognize that we need to help Canadians cope with the cost of groceries, because this is a weekly concern for people. We recognize that we need to do more to help people by reducing the gas tax. That is exactly what we have done. We have taken action on the three affordability challenges facing Canadians. We will continue to be there for them every step of the way.
Mr. Speaker, I have gone through the budget. I appreciate the opportunity, and I say to the hon. minister for heritage, good job on heritage, with creative work.

My question is to the Minister of Finance. Is accounting now a creative industry? On page 352, we see that capital investments are defined broadly as including any expenditure, which is basically anything. This is the most bizarre description of a capital cost. The Minister of Finance might turn to his colleague on his left. If he were a banker and someone showed up and said, “I want this money for advertising because it is going to end up making more money for me, so therefore, it is a capital expenditure and I can write it off right now”, would any banker give them the money? Apparently, this deduction would.

Mr. Speaker, I have enormous respect for my colleague, but I thought she would talk about the $50-million investment in our national electricity strategy, doubling the electricity generation in this country. I thought she would talk about our climate plan. I thought she would talk about our ocean plan. I am sure she will have other opportunities to rise in the House and to say we are seizing the opportunities to build a stronger Canada.
Mr. Speaker, this budget is a continuation of the betrayal on climate action.

After rolling out the red carpet for oil and gas companies and pipelines, the government continues to subsidize oil and gas. It is weakening industrial carbon pricing. It is weakening regulations on clean electricity. It is removing the zero-emissions mandate for electric vehicles. It is freezing emissions mandates for light-duty vehicles. There is no money for public transit or for climate adaptation.
Can the government explain to us why it is sacrificing our children's future and the Paris agreement, all for the sake of the oil and gas companies?

Mr. Speaker, I know there are several pages in the budget, but I think my colleague missed a few. Let us talk about heat pumps instead. A historic investment will help millions of people across the country use electricity.
Let us talk about charging stations. I am sure he has not gotten to that part yet. There is going to be some good news about charging stations.

Let us talk about our climate plan, which will transform growth across the country. There is a lot of good news in this budget, which the member has not had a chance to see yet, but we will help him out.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the budget's number one job should have been to save Canadians money.

The reality, however, is that $765 billion in debt is going to get piled on over the next five years. It is a credit card budget that is going to blow up interest rates, inflation and the cost of groceries, gas and housing. This budget is going to make life more expensive for single mothers, small businesses and seniors.
For that reason, the Conservatives are going to vote against the budget. We want to save Canadians money and make life more affordable.

The minister should have more aptly named this budget “mastered by debt”, mastered by debt that will inflate the cost of food, fuel and housing. The first priority of this budget should have been to save Canadians money, but by adding $765 billion in new debt, a record-smashing sum, over the next five years, the Prime Minister will inflate the cost of fuel, food and homes. This is a costly credit card budget that Canadians cannot afford, and Conservatives will vote no.
Let us go through the facts one by one.

First are our demands. We asked the Prime Minister to cut gas prices by 20¢ a litre and $1,200 per family by eliminating all federal taxes at the pump. Not only did the Prime Minister fail to do that, but he intends to raise gas taxes early next year, which will mean that Canadians will pay more not only at the pump but also for every single item that arrives at the grocery store.
Second, we asked the Liberals to cut waste. Instead, the Prime Minister is growing spending in this budget by an eye-watering $150 billion.

Third, we asked the Prime Minister to keep his promise from the election to lower the debt-to-GDP ratio so that our debt no longer gobbles up so much of the resources needed for health care and other basic benefits. Instead, the Prime Minister has officially broken that promise today.

As I said, the Prime Minister will add $765 billion to our national debt, the single biggest borrowing binge in Canadian history, more than Trudeau, more than during COVID and more than any other government in the history of this country, an amount that will lead to higher inflation and interest rates today and higher taxes down the road. The single biggest item of spending growth in this budget is not seniors programs, not health care, not security and not sovereignty, but the opposite: It is interest on the national debt. In fact, seniors, single moms and small businesses will now have to spend about $60 billion every year on interest to bankers and bondholders. That is right. It is money for bankers and bondholders instead of nurses and doctors.

Every family of four will spend $6,000 this year on interest alone, an amount that rises to $8,100 annually by the year 2030-31. In fact, by that year, the government will be spending $17 billion more on debt interest annually than on health care.

To cover up the growing cost of the Prime Minister's costly credit card budget, he has cooked the books. He has divided the spending onto three separate credit cards: operational, capital and Crown corporations. The only problem is that he has no rule to determine which expense goes where. There is no other government anywhere on earth that follows the accounting practices the Prime Minister is introducing.
